Clinical Vignettes - Facilitator Answer Key & Teaching Guide

22 inpatient psychiatry cases * companion to the Clinical Vignettes self-test * Joshua Moss, MD | Psychiatrist

How to use this guide

Run cases as a 5-minute warm-up, a small-group teaching block, or end-of-rotation exam review. Each case has one best answer as a teaching device - reward sound reasoning over the letter.

All cases are synthetic composites - no protected health information. Encourage learners to "think aloud": name the can't-miss mimic, the first move, and what they would document in one sentence.

"Facilitate" lines are prompts for you, the teacher - questions to pose and what to listen for. "Pairs with" points to the companion topic pages and tools.

Quick answer key

Facilitator cards

Mood & Bipolar

Case 1 - Mood * Treatment resistance

Stem.  A 52-year-old woman is referred for esketamine after "failing four antidepressants" over 18 months; PHQ-9 stays 20-24. She sleeps 4-5 hours with 3 AM waking, is alone overnight, drinks caffeine after noon, eats irregularly, gets no daylight or exercise, and has little social contact. Prior prescribers adjusted medications each visit; none assessed sleep, circadian rhythm, or daily structure.

Question.  Before escalating to interventional treatment, the best next step is to:

Answer.  C - Address sleep/circadian rhythm and daily structure, confirm adherence and adequate prior trials, and track with measurement-based care

Why.  "Treatment-resistant" requires >=2 adequate trials (adequate dose AND duration) with confirmed adherence - and assumes the basics are optimized. Here, untreated insomnia, circadian disruption, caffeine, isolation, and inactivity are unaddressed. Fix sleep/circadian rhythm (fixed wake time, morning bright light, caffeine timing), add behavioral activation, confirm adherence, and follow the PHQ-9 before labeling the depression refractory.

Teaching points.

Define TRD precisely: >=2 adequate trials (dose  duration) with adherence.

Optimize sleep, circadian rhythm, substances, and activity before escalating.

Measurement-based care (serial PHQ-9) beats impression - the spirit of STAR*D.

Facilitate.  Have the group define an adequate antidepressant trial (dose  duration  adherence). What must be optimized before accepting "treatment-resistant"? Listen for sleep, circadian rhythm, substances, adherence.

Pairs with.  Mood * Psychopharmacology Primer

Case 2 - Bipolar * Acute mania

Stem.  A 42-year-old man is brought by police after his employer found him at the office at midnight accusing coworkers of sabotage. He has not slept in four days, has pressured speech and grandiosity, and has maxed out three credit cards on impulsive "investments." This is his third such episode in five years.

Question.  Which is the most appropriate acute management?

Answer.  B - Prioritize sleep, start or optimize a mood stabilizer and/or antipsychotic, hold any antidepressant, and assess capacity and risk with collateral

Why.  Acute mania is treated with a mood stabilizer (e.g., lithium or valproate) and/or an antipsychotic, with aggressive sleep restoration and reduced stimulation. Antidepressants are held - they can worsen mania. Insight is often poor, so collateral and a capacity/risk assessment are essential. Lithium carries the strongest maintenance and anti-suicidal evidence; valproate is avoided in patients who may become pregnant.

Teaching points.

Treat mania with a mood stabilizer and/or antipsychotic; protect sleep; hold antidepressants.

Insight is often low - get collateral and assess capacity.

Lithium: best maintenance + anti-suicidal evidence; avoid valproate in pregnancy-capable patients.

Facilitate.  Ask which agents are first-line for acute mania and why antidepressants are held. Probe capacity: can a manic patient refuse care? When does collateral change the plan?

Pairs with.  Mood * Decisional Capacity

Case 3 - Bipolar * Antidepressant switch

Stem.  A 24-year-old was started on an SSRI for "depression." Two weeks later she presents with three days of decreased need for sleep, pressured speech, grandiosity, and increased goal-directed activity. Collateral reveals a similar week-long period last year that was never evaluated.

Question.  What is the most likely explanation and best next step?

Answer.  B - An antidepressant-precipitated manic episode in bipolar disorder; stop the antidepressant and start a mood stabilizer or antipsychotic

Why.  A manic episode emerging after an antidepressant - especially with a prior undiagnosed hypomanic/manic period - indicates bipolar disorder that was missed. Always screen for past mania/hypomania before starting an antidepressant. Management: stop the antidepressant, start a mood stabilizer and/or antipsychotic, protect sleep, and reassess the diagnosis.

Teaching points.

Screen every depressed patient for past mania before prescribing an antidepressant.

Antidepressant monotherapy can precipitate mania in bipolar illness.

New mania on an antidepressant -> stop it, start a mood stabilizer/antipsychotic, reassess.

Facilitate.  Ask why screening for past mania matters before any antidepressant. Have a learner distinguish a manic switch from agitation or stimulant intoxication.

Pairs with.  Mood * Psychopharmacology Primer

Psychosis

Case 4 - Psychosis * First episode

Stem.  A 16-year-old honor-roll student is brought in after two weeks of increasingly bizarre behavior: isolating, stopping school, and saying classmates send messages through the Wi-Fi to control her thoughts. She has slept under 3 hours per night for a week and barely eaten for four days. No prior psychiatric history.

Question.  Which is the most appropriate initial step?

Answer.  B - Complete a medical workup for first-episode psychosis (vitals/labs, toxicology, consider neuroimaging) while ensuring safety and restoring sleep and nutrition

Why.  First-episode psychosis warrants a medical workup - the yield of a treatable organic or substance cause is highest at first presentation (intoxication/withdrawal, autoimmune/limbic encephalitis, CNS or thyroid disease). Stabilize safety, sleep, and nutrition; don't anchor on a primary psychotic diagnosis or quote a schizophrenia prognosis before the workup. Coordinated specialty care with early family involvement improves outcomes.

Teaching points.

First-episode psychosis earns a medical workup  neuroimaging - organic yield is highest here.

Don't commit to "schizophrenia" at first presentation; duration-based diagnoses are refined over time.

Coordinated specialty care + family engagement improves first-episode trajectories (RAISE).

Facilitate.  Ask what a first-episode medical workup includes and which can't-miss organic causes to exclude (encephalitis, substances, thyroid). Why not quote a schizophrenia prognosis on day one?

Pairs with.  Psychosis * Differential Decision Trees

Case 5 - Psychosis * De-escalation

Stem.  A 28-year-old with psychosis becomes increasingly paranoid on the unit. Staff repeatedly try to reason with the patient, reality-test the delusions, and problem-solve concerns. With each conversation arousal climbs, and seclusion is now being considered.

Question.  Which approach is most appropriate?

Answer.  B - Reduce interpersonal stimulation, offer a low-stimulation space and PRN, and defer cognitive engagement until arousal settles

Why.  A hyperaroused, acutely psychotic patient is outside the window where verbal/cognitive work lands - each attempt adds stimulation. Lower the interpersonal load (quiet proximity, low-stimulation environment, PRN offered without protracted negotiation), then process content the next day once regulated. Arguing with fixed delusions acutely is counterproductive; an alliance-building approach (e.g., LEAP) comes later.

Teaching points.

Don't reality-test or debate fixed delusions in the acute, hyperaroused phase.

Lower stimulation first; verbal processing comes after regulation.

Offer PRN collaboratively before it becomes coercive.

Facilitate.  Ask why reality-testing fails in the hyperaroused phase. Contrast acute de-escalation with later alliance-building (LEAP). What concretely lowers stimulation on your unit?

Pairs with.  Psychosis * Violence Risk (FRST)

Anxiety/OCD/Trauma

Case 6 - OCD * Family accommodation

Stem.  A 16-year-old has severe contamination OCD (Y-BOCS 32); rituals consume 4+ hours daily. The family fully accommodates - washing before touching shared surfaces, barring the sibling from his room, elaborate meal rules. A prior outpatient exposure trial ended after two sessions when the distressed family called the exposures "cruel."

Question.  Which is the most appropriate treatment approach?

Answer.  B - First-line ERP (usually with an SSRI), paired with systematically reducing family accommodation and supporting the parents' own distress tolerance

Why.  Exposure and response prevention (ERP), usually with an SSRI, is first-line for OCD. Family accommodation maintains the disorder and predicts worse outcomes, so reducing it is a core target. Parent-based approaches (e.g., SPACE) lower accommodation while supporting parents through their own rising anxiety - so ERP can succeed where a standalone protocol failed.

Teaching points.

ERP  SSRI is first-line for OCD; benzodiazepines are not.

Family accommodation maintains OCD - reducing it is part of treatment.

Build distress tolerance and prepare parents before exposure work.

Facilitate.  Ask how family accommodation maintains OCD and what first-line treatment is. Why did standalone exposure fail before - and what changes the contingencies?

Pairs with.  Anxiety/Trauma/OCD * Family & Discharge

Case 7 - Trauma * Sequencing

Stem.  A 34-year-old woman with a childhood abuse history and recent intimate-partner violence presents with nightmares (sleeping 3-4 hours), hypervigilance, and dissociative episodes. A prior trial of trauma-focused exposure therapy was stopped after three sessions because she acutely destabilized.

Question.  What is the most appropriate initial treatment focus?

Answer.  B - Stabilize first - sleep (including prazosin for nightmares), present-day safety, regulation skills, and a predictable therapeutic alliance - before trauma processing

Why.  Phase-based trauma care stabilizes first - sleep and nightmares (prazosin has evidence for PTSD-related nightmares), present-day safety, arousal-regulation skills, and a reliable, predictable alliance - then graduated processing. Launching exposure before this foundation commonly retraumatizes and destabilizes, exactly as happened here. The earlier "failure" was sequencing, not the wrong protocol.

Teaching points.

Phase-based care: stabilize (safety, sleep, skills, alliance) before processing trauma.

Prazosin has evidence for PTSD-related nightmares.

Destabilization in prior therapy often signals sequencing, not a bad protocol.

Facilitate.  Ask what "stabilize before processing" looks like (sleep, safety, skills, alliance). Why did prior exposure destabilize? What is the evidence for prazosin?

Pairs with.  Anxiety/Trauma/OCD * Suicide Risk & Safety

Personality

Case 8 - Personality * Disposition

Stem.  A 24-year-old with borderline personality disorder and recurrent suicidality presents for a 5th admission in 8 months. Each time: rapid stabilization, discharge once SI drops and the patient "contracts for safety," then decompensation within weeks. Home is chaotic and isolated, sleep is poor, and there is no consistent outpatient contact between crises.

Question.  Which intervention is most likely to reduce readmission?

Answer.  C - A structured step-down with a predictable daily schedule, sleep stabilization, means restriction, and one consistent point of contact

Why.  Inpatient gains that can't be maintained outside the unit drive the revolving door. No-suicide contracts are not protective and don't reduce risk. What helps: a structured step-down (partial/IOP), restored sleep, a rehearsed daily routine, concrete means restriction, continuity with one reliable clinician - and DBT, the evidence-based treatment for recurrent self-harm in BPD.

Teaching points.

"Safety contracts" are not evidence-based - use collaborative safety planning + means restriction.

DBT is first-line for recurrent self-harm in BPD.

Continuity and structure between admissions prevent readmission more than longer stays.

Facilitate.  Ask whether no-suicide contracts reduce risk (they don't). What actually lowers readmission? Name the evidence-based therapy for recurrent self-harm in BPD.

Pairs with.  Suicide Risk & Safety * Personality

Substance

Case 9 - Substance * Dual diagnosis

Stem.  A 29-year-old man is admitted after an opioid overdose reversed with naloxone. He says, "I didn't really want to die - I just wanted to stop feeling like this." He has opioid use disorder and major depression, and has been couch-surfing since a breakup.

Question.  Which is the most appropriate management plan?

Answer.  B - Initiate medication for opioid use disorder (e.g., buprenorphine), treat the depression concurrently, complete a suicide-risk assessment with means safety, and engage social work for housing - plus naloxone at discharge

Why.  Co-occurring OUD and depression are treated concurrently, not sequentially. Medication for OUD (buprenorphine, methadone, or naltrexone) reduces overdose mortality and stabilizes the patient. A post-overdose presentation requires a full suicide-risk assessment, means safety, and naloxone education/dispensing at discharge. Unstable housing is a clinical problem - engage social work.

Teaching points.

Treat co-occurring substance use and mood disorders concurrently.

Medication for OUD (buprenorphine/methadone/naltrexone) reduces mortality - offer it.

Every opioid-overdose survivor needs naloxone and means-safety counseling at discharge.

Facilitate.  Ask whether to treat the depression or the OUD first (concurrently). Which medications reduce opioid-overdose mortality? What must every overdose survivor leave with?

Pairs with.  Substance Use * Suicide Risk & Safety

Case 10 - Substance * Alcohol withdrawal

Stem.  A 48-year-old admitted for suicidal ideation reports drinking 10-12 drinks daily; last drink was 18 hours ago. He has a prior withdrawal seizure. He now has tremor, diaphoresis, tachycardia, and anxiety.

Question.  Which is the most appropriate management?

Answer.  B - Use symptom-triggered benzodiazepine dosing guided by CIWA-Ar, give thiamine before glucose, and monitor closely for seizures and delirium tremens

Why.  This is alcohol withdrawal with high-risk features (heavy use, prior withdrawal seizure). Benzodiazepines are first-line; symptom-triggered dosing guided by the CIWA-Ar generally outperforms fixed schedules in appropriate patients. Give thiamine before glucose to prevent Wernicke's. A prior withdrawal seizure and rising scores flag risk for seizures and delirium tremens - treat early and monitor.

Teaching points.

Benzodiazepines are first-line for alcohol withdrawal; CIWA-Ar guides symptom-triggered dosing.

Thiamine before glucose.

Prior complicated withdrawal and rising CIWA predict seizures/DTs - treat early.

Facilitate.  Ask which features make this high-risk withdrawal. Why symptom-triggered over fixed-dose dosing? Why thiamine before glucose? When do you worry about DTs?

Pairs with.  Withdrawal (CIWA-Ar/COWS) * Substance Use

Acute & Safety

Case 11 - Agitation * Safety

Stem.  A 17-year-old is admitted after a suicide attempt. Over the first 48 hours, agitation worsens. The team adds one-to-one observation and PRN sedatives, but agitation keeps climbing. Chart review shows the patient has slept under 3 hours per night since admission.

Question.  What is the most appropriate next step?

Answer.  C - Prioritize sleep restoration and reduce environmental stimulation, then reassess suicidality

Why.  Sleep deprivation is a powerful, modifiable driver of agitation and apparent suicidality. Escalating observation and stimulation can worsen both. Restore sleep (sedating evening regimen, low-stimulation environment, minimal-interaction observation) and reassess risk after the patient has slept - acute SI often falls with sleep.

Teaching points.

Reassess suicidality after sleep is restored.

More observation isn't automatically safer - over-stimulation can escalate agitation.

Hunt for modifiable drivers (sleep, pain, withdrawal, akathisia) before adding restriction.

Facilitate.  Ask what's driving the escalation and why more observation can backfire. When should suicidality be re-rated? Build the modifiable-driver differential.

Pairs with.  Agitation & Restraint * Mental Status Exam

Case 12 - Delirium * Geriatric

Stem.  A 73-year-old on the medical floor becomes acutely paranoid overnight, sees insects on the wall, and pulls at his IV; by morning he is calm and lucid. He is inattentive when symptomatic. New medications include diphenhydramine for sleep and oxybutynin.

Question.  Which is the most appropriate next step?

Answer.  B - Recognize delirium: test attention, search for and treat the underlying cause, stop deliriogenic (anticholinergic) medications, and use non-pharmacologic measures first

Why.  Acute, fluctuating confusion with inattention and visual hallucinations in a hospitalized elder is delirium until proven otherwise. Find and treat the cause and remove contributors - here, anticholinergics (diphenhydramine, oxybutynin) are classic precipitants. Use non-pharmacologic measures first; reserve low-dose antipsychotics for severe agitation/safety, and avoid benzodiazepines (they worsen delirium except in withdrawal).

Teaching points.

New confusion in a hospitalized patient is delirium until proven otherwise.

Fluctuation + inattention are the hallmarks; visual hallucinations point away from primary psychosis.

Deprescribe anticholinergics; non-pharm first; benzodiazepines worsen delirium (except withdrawal).

Facilitate.  Ask for the hallmarks of delirium vs primary psychosis. Which of this patient's meds are deliriogenic? Why avoid benzodiazepines, and what's the limited role of antipsychotics?

Pairs with.  Delirium * Differential Decision Trees

Case 13 - Catatonia

Stem.  A 35-year-old with severe depression lies motionless, barely speaks, and holds odd postures; when you raise his arm it stays where you place it. Oral intake is poor. An antipsychotic was recently started for "psychotic depression."

Question.  Which is the most appropriate next step?

Answer.  B - Screen for catatonia (e.g., Bush-Francis) and perform a lorazepam challenge - diagnostic and therapeutic - while minimizing antipsychotics given NMS risk

Why.  Immobility, mutism, posturing, and waxy flexibility suggest catatonia. Confirm with the Bush-Francis scale and a lorazepam challenge, which is both diagnostic and often therapeutic. Antipsychotics can worsen catatonia and raise NMS risk, so minimize them until catatonia is treated; ECT is effective for refractory or malignant catatonia. Poor intake and immobility are safety issues.

Teaching points.

Catatonia: mutism, immobility, posturing, waxy flexibility, negativism.

Lorazepam challenge is diagnostic and therapeutic; benzodiazepines first-line.

Limit antipsychotics until catatonia is treated - NMS risk; ECT for refractory/malignant cases.

Facilitate.  Ask which signs suggest catatonia and what the lorazepam challenge accomplishes. Why minimize antipsychotics? When is ECT indicated?

Pairs with.  Catatonia

Psychopharm

Case 14 - Psychopharm * Serotonin syndrome

Stem.  A patient on an SSRI is started on tramadol for pain. Within hours she develops agitation, diaphoresis, and hyperthermia, and on exam has inducible clonus and hyperreflexia, worse in the lower extremities.

Question.  What is the diagnosis and best initial management?

Answer.  B - Serotonin syndrome; stop all serotonergic agents, provide supportive care (cooling, IV fluids, benzodiazepines), and consider cyproheptadine in severe cases

Why.  Rapid onset after adding a serotonergic agent (tramadol) with clonus and hyperreflexia (lower-extremity predominant) is serotonin syndrome. Stop serotonergic drugs, give supportive care (cooling, IV fluids, benzodiazepines for agitation/rigidity), and consider cyproheptadine if severe. Contrast with NMS: slower onset over days, "lead-pipe" rigidity with hyporeflexia, after a dopamine blocker.

Teaching points.

Serotonin syndrome: rapid onset, clonus + hyperreflexia, after serotonergic agents.

NMS: days-long onset, lead-pipe rigidity + bradyreflexia, after dopamine blockers.

Stop the offending agent + supportive care; cyproheptadine (SS) vs dantrolene/bromocriptine (NMS).

Facilitate.  Have the group separate serotonin syndrome from NMS at the bedside (onset, reflexes, rigidity, trigger). What's the antidote for each?

Pairs with.  Psychopharmacology Primer

Case 15 - Psychopharm * Lithium toxicity

Stem.  A patient with bipolar disorder on lithium develops a viral illness with vomiting and poor fluid intake, and recently started ibuprofen. She now has a coarse tremor, ataxia, slurred speech, and confusion.

Question.  Which is the most appropriate next step?

Answer.  B - Hold lithium, check a level and renal function, give IV fluids, and assess severity (hemodialysis for severe toxicity) while identifying the precipitants

Why.  Tremor, ataxia, and confusion signal lithium toxicity, usually precipitated by reduced clearance - dehydration, vomiting, renal impairment, or interacting drugs (NSAIDs, thiazides, ACE inhibitors). Hold lithium, obtain a level and renal panel, rehydrate, and consider hemodialysis for severe toxicity or very high levels. Lithium has a narrow therapeutic window.

Teaching points.

Lithium toxicity: tremor, ataxia, confusion - narrow therapeutic window.

Precipitants: dehydration, NSAIDs, thiazides, ACE inhibitors, renal decline.

Hold lithium, check level + renal function, hydrate; hemodialysis for severe toxicity.

Facilitate.  Ask what precipitates lithium toxicity (volume loss, NSAIDs, thiazides, ACE inhibitors, renal decline). What's the workup, and when is dialysis indicated?

Pairs with.  Psychopharmacology Primer * Mood

Geriatric

Case 16 - Geriatric * Failure to thrive

Stem.  A 78-year-old retired teacher is admitted for failure to thrive: 15 lb weight loss over two months, sleeping 14+ hours daily, and telling her physician "there's no point anymore." Her husband of 52 years died 18 months ago, and family report new cognitive complaints.

Question.  Which is the most appropriate initial approach?

Answer.  B - Rule out medical causes and delirium, screen cognition, and assess for a major depressive episode distinct from grief - then treat depression and address nutrition and sleep

Why.  Geriatric depression often presents as failure to thrive. New late-life presentations require a medical workup and delirium screen plus a cognitive screen (depression can cause pseudodementia). Distinguish a major depressive episode (worthlessness, anhedonia, "no point") from uncomplicated grief; treat depression (e.g., an SSRI), address nutrition and sleep, and support bereavement. Don't reflexively attribute it to grief or label dementia.

Teaching points.

Late-life depression commonly presents as failure to thrive.

New geriatric presentation -> medical workup + delirium and cognitive screens before anchoring.

Depression can mimic dementia (pseudodementia); grief and MDD can coexist but differ.

Facilitate.  Ask how late-life depression masquerades as failure to thrive or dementia. What workup precedes anchoring? How is caregiver burden itself a clinical problem?

Pairs with.  Geriatric * Mood

Perinatal

Case 17 - Perinatal * Emergency

Stem.  A woman two weeks postpartum is brought in by her husband for three days of insomnia, rapidly shifting mood, confusion, and the belief that her baby is "marked." She voices thoughts that the baby "might be better off not here."

Question.  Which is the most appropriate management?

Answer.  B - Treat as a psychiatric emergency: ensure the safety of mother and infant, admit, and begin urgent evaluation and treatment given the high suicide and infanticide risk

Why.  Postpartum psychosis is a psychiatric emergency - rapid onset (often within two weeks), waxing-and-waning confusion, mood lability, and delusions, with elevated risk of suicide and infanticide. It requires urgent hospitalization, safety measures for mother and baby, and prompt treatment (antipsychotic/mood stabilizer; lithium and ECT are effective). Distinguish it from transient baby blues and from postpartum depression/OCD.

Teaching points.

Postpartum psychosis is an emergency - high suicide and infanticide risk.

Rapid onset (~first 2 weeks): confusion, mood lability, delusions.

Admit and treat urgently; distinguish from baby blues and postpartum depression/OCD.

Facilitate.  Ask why postpartum psychosis is an emergency and how it differs from baby blues and postpartum depression/OCD. What are the immediate safety steps for mother and infant?

Pairs with.  Perinatal * Psychosis

Capacity & Legal

Case 18 - Capacity * Refusal

Stem.  A 67-year-old admitted to medicine with an infection refuses IV antibiotics, stating they are "poison." He can repeat the diagnosis but cannot explain what might happen without treatment, and he is intermittently inattentive, worse at night.

Question.  Which is the most appropriate approach?

Answer.  B - Assess the four abilities (communicate a choice, understand, appreciate, reason) for this specific decision, and screen for delirium given the fluctuating inattention

Why.  Capacity is decision-specific and assessed across four abilities (communicate a choice, understand, appreciate, reason). Disagreement - or even psychosis - does not automatically negate capacity. Here, impaired appreciation plus fluctuating inattention suggests delirium, which is itself the priority. Identify which ability is impaired and why, treat reversible causes, and follow institutional/legal process. The higher the stakes, the higher the bar.

Teaching points.

Capacity is decision-specific; assess the four abilities.

Refusal or psychosis = automatic incapacity.

Fluctuating inattention -> screen for delirium; raise the bar as risk rises.

Facilitate.  Ask the four abilities of capacity. Does refusal or psychosis equal incapacity? What does fluctuating inattention signal here, and how do stakes change the bar?

Pairs with.  Decisional Capacity

Family & Disposition

Case 19 - Family * Expressed emotion

Stem.  A 19-year-old with first-episode psychosis stabilizes on an antipsychotic and is ready for discharge. He returns to parents who are loving but frightened - critical about his medication and monitoring him constantly. Three weeks later he relapses.

Question.  Which factor most strongly predicted this relapse, and what best addresses it?

Answer.  B - High expressed emotion at home; family psychoeducation to reduce criticism/over-involvement and give parents a structured supportive role

Why.  High expressed emotion (criticism, hostility, emotional over-involvement) is among the most replicated predictors of psychotic relapse - roughly a 2-5 difference between high- and low-EE households. In first-episode psychosis the home relational climate is as prognostically important as adherence. Family psychoeducation that lowers EE and replaces surveillance with a concrete supportive role reduces relapse.

Teaching points.

High EE predicts relapse in psychosis and mood disorders - assess it before discharge.

Family psychoeducation lowers EE and reduces relapse.

Discharge planning is a family intervention, not just a patient one.

Facilitate.  Ask what expressed emotion is and its effect on relapse. What does a low-EE discharge plan look like? Why is discharge a family intervention?

Pairs with.  Week 4 - Family/Systems/EE * Psychosis

Case 20 - Family * Containment before limits

Stem.  A 16-year-old is admitted after self-harm. The parents are highly anxious - calling the unit many times a day, demanding updates, and criticizing decisions. The team plans a meeting "to set boundaries with the parents."

Question.  Which approach is most likely to succeed?

Answer.  B - First contain and validate the parents' anxiety with information and psychoeducation; introduce a communication plan only once they are regulated enough to collaborate

Why.  Limit-setting with a panicked, dysregulated family commonly backfires - frightened people experience limits as abandonment or attack. Contain first: acknowledge the fear, provide information about what's happening and why, and validate their experience. Once regulated, families can collaborate on a reasonable communication structure. Containment before limits.

Teaching points.

Regulate the family before setting limits - panicked people can't hear limits.

Validation and information reduce intrusive calling more than rules do.

Engage parents as partners, not problems to be managed.

Facilitate.  Ask why limit-setting backfires with a panicked family and what must come first. Have a learner role-play the containment opening.

Pairs with.  Week 4 - Family/Systems/EE * Family & Discharge

Case 21 - Disposition * Functional staging

Stem.  A 20-year-old college student hospitalized for severe anxiety and depression improves over two weeks. The patient and family are eager to resume a full course load next semester. The patient functions well in the structured milieu.

Question.  What is the most appropriate discharge plan?

Answer.  B - Stage functional demands: discharge to a structured home routine first, then add academic load gradually as stability holds outside the hospital

Why.  In-hospital function overestimates real-world capacity - the structured milieu supplies external rhythm and support that school does not. Returning to a full load too soon commonly precipitates relapse. Stage the demands: stabilize a daily routine at home, then add one class, increasing load only as lower-level stability is maintained.

Teaching points.

In-hospital function isn't general capacity - don't over-read it.

Stage functional demands after discharge; ramp gradually.

Match demand to current capacity to prevent relapse.

Facilitate.  Ask why in-hospital function overestimates real-world capacity. What does a staged return look like? How would they counsel an eager patient and family?

Pairs with.  Documentation & Oral Presentation * Family & Discharge

Case 22 - Disposition * Regulate before demands

Stem.  A 26-year-old with depression and anxiety has lived with parents since dropping out of college at 21. Treatment has focused on job coaching and "moving out," but plans are never executed. The patient sleeps until noon, is up until 3 AM, and the home is conflictual. Parents oscillate between enabling and ultimatums.

Question.  Which is the most appropriate initial focus?

Answer.  B - Establish a consistent sleep-wake rhythm and daily structure with steady, non-critical parental support before pushing vocational or independence goals

Why.  Apparent "resistance" is often incapacity: without a stable circadian rhythm, daily structure, and consistent relational support, the patient cannot execute higher-order plans. Fix sleep-wake timing (fixed wake time, morning light), build small reliable daily tasks, and coach parents toward consistent, non-critical structure - then introduce vocational steps once the prerequisite regulation exists.

Teaching points.

Regulate sleep/rhythm and structure before functional or vocational demands.

"Won't" is often "can't yet" - build capacity first.

Coach families toward consistent structure without criticism.

Facilitate.  Ask whether the inaction is "won't" or "can't yet." What must be stable before vocational goals? How do you coach parents toward structure without criticism?

## Source: `OPENEVIDENCE RAW FILES TO REVIEW/Acute Agitation in Adult Inpatient and Emergency Psychiatry_ Comprehensive Evidence Review.docx`

Acute Agitation in Adult Inpatient and Emergency Psychiatry: Comprehensive Evidence Review

Scope and Framing

This review synthesizes current evidence on the pharmacologic and nonpharmacologic management of acute agitation in adult psychiatric emergency and inpatient settings. It integrates Project BETA (Best practices in Evaluation and Treatment of Agitation) consensus statements, ACEP and APA guidance, systematic reviews, network meta-analyses, and comparative medication trials through mid-2026. The review addresses verbal de-escalation, trauma-informed care, pharmacotherapy (including route comparisons and combination strategies), eight special populations, restraint/seclusion reduction, and safety outcomes. It concludes with a risk-stratified PRN algorithm, medication table by scenario, contraindications summary, and a resident bedside checklist.

---

I. Verbal De-Escalation

Project BETA Framework

Project BETA, published in 2012 by the American Association for Emergency Psychiatry (AAEP), established noncoercive de-escalation as the intervention of choice for acute agitation.[1] The De-Escalation Workgroup (Richmond et al., 2012) articulated a 3-step paradigm: (1) verbally engage the patient, (2) establish a collaborative relationship, and (3) verbally de-escalate the patient out of the agitated state.[1] Four overarching objectives guide every encounter: ensure safety, help the patient regain behavioral control, avoid restraint, and avoid coercive interventions that escalate agitation.[1]

The workgroup's 10 Domains of De-Escalation provide a structured framework encompassing: respecting personal space, being non-provocative, establishing verbal contact, being concise, identifying wants and feelings, listening closely, agreeing or agreeing to disagree, setting clear limits, offering choices and optimism, and debriefing the patient and staff.[1] Effective de-escalation should take approximately 5-10 minutes to return an agitated person to a calm state.[2]

APA Guidance and the ERASER Mnemonic

The APA Resource Document on Seclusion or Restraint (2022) designates verbal de-escalation as first-line treatment, effective for a majority of patients in behavioral health crisis within 5 minutes.[3] The APA recommends all staff-including security and observation personnel-be trained in de-escalation, referencing the ERASER mnemonic as a teaching tool.[3] Environmental interventions endorsed by the APA include quiet rooms, sensory rooms, music, warm showers, weighted blankets, aromatherapy, exercise, and 1:1 observation with de-escalation-trained staff.[3]

Effectiveness Evidence

A cluster-randomized controlled trial across all psychiatric hospitals in Slovenia demonstrated that de-escalation training reduced aggressive events by 73% (IRR 0.268, 95% CI 0.221-0.342), severe aggressive events by 86%, and physical restraints by 70% compared to controls.[4] Implementation of Project BETA-aligned initiatives at a large county hospital ED reduced physical assaults on emergency medicine residents from 28% to 11.3% (p = 0.032), though gains eroded when in-person training was disrupted by COVID-19.[5] A systematic review of de-escalation training in health professions education (56 studies) found that curricula incorporating both didactic education and active skills practice (role-play/simulation) produced the strongest evidence of effectiveness.[6]

Critically, two Cochrane systematic reviews found no RCTs meeting inclusion criteria for de-escalation techniques alone, highlighting that the evidence base remains predominantly consensus-driven and observational despite universal guideline endorsement.[7][2]

---

II. Trauma-Informed Approaches

Trauma-informed care (TIC) applied to agitation management rests on three core recognitions: the prevalence of trauma, how trauma affects all individuals involved, and the need to prevent retraumatization.[8] The SAMHSA model emphasizes five interpersonal principles: safety, trustworthiness, choice, collaboration, and empowerment.[9]

The Six Core Strategies (6CS) framework-developed by the National Association of State Mental Health Program Directors-is the most extensively studied TIC-based restraint reduction model. A federally funded multisite study of 43 inpatient psychiatric facilities found that stabilized 6CS implementation reduced the percentage of patients secluded by 17% (p = .002), seclusion hours by 19% (p = .001), and proportion restrained by 30% (p = .03).[10] The Pennsylvania State Hospital System achieved near-complete cessation of mechanical restraint and seclusion over a 10-year period through continuous 6CS adherence, with all safety measures (assaults, aggression, self-injurious behavior) improved or unchanged.[11] A cluster-RCT in Finnish forensic wards demonstrated that seclusion-restraint-observation days declined from 30% to 15% in intervention wards without any increase in violence (p = .91).[12]

A scoping review of 31 studies found that TIC approaches (most commonly 6CS and the Sanctuary Model) were associated with decreased restraint and seclusion rates, though most evidence remains preliminary.[13]

---

III. Pharmacotherapy: Comparative Evidence

Antipsychotic-Benzodiazepine Combinations vs. Monotherapy

The largest and most recent evidence comes from the 2026 individual participant data network meta-analysis (IPD-NMA) by Siafis et al. (18 trials, 3,411 participants), published in The Lancet Psychiatry.[14] For moderate agitation, antipsychotic-benzodiazepine combinations were substantially more effective than haloperidol monotherapy for achieving sedation within 15-30 minutes (OR 12.93, 95% CrI 3.00-50.91; RR 1.58), followed by benzodiazepines alone (OR 5.52, 95% CrI 1.37-21.02) and other antipsychotics (OR 4.54, 95% CrI 1.35-14.45).[14] For severe agitation, combinations remained superior (OR 4.86, 95% CrI 1.28-17.54), but results for monotherapy were uncertain.[14] Haloperidol monotherapy was among the least effective options and carried the highest risk of extrapyramidal side effects; benzodiazepines (alone or in combination) increased hypotension risk.[14] Confidence in all estimates was very low.[14]

The Cochrane review on haloperidol for psychosis-induced aggression found that haloperidol alone produced significantly more adverse effects than haloperidol + promethazine (RR 2.01, 95% CI 1.07-3.80), with acute dystonia so common in the haloperidol-alone arm that the trial steering group deemed continuing monotherapy unethical.[15]

Oral vs. Intramuscular Strategies

A landmark quality-improvement study (n = 1,178 prospectively observed patients) from a safety-net ED found no difference in time to adequate sedation between oral and IM medications: median 15 minutes for both routes (median difference 1 min, 95% CI -0.6 to 2.6).[16] Additional sedation rates and adverse drug reaction rates were comparable.[16] This finding supports the Project BETA and APA recommendation to offer oral medications first whenever patients are cooperative.[3][17]

Expert Tiered Rankings (Stetson & Osser, 2022)

Based on qualitative synthesis of meta-analyses and Cochrane reviews:[25]

IM Olanzapine + Benzodiazepine: The FDA-ACEP Discordance

The FDA label warns against concomitant IM olanzapine and parenteral benzodiazepines due to potential for excessive sedation and cardiorespiratory depression.[28][29] Postmarketing data identified 29 fatalities among an estimated 539,000 exposures, with 66% involving concomitant benzodiazepines.[30] However, a large retrospective ED study (n = 693) found no difference in intubation rates between olanzapine-only (3.8%) and olanzapine + benzodiazepine (3.5%; difference 0.3%, 95% CI -3.0% to 3.7%).[31] The ACEP clinical policy recommends coadministration for severe agitation, creating a guideline-label discordance that clinicians must navigate.[31]

---

IV. Special Populations

Older Adults

Nonpharmacologic strategies are first-line per AGS 2023 Beers Criteria guidance.[32] Benzodiazepines should generally be avoided due to cognitive impairment, falls, and delirium risk; a Geriatric ED Guidelines 2.0 systematic review found midazolam had the highest adverse event rate (53%; OR 5.25 vs. haloperidol, 95% CI 2.64-10.45).[33] Quetiapine was the only agent with lower adverse events than haloperidol (OR 0.27, 95% CI 0.08-0.97).[33] All antipsychotics carry an FDA black box warning for increased mortality in dementia-related psychosis.[34] Recommended starting doses: quetiapine 12.5-25 mg PO, olanzapine 2.5-5 mg PO/IM, haloperidol 0.5-1 mg PO/IM.[35]

Pregnancy

No efficacy or safety RCTs exist for acute agitation management in pregnancy.[36] Haloperidol (high-potency antipsychotic) is the most commonly administered agent, based on retrospective data from a psychiatric emergency service.[36][37] Lorazepam is preferred among benzodiazepines due to lack of active metabolites, though 20-40% of neonates exposed in late pregnancy develop withdrawal symptoms.[38] Nonpharmacologic approaches should be attempted first.[37]

Alcohol/Substance Intoxication

Droperidol (5-10 mg IM) or olanzapine (where droperidol is unavailable) are recommended first-line for undifferentiated agitation including intoxication.[39][40] Benzodiazepines are specifically indicated for stimulant intoxication and alcohol/sedative-hypnotic withdrawal.[39][41] For alcohol withdrawal delirium, benzodiazepines should be administered IV to achieve light somnolence; antipsychotics may be used as adjuncts but not monotherapy.[41]

Delirium

Nonpharmacologic multicomponent interventions are the cornerstone.[42][32] No medications are FDA-approved for delirium.[34] When pharmacotherapy is needed for severe agitation, second-generation antipsychotics (quetiapine, olanzapine, risperidone) are preferred over haloperidol for faster onset and fewer EPS.[34] Benzodiazepines should be avoided unless the etiology is alcohol/benzodiazepine withdrawal or end-of-life delirium.[42][43] Trazodone is an alternative with lower EPS and QTc risk.[44]

Autism Spectrum Disorder / Intellectual Developmental Disability

Environmental modification is critical: quiet rooms, dimmable lights, reduced stimulation, clear/concrete communication, and family involvement.[45] Risperidone and aripiprazole are the only FDA-approved medications for irritability/aggression in ASD, with meta-analytic effect sizes of SMD 1.07 and 1.18, respectively.[46][47] Evaluate for organic causes (pain, infections) especially in nonverbal patients.[45] No specific RCTs exist for acute agitation management in ASD/IDD populations in emergency settings.

QTc Prolongation

Ziprasidone and iloperidone carry the highest QTc prolongation risk among antipsychotics; aripiprazole and lurasidone have minimal risk.[48] Benzodiazepines do not prolong QTc and are a reasonable alternative.[49] A clinical decision analysis found quetiapine optimal for delirium patients with baseline QTc >=450 ms.[50] The Association of Medicine and Psychiatry recommends baseline ECG for patients with risk score >=2; if QTc >500 ms, medication adjustments should be considered.[51] A secondary analysis of the MIND-USA trial found that neither haloperidol nor ziprasidone was associated with clinically significant QTc changes compared to placebo in ICU patients with normal baseline QTc.[52]

Parkinson Disease

Avoid all dopamine D2-blocking antipsychotics (haloperidol, olanzapine, risperidone, ziprasidone, aripiprazole), which worsen parkinsonism.[53][54] Only three antipsychotics are considered acceptable: pimavanserin (FDA-approved for PD psychosis), clozapine (efficacious but requires REMS), and quetiapine (most commonly prescribed, generally well tolerated).[53][55] For acute agitation, short-acting benzodiazepines (lorazepam, alprazolam) are the mainstay.[56] Optimize motor fluctuation treatment and taper anxiogenic antiparkinsonian drugs in order: anticholinergics -> MAO-B inhibitors -> amantadine -> dopamine agonists -> reduce levodopa.[56]

Catatonia

Recognition is critical: catatonia presents in 5-18% of psychiatric inpatients.[57] Lorazepam is both diagnostic and therapeutic-the lorazepam challenge test (1-2 mg IV) has response rates of 66-100%.[57] Scheduled lorazepam (minimum TID, up to 16 mg/day) is first-line treatment.[57][58] ECT is second-line, improving 80-100% of cases including up to 60% of benzodiazepine-refractory cases.[58] NMDA receptor antagonists (amantadine, memantine) are third-line options.[59][58] Antipsychotics may worsen catatonia and should be held; if needed for coexisting psychosis, clozapine is preferred.[59][57]

---

V. Restraint and Seclusion Reduction

The evidence consistently demonstrates that multimodal, trauma-informed programs can substantially reduce restraint and seclusion without increasing violence or adverse safety outcomes. The Pennsylvania State Hospital System's 10-year experience with 6CS showed physical restraint duration fell by 64% (6.6 to 2.4 minutes, p < .001) while all safety measures improved or were unchanged.[11] The Finnish cluster-RCT confirmed no increase in violence with seclusion-restraint reduction (p = .91 for between-group difference).[12] An ED-based agitation code team achieved a 27.3% proportionate decrease in restraint rates over 5 years.[60]

The CMS Inpatient Psychiatric Facility Quality Reporting program, requiring public reporting of restraint and seclusion measures, reduced restraint duration by 49% and seclusion by 54%.[61] Joint Commission 2024/2025 updated standards (effective January 1, 2025) require continuous in-person observation, regular interval assessments, physician evaluation before order expiration, and face-to-face evaluation within 1 hour of initiation.[62]

---

VI. Safety Outcomes and Monitoring

Staff Safety

Government-sector mental health workers experience the highest rate of nonfatal workplace violence at 77.1 incidents per 1,000 workers.[8] In a prospective ED study, staff received injuries in 12% of sedation events.[63] The APA 2025 resource document endorses the Assaulted Staff Action Program (ASAP) for post-assault support.[8]

Patient Adverse Events

A prospective Australian study of 904 patients receiving parenteral sedation found 15.9% experienced at least one adverse event, most commonly oxygen desaturation (7.4%), airway obstruction (3.6%), and bradycardia (1.9%). Risk factors included age >=65 (OR 2.8), multiple sedatives within 60 minutes (OR 2.1), and alcohol intoxication (OR 1.8).[64] In older adults, adverse events occurred in 16.8% of patients, with midazolam posing the highest risk.[33]

Post-Sedation Monitoring Protocol

Expert recommendations for post-sedation monitoring include, at minimum: regular vital signs, level of sedation assessment, and continuous pulse oximetry (without supplemental oxygen); end-tidal CO2 monitoring when available.[39] Clinical trials typically employed 1:1 nursing with sedation level and vital sign monitoring at 10, 20, 30, 45, and 60 minutes post-dose, along with cardiac rhythm monitoring.[22] The British National Formulary recommends monitoring for a minimum of 4 hours following IM antipsychotic administration.[65]

X. Resident Bedside Checklist for Acute Agitation

[ ] SAFETY FIRST

- Ensure clear exit path; remove potential weapons from environment

- Activate team response if patient is violent or imminently dangerous

- Maintain >=2 arm lengths of personal space

[ ] ASSESS

- Vital signs (HR, BP, SpO2, temperature, glucose) when safely obtainable

- Rapid etiology screen: psychosis vs. delirium vs. intoxication/withdrawal vs. medical vs. catatonia

- Check medication list for QT-prolonging drugs; review allergies

- Screen for special populations: age >=65, pregnancy, Parkinson disease, ASD/IDD, known QTc prolongation

[ ] DE-ESCALATE (Project BETA 10 Domains)

- Respect personal space; use calm, non-provocative tone

- Introduce yourself; establish verbal contact concisely

- Identify wants and feelings; listen actively

- Offer choices ("Would you prefer a pill or a drink?")

- Set clear, enforceable limits

- Allow 5-10 minutes for de-escalation before pharmacotherapy

[ ] OFFER ORAL MEDICATION FIRST

- Olanzapine 5-10 mg ODT, OR lorazepam 1-2 mg PO, OR haloperidol 5 mg + lorazepam 2 mg PO

- Frame as collaborative: "This medication can help you feel calmer"

- Document patient preference and response

[ ] IF ORAL REFUSED OR INEFFECTIVE -> IM MEDICATION

- Select agent based on etiology and population (see medication table)

- Default: IM olanzapine 10 mg, OR IM haloperidol 5 mg + promethazine 25-50 mg, OR IM droperidol 5-10 mg

- Do not combine IM olanzapine with parenteral benzodiazepine (FDA label)[28]

- Reassess in 15-30 minutes; may repeat dose once

[ ] POST-MEDICATION MONITORING

- Continuous pulse oximetry (no supplemental O2 unless SpO2 <92%)

- Vital signs + sedation level at 10, 20, 30, 45, 60 minutes post-dose[22]

- Assess for: airway compromise, SpO2 <90%, SBP <90, dystonic reactions, seizures, vomiting

- ECG within 30 minutes of sedation if QTc-prolonging agent used[22]

- Patient should remain recumbent if drowsy; assess orthostatic vitals before ambulation[29]

- Monitor for minimum 4 hours after IM antipsychotic[65]

[ ] RESTRAINT (LAST RESORT ONLY)

- Document less restrictive interventions attempted and failed

- Physician order required; specify type, duration, and clinical justification

- Face-to-face evaluation within 1 hour of initiation (CMS requirement)[3]

- Maximum order duration: 4 hours for adults (Joint Commission)[62]

- Continuous in-person observation; reassess readiness for discontinuation at each interval[62]

- Pulse, BP, range of motion every 15 minutes; nutrition/hydration/elimination ongoing[68]

[ ] DEBRIEF

- Debrief with patient after de-escalation (trauma-informed practice)

- Debrief with team; document in chart

- Report any staff or patient injuries per institutional protocol

---

XI. Evidence Gaps and Emerging Data

Several critical uncertainties persist. No RCTs of verbal de-escalation alone have met Cochrane inclusion criteria, meaning the universal first-line recommendation rests on consensus and observational data.[7][2] The sustainability of restraint reduction programs without external oversight remains a significant concern, as demonstrated by the resumption of high seclusion/restraint use when 6CS adherence was discontinued.[69] The FDA warning against IM olanzapine + parenteral benzodiazepines conflicts with emerging ED safety data and ACEP recommendations, creating unresolved clinical uncertainty.[31] Evidence on equity in agitation management is limited, though some data suggest disproportionate restraint use among Black patients.[70] The role of underlying etiology in treatment selection remains poorly studied in comparative trials.[14] Emerging agents and formulations-including sublingual dexmedetomidine and novel rapid-acting formulations-may expand the therapeutic armamentarium but lack robust agitation-specific trial data.

---

XII. Summary

The totality of evidence supports a stepwise, etiology-informed approach to acute agitation: verbal de-escalation and environmental modification as universal first-line interventions, oral medication offered before intramuscular when feasible, and pharmacotherapy guided by clinical scenario and patient-specific factors. Haloperidol monotherapy should no longer be considered standard practice given its inferior efficacy and high EPS risk.[14][15] Antipsychotic-benzodiazepine combinations appear most effective for rapid tranquilization but carry increased hypotension risk.[14] Trauma-informed, multimodal programs (particularly the Six Core Strategies) can substantially reduce restraint and seclusion without compromising safety.[11][12] Sustained organizational commitment, ongoing training, and external oversight are essential to maintain gains.

## Source: `OPENEVIDENCE RAW FILES TO REVIEW/Alcohol Withdrawal and Alcohol Use Disorder Management on Adult Inpatient Psychiatry Units.docx`

Alcohol Withdrawal and Alcohol Use Disorder Management on Adult Inpatient Psychiatry Units

Scope and Framing

This review synthesizes current evidence and guideline recommendations for managing alcohol withdrawal syndrome (AWS) and alcohol use disorder (AUD) on adult inpatient psychiatry units. It covers assessment tools, pharmacotherapy for withdrawal and long-term treatment, special populations, thiamine repletion, and discharge planning. The inpatient psychiatry setting presents unique challenges - psychiatric comorbidity, communication barriers, limited medical monitoring infrastructure compared to ICUs, and the opportunity to initiate long-term AUD treatment during a "reachable moment." Key sources include the ASAM 2020 Clinical Practice Guideline on Alcohol Withdrawal Management, the VA/DoD 2021 SUD Clinical Practice Guideline, the APA 2018 Pharmacotherapy Guideline, and recent systematic reviews and practice-changing studies.

---

1. CIWA-Ar: Utility and Limitations

The Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment for Alcohol-Revised (CIWA-Ar) is the most widely used withdrawal severity scale, with excellent inter-rater reliability (r > 0.8) in research settings.[1][2] However, several critical limitations are particularly relevant to inpatient psychiatry:

Reliance on patient self-report. Six of 10 CIWA-Ar items require the patient to answer questions (nausea, anxiety, tactile/auditory/visual disturbances, headache).[1][3] This renders the scale unreliable or impossible to administer in patients with delirium, psychosis, severe cognitive impairment, or communication barriers - all common on psychiatry units. The ASAM guideline explicitly recommends not using the CIWA-Ar in patients with delirium.[1]

Confounding by comorbid conditions. Scores can be falsely elevated by fever, concurrent substance withdrawal, or traumatic brain injury, and falsely suppressed by beta-blockers or other sympatholytic medications.[1][3] A Lancet review concluded that no withdrawal scale has been validated in the inpatient setting where comorbidity is prevalent, and that serious comorbidity is "probably better managed without use of a scale".[1]

Protocol misapplication. A retrospective chart review of 118 encounters found that 57% of patients placed on a CIWA-Ar protocol had zero or one documented risk factor for AWS, 20% had no documentation of recent alcohol use, 14% were unable to communicate, and benzodiazepine-associated adverse events occurred in 15%.[1]

Severity thresholds are not empirically derived. The commonly used cutoffs (<10, 10-20, >20) were based on the original authors' clinical experience, not empirical data, and there is wide variation in practice regarding which scores delineate severity categories.[1]

Alternative scales include the mMINDS (does not require patient self-report; preferred by 70% of ICU nurses over CIWA-Ar; r = 0.814 correlation with CIWA-Ar), the BAWS (5 objective items), and the mRASS-AW (observation-based, with no worsening of LOS or complications vs.[3][4] CIWA-Ar in a retrospective comparison of 1,073 patients).[5] For patients with delirium, the ASAM guideline recommends the CAM-ICU, RASS, or Delirium Detection Score.[1]

---

2. Symptom-Triggered vs. Fixed-Dose Benzodiazepine Protocols

Symptom-Triggered Therapy (STT)

A 2019 systematic review and meta-analysis of 6 RCTs (n = 664) found STT reduced treatment duration by 60.4 hours (95% CI 39.7-81.1; P < .001) and total benzodiazepine dose by 10.5 mg lorazepam-equivalents (95% CI 7.1-13.9; P = .011) compared to fixed-dose regimens, with no significant differences in delirium, seizures, or mortality.[6] A landmark RCT demonstrated that symptom-triggered chlordiazepoxide reduced mean treatment duration from 68 to 9 hours and total dose from 425 to 100 mg.[7]

Critical caveat: The evidence was derived primarily from specialized detoxification settings with low-risk patients; applicability to general hospital and inpatient psychiatry settings was rated as low.[6] There was insufficient evidence to draw conclusions about hard outcomes (mortality, seizures, delirium) in any setting.[6]

Fixed-Dose Therapy

Fixed-dose regimens (e.g., chlordiazepoxide 50 mg q6h with taper) are appropriate when STT cannot be reliably implemented - specifically when patients cannot self-report symptoms due to psychiatric comorbidity, cognitive impairment, or communication barriers.[1] The ASAM guideline recommends that when fixed-dose schedules are used, symptoms should still be monitored and additional PRN doses provided.[8]

Front-Loading

Front-loading involves administering moderate-to-high doses of long-acting benzodiazepines (typically diazepam 10-20 mg PO every 1-2 hours) to achieve rapid symptom control, then allowing the drug to self-taper. The ASAM guideline specifically recommends front-loading for severe withdrawal (CIWA-Ar >= 19), as it reduces treatment duration, seizure incidence, and delirium duration.[8]

Guideline Positions

The ASAM 2020 guideline designates STT as the preferred benzodiazepine dosing method (Recommendation V.23), with diazepam or chlordiazepoxide as preferred agents.[8] The VA/DoD 2021 guideline recommends benzodiazepines as first-line for AWS (CIWA-Ar >= 10), noting they reduce seizure risk by 84% vs. placebo (RR 0.16; 95% CI 0.04-0.69).[8][1] For mild-to-moderate withdrawal where benzodiazepine risks outweigh benefits, gabapentin, carbamazepine, or valproic acid are suggested alternatives.[9]

---

3. Phenobarbital Protocols

Phenobarbital use in US hospitals increased from 6.1% to 18.4% between 2016 and 2020.[10] Its dual mechanism - GABA-A receptor agonism plus direct glutamate antagonism - addresses both pathophysiologic arms of AWS, unlike benzodiazepines which only enhance GABA signaling.[11] Its long half-life (80-120 hours) enables "auto-tapering" after a loading dose.[12]

Evidence Base

No large, multicenter RCT comparing phenobarbital monotherapy to benzodiazepines has been published.[13][1] The evidence base consists of two small ED-based RCTs and numerous observational studies. A meta-analysis of 12 studies (n = 1,934) found no differences in intubation (RR 0.70; 95% CI 0.36-1.38), seizures (RR 0.73; 95% CI 0.29-1.89), or length of stay vs. benzodiazepines.[1] The largest comparative study to date - a multicenter propensity-matched analysis (n = 4,712 per cohort) - found phenobarbital monotherapy was associated with significantly lower seizures (RR 0.70; 95% CI 0.58-0.85) and delirium tremens (RR 0.52; 95% CI 0.41-0.65).[14]

A hospital-wide QI study implementing an EHR-based phenobarbital monotherapy order set (10-15 mg/kg IV loading) demonstrated 67% uptake, reduced benzodiazepine use, improved symptom control, and a 2-day reduction in time to discharge with no increase in adverse safety events.[10] On VA general medical wards, serious adverse events occurred in only 0.4% of 244 hospitalizations using phenobarbital.[15]

Dosing Protocols

The American Family Physician review provides a clinical decision algorithm for phenobarbital dosing that branches based on prior benzodiazepine exposure and sedation status, incorporating RASS monitoring.

eFigure A Treatment of alcohol withdrawal syndrome with phenobarbital. Information from Farkas J. Phenobarbital monotherapy for alcohol withdrawal: simplicity and power. October 18, 2015. Accessed January 17, 2023. https://emcrit.org/pulmcrit/phenobarbital-monotherapy-for-alcohol-withdrawal-simplicity-and-power

Guideline Positions

The ASAM 2020 guideline positions benzodiazepines as first-line but endorses phenobarbital as an appropriate alternative for moderate-to-severe/complicated withdrawal, as monotherapy when benzodiazepines are contraindicated, or as an adjunct in severe withdrawal.[11][6] Parenteral phenobarbital should only be used in highly supervised settings (ICU/CCU) due to risk of oversedation and respiratory depression.[6] The VA/DoD 2021 guideline does not specifically highlight phenobarbital as a recommended alternative.[9] The SAEM GRACE-4 guideline (2024) recommends adjunctive phenobarbital in the ED but states there is insufficient evidence to recommend any specific dosing protocol.[1]

Safety Considerations for Psychiatry Units

Phenobarbital has no reversal agent, a narrow therapeutic window, and requires experienced clinicians.[12][6] Combination with benzodiazepines may carry higher risk than monotherapy with either agent.[18] These factors make phenobarbital loading protocols challenging on most inpatient psychiatry units, which typically lack continuous cardiopulmonary monitoring. If used, fixed-dose regimens with RASS-guided monitoring are preferred over symptom-triggered approaches given phenobarbital's long half-life.[12]

---

4. Special Populations

Delirium Tremens

Delirium tremens typically presents 72-96 hours after the last drink, carries 1-4% mortality among hospitalized patients, and often necessitates ICU admission.[8][1] Benzodiazepines are first-line, with the goal of achieving light somnolence; IV administration is preferred.[19] Very large doses may be required (>2,000 mg diazepam in the first 2 days in some patients).[19][20] Phenobarbital can be used as an adjunct when DT is not controlled by benzodiazepines alone.[19] Antipsychotics may be used as adjuncts for hallucinations but should not be used as monotherapy.[5] Alpha-2 agonists and beta-blockers should not be used to treat DT.[5]

Seizure History

Prior withdrawal seizures and prior DT are among the strongest predictors of severe withdrawal.[21] The kindling effect is well-supported: patients with >=5 prior detoxifications had a 48% rate of withdrawal seizures vs. 12% in controls.[22] Front-loading with benzodiazepines is specifically recommended for high-risk patients.[1] Following a withdrawal seizure, IV lorazepam or diazepam should be administered immediately.[1] Phenytoin should not be used for alcohol withdrawal seizures unless treating a concomitant underlying seizure disorder.[1]

Hepatic Impairment

Lorazepam and oxazepam are preferred in patients with advanced liver disease - both are metabolized by glucuronidation (not hepatic oxidation), lack active metabolites, and lorazepam metabolites are eliminated renally.[19][23][24] The ACG 2024 guideline recommends avoiding diazepam and chlordiazepoxide in patients with decompensated cirrhosis.[23] Phenobarbital is not recommended in liver disease.[19] Benzodiazepines may precipitate or worsen hepatic encephalopathy, requiring careful dose titration.[23]

Older Adults (>=65 years)

Withdrawal onset may be delayed by several days, and confusion rather than tremor and tachycardia is often the predominant sign.[26] No age-specific dosing guidelines exist.[26] Longer-acting benzodiazepines can accumulate and lead to oversedation, with signs (ataxia, confusion) that may be difficult to differentiate from withdrawal-related delirium.[27] A retrospective study of patients >=70 years found that implementing a symptom-triggered protocol significantly reduced median treatment duration (96->48 hours), cumulative benzodiazepine dose (9->3 mg lorazepam equivalents), and severe AWS complications.[28] Prefer shorter-acting agents (lorazepam, oxazepam) and implement falls precautions.[27]

Polysubstance Use

The VA/DoD guideline lists comorbid substance use as an indication for inpatient treatment.[8][1] For concurrent opioid use, the ASAM guideline recommends stabilizing OUD concomitantly (with methadone or buprenorphine) while treating alcohol withdrawal, with close monitoring for respiratory depression.[29] Concurrent withdrawal from alcohol and another sedative-hypnotic is more clinically complicated than withdrawal from a substance with different pharmacologic effects and typically requires a longer taper.[30] Gabapentin, carbamazepine, and valproic acid may be useful alternatives when benzodiazepine risks outweigh benefits (e.g., history of sedative abuse).[9]

---

5. Thiamine Dosing for Wernicke Prevention and Treatment

The Evidence Gap

The Cochrane systematic review (Day et al., 2013) concluded there is insufficient evidence from RCTs to guide the optimum dose, frequency, route, or duration of thiamine for either prophylaxis or treatment of Wernicke encephalopathy (WE).[31] The only major dose-comparison RCT (Dingwall et al., 2022; N = 520) found no significant differences between parenteral thiamine dose tiers, but the authors acknowledged substantial limitations and recommended patient-specific treatment.[19]

Why Oral Thiamine 100 mg Is Inadequate for High-Risk Patients

Chronic alcohol consumption inhibits intestinal thiamine transport via reduced thiamine transporter-1 (THTR-1) expression.[25] Doses of 100-250 mg/day "apparently may not restore vitamin status, improve clinical signs, or prevent death" in patients with established WE.[25] When WE is inappropriately treated with low doses, estimated mortality is ~20%, and ~85% of survivors develop irreversible Korsakoff syndrome.[25] The classic triad (oculomotor dysfunction, ataxia, encephalopathy) is present in less than one-third of cases, making clinical diagnosis unreliable.[32]

Recommended Dosing

Magnesium should be corrected concurrently (cofactor for thiamine-dependent transketolase reactions).[1] Thiamine should be given before or concurrently with IV glucose in thiamine-deficient patients.[25][1] Parenteral thiamine has an excellent safety profile; anaphylaxis is rare.[17]

Practical Recommendation for Inpatient Psychiatry

All patients admitted with AUD should receive parenteral thiamine 200-500 mg IV/IM daily for at least 3 days before transitioning to oral supplementation. The standard "banana bag" containing 100 mg thiamine is pharmacokinetically inadequate for CNS repletion.[1] If any signs of WE are present (confusion, ataxia, oculomotor abnormalities - even in isolation), escalate immediately to 500 mg IV TID.

---

6. Pharmacotherapy for Alcohol Use Disorder

Initiating MAUD During Hospitalization

The ASAM guideline explicitly recommends that AUD treatment, including pharmacotherapy, should be initiated concurrently with withdrawal management as cognitive status permits.[1] A target trial emulation using Medicare data (n = 9,834) found that discharge MAUD initiation was associated with a 42% decreased incidence of the composite outcome of all-cause mortality or return to hospital within 30 days (IRR 0.58; 95% CI 0.45-0.76).[1] The ADOPT trial (RCT, N = 248) demonstrated that both oral and injectable naltrexone initiated at hospital discharge produced substantial reductions in heavy drinking days (66.7%->27.4% for oral; 70.7%->23.8% for injectable at 3 months).[34] Addiction consult services dramatically increase inpatient MAUD initiation (33.0% vs. 0.9%; OR 52.5).[1]

Medication Comparison

The 2023 JAMA systematic review and meta-analysis (118 RCTs, 20,976 participants) provides the most comprehensive comparative efficacy data:[35]

Table 1 Summary of Findings and Strength of Evidence From Trials Assessing Efficacy of Medications With at Least Low Strength of Evidence for Benefit for Alcohol Use Disordera

Guideline Discrepancies

The VA/DoD 2021 guideline elevated topiramate to first-line (alongside naltrexone) and downgraded acamprosate and disulfiram to "suggested," based on more stringent evidence criteria.[9] The APA 2018 guideline maintains naltrexone and acamprosate as co-first-line.[40] The COMBINE trial (N = 1,383) found naltrexone effective (80.6% vs. 75.1% days abstinent; P = .009) but no evidence of efficacy for acamprosate in any arm - a finding that has not been replicated in European trials.[40][1]

7. Discharge Linkage and Relapse Prevention

Up to 75% of patients relapse in the year after treatment, with risk highest during the first 3 months.[42] The ASAM guideline states that the success of withdrawal management is defined not only by acute symptom control but by engagement in continued AUD treatment.[1]

Evidence-Based Discharge Strategies

Warm handoffs and addiction consult services. The ASAM guideline recommends proactively connecting patients to treatment services with a warm handoff to treatment providers.[1] The IMPACT addiction consult service increased post-discharge SUD treatment engagement from 23.3% to 38.9% (aOR 2.15; 95% CI 1.29-3.58).[1] A pharmacy-guided AUD discharge workflow produced a 195% increase in MAUD prescriptions, 61% reduction in 90-day total readmissions, and 92% reduction in alcohol-related readmissions.[43]

Mutual aid referral. A 2020 Cochrane review (27 studies, 10,565 participants) found manualized AA/twelve-step facilitation (TSF) produced higher rates of continuous abstinence at 12 months (367 vs. 304 per 1,000; high-certainty evidence) compared to other established treatments like CBT, with benefits persisting to 36 months.[38] The VA/DoD guideline strongly recommends TSF, network support, or peer linkage to promote active involvement in mutual help programs.[44] Peer linkage (3 sessions linking patients with a 12-step peer) produced higher AA attendance and greater reductions in alcohol use severity over 12 months compared to standard referral.[18]

Motivational interviewing. A 2023 Cochrane review found a small-to-moderate benefit vs. no intervention post-intervention (SMD 0.48; 95% CI 0.07-0.89; low certainty), diminishing at follow-up.[1] An RCT in a psychiatric emergency unit found that two MI sessions produced 7.3 fewer days of substance use per month at 2-year follow-up (95% CI 1.9-12.6; P < .01).[44]

Technology-based continuing care. The A-CHESS smartphone app (RCT, n = 349) significantly increased abstinence at 8 and 12 months.[18] A systematic review and meta-analysis (34 RCTs, 6,461 participants) found remote interventions supplementing in-person care reduced relapse odds by 39% (OR 0.61; 95% CI 0.46-0.81).[1] The VA/DoD guideline suggests technology-based interventions and structured telephone-based care as adjuncts.[45]

Follow-up timing. The ASAM quality measure recommends outpatient follow-up within 7 days after withdrawal management.[46] Weekly follow-up for a month after detoxification, with decreasing frequency thereafter, is recommended.[1]

---

8. Resident Algorithm for Alcohol Withdrawal on Inpatient Psychiatry

Step 1: Risk Stratification (Admission)

- Obtain detailed alcohol use history: quantity, frequency, time of last drink, prior withdrawal severity (seizures, DT)

- Assess for kindling (>=5 prior detoxifications -> 48% seizure rate)[22]

- Check vitals, CBC, CMP, Mg2+, phosphorus, hepatic panel, BAL, UDS

- High-risk features requiring medical floor/ICU consideration: CIWA-Ar >= 20, prior DT or withdrawal seizures, active medical illness, decompensated cirrhosis, age >65 with comorbidities

Step 2: Thiamine Repletion (Day 1)

- All patients: Thiamine 200-500 mg IV/IM daily  3-5 days -> 100 mg PO daily[25][29]

- If any WE signs (confusion, ataxia, oculomotor abnormalities): Thiamine 500 mg IV TID  2-3 days[25]

- Correct magnesium concurrently; give thiamine before IV dextrose[25][1]

Step 3: Withdrawal Management

- If patient can reliably self-report and no delirium/psychosis: Symptom-triggered protocol (CIWA-Ar q1-2h; treat if >=10)[8]

- Lorazepam 2 mg PO/IM q1h PRN (preferred in liver disease, elderly)[19]

- OR Chlordiazepoxide 25-50 mg PO q1h PRN (preferred if no liver disease)[8]

- If patient cannot self-report (delirium, psychosis, cognitive impairment): Fixed-dose protocol with objective monitoring (vitals, RASS)[1]

- Lorazepam 1-2 mg PO/IM q6h scheduled  3 days with taper + PRN

- If severe withdrawal (CIWA-Ar >= 19) or high-risk: Front-loading[8]

- Diazepam 10-20 mg PO q1-2h until light sedation (if no liver disease)

- OR Lorazepam 2-4 mg IV q15-30 min (if liver disease or IV access needed)

- Escalation triggers -> transfer to medical floor/ICU: Refractory symptoms despite adequate dosing, seizure, DT, respiratory depression, hemodynamic instability

Step 4: Initiate AUD Pharmacotherapy (Days 2-3, as cognition clears)

- Default first-line: Naltrexone 25 mg PO  3 days -> 50 mg PO daily[1]

- Contraindicated if: current opioid use, acute hepatitis, liver failure

- If opioid use or liver disease: Acamprosate 666 mg PO TID (requires CrCl >30)[1]

- If prominent withdrawal symptoms/insomnia/anxiety: Gabapentin 300 mg -> titrate to 600 mg TID[38][39]

- If obesity or prior MAUD failure: Topiramate 25 mg/d -> titrate over 5-6 weeks[1]

- If highly motivated with supervised administration available: Disulfiram 250 mg PO daily[1]

Step 5: Discharge Planning (Begin Day 1)

- Warm handoff to outpatient addiction/psychiatry provider[1]

- Schedule follow-up within 7 days[46]

- Prescribe MAUD with >=30-day supply

- Provide AA/mutual aid referral with specific meeting times/locations; consider peer linkage[38][18]

- Brief MI session during hospitalization[1][44]

- Provide crisis resources and relapse prevention plan

- Consider injectable naltrexone if adherence concerns (aOR 3.88 for adherence vs. oral)[1]

---

9. Common Pitfalls

1. Using CIWA-Ar in patients who cannot self-report - delirious, psychotic, or cognitively impaired patients produce unreliable scores; use objective scales (RASS, mMINDS) or fixed-dose protocols instead.[1]

2. Prescribing oral thiamine 100 mg as sole repletion - inadequate for hospitalized patients with AUD; parenteral 200-500 mg daily is the minimum standard.[25][1]

3. Using phenytoin for alcohol withdrawal seizures - phenytoin is ineffective for withdrawal seizures and should not be used unless treating a concomitant underlying seizure disorder.[1]

4. Choosing chlordiazepoxide or diazepam in decompensated liver disease - these agents undergo hepatic oxidation with active metabolites that accumulate; use lorazepam or oxazepam.[19][23]

5. Discharging without initiating MAUD - only ~2% of alcohol-related hospitalizations involve discharge MAUD initiation despite evidence of a 42% reduction in 30-day mortality/readmission.[1]

6. Treating beta-blocker-suppressed vital signs as "mild withdrawal" - sympatholytic medications mask tachycardia and hypertension without preventing seizures or delirium.[1]

7. Using antipsychotics as monotherapy for withdrawal-related agitation - antipsychotics lower the seizure threshold and should only be used as adjuncts to benzodiazepines.[5]

8. Underdosing benzodiazepines in severe withdrawal/DT - very large doses may be required; clinicians should not hesitate to provide adequate dosing to achieve light somnolence.[19][20]

9. Failing to assess for concurrent sedative-hypnotic dependence - concurrent benzodiazepine/sedative withdrawal is more complicated and requires longer tapers.[30]

10. Passive referral at discharge ("here's a phone number") - warm handoffs, peer linkage, and scheduled appointments within 7 days are far more effective than passive referral alone.[1]

## Source: `OPENEVIDENCE RAW FILES TO REVIEW/Brief Psychotherapeutic Interventions on Adult Inpatient Psychiatry Units_ A Comprehensive Evidence Review.docx`

Brief Psychotherapeutic Interventions on Adult Inpatient Psychiatry Units: A Comprehensive Evidence Review

Scope and Framing

This review synthesizes the evidence for brief psychotherapeutic interventions deliverable by psychiatry residents during short (3-7 day) adult inpatient psychiatric admissions. It covers safety planning, brief CBT, behavioral activation, DBT-informed skills, motivational interviewing, problem-solving therapy, supportive psychotherapy, crisis intervention, and psychoeducation. The focus is on interventions with RCT or meta-analytic support, guideline endorsement, and practical feasibility in acute settings. Pediatric and long-stay (>3 month) inpatient data are excluded except where directly informative.

---

I. The Overarching Evidence Base: Does Inpatient Psychotherapy Work?

Multiple meta-analyses converge on a small-to-moderate benefit of adding psychotherapy to standard inpatient care. The Schefft et al. (2019) meta-analysis of 14 RCTs (1,080 patients with MDD) found a pooled effect of SMD 0.24 (95% CI 0.12-0.37; NNT = 7.4) with zero heterogeneity across CBT, behavioral activation, psychodynamic, and interpersonal modalities.[1] Cuijpers et al. (2021) extended this to 32 RCTs in institutional settings, finding g = 0.42 (0.29-0.56), sustained at 9-15 months.[2] The Cohen-Chazani et al. (2022) meta-analysis (37 samples, 4,443 patients across diagnoses) found d = 0.43 for the specific contribution of psychotherapy beyond ward treatment, with no significant effect of therapy orientation - diagnosis moderated outcomes more than modality.[3] The Paterson et al. (2018) meta-analysis confirmed small-to-moderate improvements in depression, anxiety, and readmissions, though blinded RCTs showed smaller effects.[4]

The following forest plot from Schefft et al. illustrates the consistent small benefit across modalities for inpatient depression treatment:
