A critical 2026 JAMA Psychiatry viewpoint by Kleiman et al. argues that the field must stop treating inpatient units as "short-term outpatient" and instead design interventions around stand-alone, open-enrollment modules targeting transdiagnostic crisis mechanisms (emotion dysregulation, cognitive inflexibility, behavioral inactivity, life-threatening behaviors), deliverable by non-specialist staff.[5]

---

II. Safety Planning Intervention (SPI) and Suicide Prevention

The Stanley-Brown Safety Planning Intervention

The strongest evidence for any single brief inpatient intervention comes from safety planning. The Stanley et al. (2018) VA cohort comparison (N = 1,640 across 9 EDs) found SPI with structured follow-up calls (SPI+) was associated with ~45% fewer suicidal behaviors (OR 0.56; 95% CI 0.33-0.95) and more than double the odds of outpatient engagement over 6 months.[6] Critically, the protective effect was not mediated by increased treatment engagement, suggesting SPI has an independent mechanism.[6]

Figure 1 Suicidal Behavior in 6-Month Follow-up for Safety Planning Intervention With Structured Follow-up Telephone Contact (SPI+) and Usual Care

The Nuij et al. (2021) meta-analysis of 6 studies (N = 3,536) confirmed safety planning-type interventions reduce suicidal behavior (RR 0.57; 95% CI 0.41-0.80; NNT = 16), though not suicidal ideation.[7] Safety plan quality matters: among hospitalized veterans, higher whole-plan quality was associated with decreased suicide attempts (AHR 0.79; 95% CI 0.66-0.95), with Step 1 (warning signs) quality most strongly protective (HR 0.48).[8] Alarmingly, 52.5% of at-risk veterans in one sample lacked a documented safety plan.[8]

Crisis Response Planning

Bryan et al. (2017) demonstrated that crisis response planning (an abbreviated 4-step SPI) significantly reduced suicide attempts and improved treatment engagement compared to no-suicide contracts in active-duty military.[9] The 2024 VA/DoD guideline recognizes SPI as standard of care in both VA and DoD settings.[10]

Brief Cognitive Behavioral Therapy for Suicide Prevention (BCBT-Inpatient)

The Diefenbach et al. (2024) RCT (N = 200) is the largest and most definitive inpatient suicide prevention psychotherapy trial. Up to 4 sessions of BCBT-Inpatient added to TAU (which already included safety planning and caring contacts) reduced post-discharge suicide attempts by 60% (OR 0.40; 95% CI 0.20-0.80; NNT = 7) and psychiatric readmissions by 71% in patients without SUD over 6 months.[11]

The MSPIRE RCT (Bryan et al., 2025) replicated these findings in military populations, with BCBT reducing cumulative attempt rates to ~6% vs. ~28% for present-centered therapy.[12]

Caring Contacts

The 2024 VA/DoD guideline suggests sending periodic caring communications for 12 months post-hospitalization to reduce suicide attempts (moderate quality evidence).[10] A systematic review found caring contacts may reduce attempts by ~43% at 1-year follow-up, though a single postcard is insufficient - repeated communication for >=12 months is required.[10][9]

Post-Discharge Risk Window

The post-discharge period carries extraordinary risk: pooled suicide rates are 2,950 per 100,000 person-years in the first week and 2,060 per 100,000 person-years in the first month after psychiatric discharge.[13] Only 35% of patients attend follow-up within 1 week.[14] The Doupnik et al. (2020) JAMA Psychiatry meta-analysis of 14 studies (N = 4,270) found brief suicide prevention interventions in acute care reduced subsequent attempts (pooled OR 0.69) and increased linkage to follow-up (pooled OR 2.74).[15]

Figure 2 Forest Plots for 3 Study Outcomes: Depression, Linkage to Follow-up Care, and Subsequent Suicide Attempts

III. DBT-Informed Skills Training

Inpatient Evidence

The evidence for DBT in acute inpatient settings is consistently positive but methodologically limited, consisting primarily of retrospective studies and small trials.[16] Bohus et al. (2004) demonstrated that 3-month inpatient DBT for BPD (N = 50) was superior to waitlist on 7 of 9 psychopathological variables, with 42% achieving clinical recovery.[17] Kujovic et al. (2024) found that 8-week and 12-week adapted inpatient DBT produced comparable large effect sizes (BSL-23: d = 1.29 vs. 1.16), suggesting shorter programs may be viable.[18]

Jones et al. (2025) conducted a feasibility RCT of digital DBT (5 online modules over 5-10 days) for acutely suicidal inpatients (N = 42), finding a large effect on suicidality (Cohen's d = -1.0) with 75% adherence.[19] The "Living Through Distress" DBT-informed skills group showed significant reductions in self-harm and increased distress tolerance maintained at 3-month follow-up.[20][21]

The Dismantling Evidence: Skills Training as the Active Ingredient

The landmark Linehan et al. (2015) dismantling RCT (N = 99) compared standard DBT, DBT skills training + case management, and DBT individual therapy + activities group. Conditions including skills training were significantly superior for reducing NSSI (F = 59.1, p < .001) and depression, while all three reduced suicide attempts comparably.[22] This supports skills training as a necessary and potentially sufficient component - directly relevant to inpatient settings where individual DBT therapy is impractical.

The following figure from McMain et al. (2017) illustrates outcomes from a brief DBT skills training trial, showing steep declines in self-harm reaching near-zero rates:

Figure 2 Outcomes for dialectical behaviour therapy ( N = 42) and waitlist ( N = 42) groups over 32 weeks after randomization. Estimated marginal means and 95% confidence intervals over specific outcomes. DSHI , Deliberate SelfHarm Inventory; LSASI , Lifetime Suicide Attempt SelfInjury. Estimates of the marginal means were derived from multilevel generalized linear models. Estimates are incident rate ratios for the selfharm measures and probabilities for the occurrence of Emergency Room Visits and Hospitalizations.

Meta-Analytic Evidence

DeCou et al. (2019; 18 controlled trials) found DBT significantly reduced self-directed violence (d = -0.32) and crisis service use (d = -0.38), but the effect on suicidal ideation was not significant.[24] The 2024 VA/DoD guideline concluded there is insufficient evidence to recommend for or against DBT specifically for suicide attempts, reflecting uncertainty about DBT's effect on attempts as distinct from self-harm broadly.[10]

IV. Behavioral Activation (BA)

BA's simplicity and low cognitive demands make it particularly well-suited to acute inpatient settings. Hopko et al. (2003) conducted the first inpatient BA pilot RCT, demonstrating superiority over supportive treatment with a large effect size.[26] Folke et al. (2015) showed that a 5-day, 10-session BA protocol produced marked improvements in 4 of 6 inpatients.[27] Melicherova et al. (2024; N = 375) found group BA and group CBT produced comparable depression reductions (d = 0.83 vs. 1.08) with no significant between-group differences.[28]

The Cochrane review by Uphoff et al. (2020; 15 RCTs, 2,208 participants) found BA superior to TAU for depression (SMD -0.78; 95% CI -1.05 to -0.51) and anxiety (SMD -0.33).[29] A 2024 JAMA review confirmed BA's effect on depression vs. usual care (SMD 0.73; 95% CI 0.52-0.95), comparable to CBT (0.67) and problem-solving therapy (0.64).[30] BA is not significantly different from other active treatments, supporting its use as a pragmatic, easily taught alternative to more complex modalities.[31]

---

V. Motivational Interviewing (MI)

Inpatient Psychiatric Settings

The Bagien et al. (2013) RCT is the most directly relevant trial: 135 patients with comorbid substance use admitted to a psychiatric emergency unit received 2 sessions of MI + TAU vs. TAU alone. At 2-year follow-up, the MI group showed a net reduction of 7.3 days of substance use per month (95% CI 1.9-12.6, p < 0.01), suggesting a delayed but substantial benefit from a very brief intervention.[32] Baker et al. (2002) found a single 30-45 minute MI session for psychiatric inpatients with SUD produced modest short-term effects on polydrug use, though effects were not sustained at 12 months.[33]

Treatment Engagement

A meta-analysis by Lawrence et al. (2017) found MI as a pre-treatment intervention significantly increased subsequent treatment attendance, with effects concentrated in non-treatment-seeking populations (OR ~ 5, no heterogeneity).[34] This supports MI's particular value for engaging ambivalent or involuntary patients encountered on inpatient units.

Figure 2 Forest plot: attendance to treatment [Colour figure can be viewed at wileyonlinelibrary.com]

Medication Adherence

Palacio et al. (2016; 17 RCTs) found MI improved medication adherence (pooled RR 1.17; 95% CI 1.05-1.31).[35] For bipolar disorder, Pakpour et al. (2017; N = 270) found 5 sessions of MI + psychoeducation significantly improved adherence scores.[36] The VA/DoD SUD guideline emphasizes using MI style during all therapeutic encounters as a fundamental engagement strategy.[37]

Cochrane Evidence

The 2023 Cochrane review (93 studies, 22,776 participants) found MI showed small-to-moderate benefit vs. no intervention post-treatment (SMD 0.48), weakening over time, with no clear benefit vs. TAU at most time points.[38]

---

VI. Problem-Solving Therapy (PST)

The Hatcher et al. (2011) Zelen RCT (N = 1,094) found that among patients with repeat self-harm history, PST significantly reduced re-presentations (13.5% vs. 22.1%, RR = 0.39, NNT = 12).[39] Turgut & Eskin (2025; N = 39) showed both individual and group PST produced large effect sizes for reducing suicide probability and depression.[40] A 2026 meta-analysis found PST demonstrated a 55% reduction in suicide deaths at 6-12 month follow-up - one of only two intervention types to show significant effects on suicide mortality.[41]

Figure 3 Forest plots of selfharm recurrence (a) and suicide deaths (b) at T2 (> 6 to 12 months).

The VA/DoD guideline describes PST as "brief, easily taught, and usable by various providers".[10] The 2024 JAMA review confirmed PST's effect on depression (SMD 0.64) is comparable to CBT and BA.[30]

---

VII. Psychoeducation

The Cochrane review by Xia et al. (2011; 44 RCTs, 5,142 participants, mostly inpatients with schizophrenia) found psychoeducation significantly reduced non-compliance (RR 0.52, NNT = 11), relapse (RR 0.70, NNT = 9), and readmission (RR 0.71, NNT = 5).[42] Barnicot et al. (2020) confirmed psychoeducation as having the strongest evidence base among psychological interventions for acute inpatients with schizophrenia-spectrum disorders.[43] Vickar et al. (2009) found intensive inpatient-initiated psychoeducation reduced 6-month rehospitalization from 56% to 20% (p = 0.038).[44]

Despite this evidence, a survey of psychiatry trainees found 81-84% reported non-uniform psychoeducation content and delivery, with 98% using unstructured conversation and only 25% using supplemental materials.[45]

---

VIII. Supportive Psychotherapy and Common Factors

Direct RCT evidence for manualized supportive psychotherapy in inpatient settings is sparse - it typically serves as the control condition rather than the experimental intervention.[26] The Massachusetts General Hospital model teaches four key brief inpatient psychotherapy techniques: support, affective experience and expression, chain analysis, and identification of relational styles/maladaptive relational patterns.[46] Qualitative evidence highlights that patients value the "human" therapeutic relationship as the foundation for therapeutic work in acute settings, with psychological formulation providing meaning-making and hope.[47] The finding that no single therapy orientation demonstrates superiority in inpatient settings (Cohen-Chazani et al., 2022) suggests common therapeutic factors - alliance, validation, support - account for much of the benefit.[3]

---

IX. Guideline Recommendations

---

X. Contraindications and Common Pitfalls

Structural pitfalls are the most consequential barriers. Kleiman et al. (2026) identify the fundamental mismatch: outpatient evidence-based treatments assume stable attendance, cumulative learning, and continuity - assumptions that rarely hold in inpatient settings with rapid turnover, frequent cancellations, and diagnostic heterogeneity.[5] Even the briefest manualized treatments often exceed typical lengths of stay.[5]

Clinical contraindications and cautions:

- Acute psychosis with disorganization: Insight-oriented or cognitively demanding interventions (CBT restructuring, PST) are poorly tolerated; prioritize supportive contact, simple behavioral strategies, and psychoeducation[55]

- Severe intoxication or withdrawal: Defer MI and structured interventions until the patient is alert and oriented; SAMHSA recommends providing brief interventions "as early as possible during hospitalization when the patient is alert and oriented"[54]

- Involuntary admission and coercion: The therapeutic alliance is uniquely challenged; Bolsinger et al. (2019) found that coercive admission circumstances, lack of autonomy, and environmental factors (noise, lack of privacy) significantly impair relationship-building. MI spirit (autonomy support, collaboration) is particularly important here[56][34]

- Trauma exposure: Avoid detailed trauma processing during acute crisis; focus on stabilization, grounding, and safety[57]

- Substance use disorder comorbidity: Moderates treatment effects - BCBT-Inpatient's readmission benefit was attenuated in patients with SUD; bipolar disorder patients did not benefit from SPI+ in the Stanley et al. study[11][6]

- Safety plan quality: Mandating safety plans without ensuring quality is insufficient - poor-quality plans may provide false reassurance[8][58]

- No-suicide contracts: Should be abandoned - they have no evidence of efficacy and crisis response planning is significantly superior[9]

Resident-specific pitfalls:

- Attempting multi-session manualized protocols that exceed the patient's length of stay

- Providing unstructured psychoeducation without standardized content[45]

- Neglecting to document and communicate psychotherapeutic interventions to the outpatient team

- Failing to match intervention intensity to patient acuity and cognitive capacity

XIII. Top 10 Bedside Psychotherapy Skills for Inpatient Psychiatry

1. Safety Planning (Stanley-Brown 6-Step Model)

The single most evidence-based brief intervention. Complete all 6 steps: warning signs, internal coping strategies, social contacts for distraction, people to contact for help, professionals/agencies to contact, making the environment safe. Personalize each step; quality predicts outcomes.[6][8]

2. Validation and Therapeutic Alliance

The foundation for all other interventions. Reflect the patient's emotional experience without judgment. In acute settings marked by coercion and loss of autonomy, the "human" relationship is what patients value most.[47][56] Use Linehan's 6 levels of validation: being present, accurate reflection, articulating the unverbalized, validating in terms of past history, validating in terms of present context, radical genuineness.

3. Chain Analysis

Map the behavioral sequence from vulnerability factors through prompting event, thoughts, emotions, urges, behavior, and consequences. Identifies intervention points and builds patient insight. Core to both DBT and the MGH inpatient psychotherapy model.[46][22]

4. Behavioral Activation Scheduling

Collaboratively schedule one concrete pleasant or mastery activity. Start small - even getting out of bed, showering, or walking the hallway counts. Track mood before and after. BA's simplicity and low cognitive demands make it ideal for acutely ill patients.[26][29]

5. Distress Tolerance Skills (TIPP)

Teach one concrete skill: Temperature (ice water on face), Intense exercise (wall push-ups, pacing), Paced breathing (exhale longer than inhale), Progressive/Paired muscle relaxation. These produce immediate physiological down-regulation and are the most immediately applicable DBT skills.[22][20]

6. Motivational Interviewing Spirit

Use OARS (Open questions, Affirmations, Reflections, Summaries) in every encounter. Elicit change talk with the "readiness ruler." Particularly valuable for medication ambivalence, substance use, and treatment engagement in non-treatment-seeking patients.[34][32]

7. Psychoeducation Delivery

Provide structured, diagnosis-specific information about the illness, medications, warning signs of relapse, and when to seek help. Use standardized materials when available. The strongest evidence base of any inpatient psychological intervention for psychosis.[42][43]

8. Problem-Solving in 4 Steps

Define the problem concretely -> brainstorm solutions without judgment -> evaluate pros/cons -> select and plan implementation of one solution. Effective for patients with concrete stressors (housing, relationships, finances) driving the crisis.[39][10]

9. Collaborative Formulation

Develop a brief, shared understanding of why the crisis happened now - linking history, vulnerabilities, triggers, and maintaining factors. This provides meaning-making and hope, and improves staff understanding of the patient's presentation.[47][55]

10. Discharge Preparation and Bridging

Review the safety plan, confirm follow-up appointments, identify the highest-risk period (first week post-discharge), rehearse coping strategies for anticipated stressors, and ensure the patient has crisis line numbers. This is the intervention with the highest potential impact given the extreme post-discharge risk window.[13][15]

---

XIV. Suggested Resident Teaching Handout

"BRIEF THERAPY ON THE INPATIENT UNIT: A Pocket Guide for Psychiatry Residents"

Core Principle: Every patient encounter is a therapeutic opportunity. Even 5-minute interactions can be structured to deliver evidence-based interventions. The goal is not to replicate outpatient therapy but to target crisis mechanisms, build coping skills, and bridge to post-discharge care.[5]

The 4 Transdiagnostic Targets (Kleiman et al., 2026):[5]

1. Emotion dysregulation -> Distress tolerance skills, validation

2. Cognitive inflexibility -> Collaborative formulation, psychoeducation

3. Behavioral inactivity -> Behavioral activation scheduling

4. Life-threatening behaviors -> Safety planning, chain analysis, means restriction

Before Every Encounter, Ask Yourself:

- What is this patient's primary crisis mechanism?

- What is one skill or insight this patient can leave with today?

- What is the discharge plan, and how does today's work support it?

The "3-3-3" Framework for Each Admission:

- 3 assessments: Suicide risk (C-SSRS), substance use (AUDIT/DAST), readiness for change

- 3 interventions: Safety plan, one skills-based intervention matched to diagnosis, psychoeducation

- 3 discharge tasks: Confirm follow-up within 7 days, review safety plan, provide crisis resources

What NOT to Do:

-  No-suicide contracts (no evidence; use safety planning instead)[9]

-  Detailed trauma processing during acute crisis (stabilize first)

-  Unstructured "how are you feeling?" without a therapeutic frame

-  Attempting a full course of manualized therapy in 3 days

-  Assuming psychoeducation happened if it wasn't documented

---

XV. Algorithm: Matching Intervention to Clinical Scenario

Decision Logic:

1. All patients -> Safety plan + psychoeducation + discharge bridging (non-negotiable minimum)

2. Suicidal? -> Add BCBT-Inpatient session if >=4 days of stay; if shorter, prioritize high-quality SPI

3. Self-harm/BPD? -> Chain analysis + distress tolerance skill + DBT skills group

4. Depressed? -> Behavioral activation scheduling (lowest cognitive demand, highest feasibility)

5. Substance use? -> MI session; SBIRT if not yet screened

6. Psychotic? -> Psychoeducation first; brief CBTp formulation if patient is engaged and able

7. Disengaged/involuntary? -> Lead with MI spirit and validation; avoid confrontation

---

Summary

The evidence supports a small-to-moderate benefit (d = 0.24-0.43) of adding psychotherapy to standard inpatient care, with no single modality demonstrating superiority - common therapeutic factors likely account for much of the benefit.[3][1] The strongest evidence for specific brief interventions comes from safety planning (RR 0.57 for suicidal behavior),[7] BCBT-Inpatient (60% reduction in post-discharge attempts),[11] psychoeducation for psychosis (NNT = 5 for readmission), and[42] behavioral activation for depression (SMD -0.78 vs. TAU).[29] DBT skills training appears to be the active ingredient of DBT for reducing NSSI, and MI is most effective for engaging non-treatment-seeking patients.[22][34] The critical gap is that most evidence comes from studies with longer stays than typical US admissions, and the field needs interventions designed specifically for the inpatient context - stand-alone, modular, transdiagnostic, and deliverable by trainees.[5] Every patient encounter, however brief, can be structured to deliver an evidence-based micro-intervention.

## Source: `OPENEVIDENCE RAW FILES TO REVIEW/Child and Adolescent Psychiatry for Adult Psychiatrists_ A Comprehensive Evidence Review.docx`

Child and Adolescent Psychiatry for Adult Psychiatrists: A Comprehensive Evidence Review

Scope and Framing

This review synthesizes the evidence on ten domains of child and adolescent psychiatry most commonly encountered by adult psychiatrists working in emergency departments and inpatient units. It emphasizes adolescents (13-17) while covering the full pediatric range where relevant. The review draws on AACAP practice parameters, AAP clinical reports, systematic reviews, landmark RCTs, and emergency psychiatry consensus statements. It is designed as a resident education and teaching resource.

---

I. Adolescent Psychiatric Boarding

Scale of the Crisis

Pediatric mental health ED visits approximately doubled from 2011 to 2020, rising from 4.8 million (7.7% of all pediatric ED visits) to 7.5 million (13.1%), with suicide-related visits showing the greatest increase (average annual percent change 23.1%).[1] Among youth requiring inpatient psychiatric care, 23-58% experience boarding, with average ED boarding durations of 5-41 hours and inpatient medical unit boarding of 2-3 days.[2] The COVID-19 pandemic dramatically worsened the crisis: prolonged boarding (>=2 midnights) increased by 76.4% in pandemic year 2, with adolescents aged 13-17 disproportionately affected (87.2% increase).[3]

More than 1 in 10 mental health ED visits among Medicaid-enrolled youth lasted >2 days, with striking state-level variation (3-27%).[4] In Massachusetts, 45% of pediatric psychiatric ED visits resulted in boarding >=12 hours, and nearly half of boarding episodes did not result in inpatient admission.[5] In October 2021, the AAP, AACAP, and Children's Hospital Association jointly declared a national emergency in child and adolescent mental health.[5]

Disparities and Risk Factors

Transgender youth board longer with lower admission rates; Hispanic ethnicity is associated with nearly threefold odds of ED length of stay >12 hours; and youth with autism spectrum disorder have higher baseline boarding rates (18.4% vs. 10.3%) that widened further during the pandemic.[3][5][6] Aggressive behaviors increase boarding duration by 193%, and prior psychiatric admissions by 88%.[7]

Harms

The majority of boarding youth report worsening mental health symptoms, with 72.7% reporting increasing anxiety.[8] Only 14% of pediatric hospitalists report that boarding youth receive medication management, and only 18% report psychotherapy access.[3] Parents frequently liken the environment to incarceration.[3] Disposition is often driven by bed availability rather than clinical need - only 56% of youth determined to need inpatient care actually received it after boarding.[5]

Guidelines and Interventions

The AAP 2023 policy statement recommends trauma-informed ED protocols, low-stimulation safe areas, embedded mental health professionals, telehealth consultation, and lethal means restriction counseling.[9] A national Delphi consensus panel (2023) recommended a 24-hour threshold for transferring boarding patients from the ED to an inpatient floor, that pediatric patients should not be cared for in the same space as adults (87% agreement), and that emergency medicine or hospitalists maintain primary ownership with child psychiatry in a consultative role.[10]

Comprehensive hospital-level interventions at one institution reduced mean boarding by 53% (9.1 to 4.3 days) and increased access to acute psychiatry programs.[7] Standardized ED stabilization protocols significantly reduced psychiatric facility admissions (22.6% vs. 58.2%) and increased safe discharges home.[11]

---

II. First-Episode Psychosis in Minors

Presentation Differences from Adults

Approximately 100,000 adolescents and young adults in the U.S. experience FEP annually, with peak onset between ages 15-25.[12] Key developmental differences include: perceptual symptoms (hallucinations) are more prominent in younger patients while delusions and thought disorder increase with age; flat affect is more severe in younger patients; visual hallucinations are more common in children; and delusions are less elaborate.[13][14] Auditory hallucinations are common in children (median 17% of 9-12-year-olds) but most do not signify psychotic disorder.[12]

Early-onset patients have significantly longer duration of untreated psychosis (median 91 vs. 58 days in adults), more prodromal symptoms, and higher rates of premorbid neurodevelopmental difficulties.[15][16] DUP is the strongest predictor of functional outcome at 2-year follow-up in pediatric FEP.[17]

Diagnostic Complexity

A thorough differential is essential: psychotic mood disorders, ASD, intellectual disability, substance-induced psychosis, trauma-related presentations, and medical causes (autoimmune encephalitis, seizure disorders, 22q11.2 deletion syndrome, metabolic disorders) must be excluded.[18][19] Notably, 23.5% of children admitted for first psychotic symptoms had substance-/medication-induced or medically-associated psychosis.[20] Daily cannabis use confers 3.2 higher odds of psychotic disorder, and cannabis-induced psychosis has a 36-46% transition rate to schizophrenia spectrum disorders.[12]

AACAP Practice Parameter

The AACAP Practice Parameter (2001, updated 2013) establishes that EOS is diagnosed using the same DSM criteria as adults and recommends antipsychotic medications as first-line, with SGAs generally favored due to lower EPS risk.[18][21] Clozapine is reserved for treatment-resistant cases after failure of at least two adequate antipsychotic trials.[18] First-episode patients should receive maintenance treatment for 1-2 years after the initial episode.[18]

Coordinated Specialty Care

The landmark RAISE-ETP trial (N = 404, ages 15-40) demonstrated that NAVIGATE (a CSC program including individualized medication management, family education, CBT-based individual therapy, and supported employment/education) produced greater improvement in quality of life and psychopathology, with effects more pronounced with shorter DUP.[22] OnTrackNY increased education/employment rates from 40% to 80% and decreased hospitalization rates from 70% to 10%.[23]

---

III. Adolescent Suicidality

Epidemiology

Suicide is the second leading cause of death for youth aged 10-24, with 59,827 deaths from 2011-2020.[24] The suicide rate among 10-19-year-olds increased 85.3% between 2007 and 2017.[25] During 2020-2021, ED visits for suspected suicide attempts among girls aged 12-17 increased 50.6% compared to 2019.[26] Firearms (51%), suffocation (33.5%), and overdose (5.9%) are the leading methods.[24]

The following figure illustrates the mean annual rates of ED visits and hospitalizations for suicidality among children and adolescents, demonstrating that females have approximately twice the rate of males and rates peak at ages 16-17:

Figure 1 Mean Annual Rates of Emergency Department Visits and Hospitalizations for Suicidal Ideation and Suicide Attempts Among Children and Adolescents Aged 10 to 18 Years, 2016-2021

Screening Tools

The Ask Suicide-Screening Questions (ASQ) is the most validated pediatric suicide screening tool: 97% sensitivity, 88% specificity in the pediatric ED, validated for ages 10-21.[24][28] The C-SSRS provides severity assessment and is recommended by the Joint Commission, with worst-point lifetime suicidal ideation predicting future attempts.[29] The CASSY (computerized adaptive screen) shows similar sensitivity to the ASQ but performs significantly better among patients already presenting with psychiatric symptoms (AUROC 0.72 vs. 0.57).[30]

The USPSTF (2022) found insufficient evidence to recommend for or against universal suicide risk screening in pediatric primary care, creating tension with AAP, AACAP, and Joint Commission recommendations for universal screening.[31]

Safety Planning in Adolescents - A Critical Caveat

A 2025 JAMA Pediatrics meta-analysis (10 studies) - the first dedicated to standalone SPIs in youth - found no association between SPI and reduction in suicidal ideation, suicide-related behaviors, or suicide attempts at 1-6 months.[32] This contrasts sharply with the adult evidence base. Family-based adaptations showed more promising results.[32] MI-enhanced safety planning (MI-SafeCope) for hospitalized adolescents showed significantly higher self-efficacy to refrain from suicidal action and greater likelihood of safety plan use.[33]

Evidence-Based Interventions

DBT-A is the only well-established (Level 1) intervention for reducing self-injurious thoughts and behaviors in youth.[34] The McCauley et al. (2018) multisite RCT (N = 173) found DBT reduced suicide attempts (OR 0.30), NSSI (OR 0.32), and total self-harm (OR 0.33) compared to supportive therapy, though the advantage diminished during 6-12 month follow-up.[35] Long-term follow-up at 12.4 years showed lower odds of suicidal ideation in adulthood (OR 0.16).[36]

The following figure from McCauley et al. shows the trajectory of suicide attempts, NSSI, and self-harm over 12 months, demonstrating DBT's advantage during active treatment:

Figure 2 Changes in Suicide Attempts, Nonsuicidal Self-injury, Self-harm, and Suicidal Ideation

Family-based interventions are classified as Level 2 (probably efficacious) for reducing youth suicidal ideation.[34] The SAFETY program (CBT/DBT-informed family treatment) showed 100% survival without suicide attempt at 3 months vs. 67% for enhanced TAU (NNT = 3).[37]

Means Restriction

For adolescent suicide by firearm, parents owned the firearm 66% of the time for ages 10-14 and 51% for ages 15-19.[38] Only 21.9% of pediatric primary care providers consistently screen for firearms.[39] The AAP, AACAP, and SAMHSA all recommend assessing for access to lethal means and counseling on safe storage.[24]

---

IV. Family Engagement

Evidence for Family Involvement

Family-based crisis intervention (FBCI) in the ED resulted in significantly more suicidal adolescents discharged home safely with outpatient follow-up compared to TAU, with higher family empowerment and no completed suicides.[40] Any family involvement with inpatient staff was significantly associated with attending outpatient follow-up within 7 days (OR 2.79) and 30 days (OR 3.07) after discharge.[41]

A structured psychoeducational group for adolescents with early-onset psychosis and their families reduced ED visits from 39% to 15% at initial follow-up and from 50% to 13% at 2-year follow-up.[42][43] The Cochrane review of family-based interventions for schizophrenia found reduced days in hospital (MD -2.43 days) and probable reduction in relapse.[44]

AACAP Guidance on Family Assessment

The AACAP Practice Parameter for Assessment of the Family (2007) establishes that a family assessment is always indicated in the psychiatric evaluation of a child or adolescent.[45] The clinician begins by identifying family strengths, then defines the problem while observing family interactions. An individual interview with the adolescent is essential, and the clinician must maintain neutrality.[45]

---

V. Consent, Assent, and Confidentiality

Consent Framework

Parents provide informed permission for diagnosis and treatment, with the assent of the child whenever developmentally appropriate.[46] The AACAP Practice Parameter on Psychotropic Medication (2009) requires documenting assent of the child and consent of the parents before initiating medication and at important treatment transitions.[46]

Psychiatric Hospitalization

In practically all states, if a physician determines hospitalization is medically indicated and a parent consents, the minor is admitted - even if the minor objects (Parham v. J.R., 1979).[47] About two-thirds of states allow some minors to independently consent to mental health hospitalization, with minimum ages ranging from no minimum to age 16.[47]

Confidentiality

Confidentiality is essential for adolescent care - adolescents are less likely to seek care or disclose sensitive information without it.[48] Key domain-specific rules:

- Substance use: 42 CFR Part 2 provides strong protections; records cannot be shared with parents without the minor's written consent at federally funded facilities[48]

- Sexual/reproductive health: All states allow minor consent for STI services[48]

- Mental health: ~2/3 of states allow some minor consent; ages vary widely[48]

- Mandatory breach: Required for danger to self or others, abuse, or severe disorganization[12][24]

The 21st Century Cures Act creates significant confidentiality risks through mandated easy access to electronic health information, though confidentiality rights themselves have not been altered.[49][50]

---

VI. Neurodevelopmental Disorders

Disproportionate ED Utilization

Adolescents with ASD have a psychiatric ED visit rate 9.9 times higher than those without ASD or ADHD.[51] The most common presenting complaint is aggression toward others (36.4%), followed by suicidal thoughts and self-injurious behaviors.[52] ASD is an independent risk factor for boarding >=24 hours (OR 1.82).[53]

Diagnostic Overshadowing

Psychiatric disorders occur at least 3 times more often in children with ID than in typically developing children.[54] Symptoms are frequently assumed to be inherent to the underlying disability, leading to substantial underdiagnosis.[54] Behavioral outbursts in ASD/ID may be driven by co-occurring medical issues causing pain (ear infections, abdominal pain), particularly in nonverbal children.[9]

Suicidality Risk

Suicidality risk is elevated and often overlooked: ASD without ID with comorbid ADHD carries the highest suicide risk (attempt OR 7.25; suicide OR 13.09).[55] Suicidality assessment tools have not been validated specifically for individuals with ID or minimally verbal ASD.[24]

Management Adaptations

ASD-specific de-escalation strategies include clear, concrete, short statements; reduced sensory stimulation; lower-volume tone; refraining from physical contact; and consulting families for calming strategies.[9] Children with ASD are significantly more likely to be physically restrained (RR 2.8), managed in seclusion (RR 3.3), and receive medication for behavioral de-escalation (RR 2.8).[56]

Medication Cautions

Risperidone (>=5 yr) and aripiprazole (>=6 yr) are the only FDA-approved medications for irritability in ASD.[57][58] Methylphenidate is effective for ADHD symptoms in ASD but with lower response rates and higher discontinuation rates due to increased adverse events, including behavioral activation.[58][59] The AACAP Practice Parameter for ID states that children with ID/IDD may be more sensitive to medication side effects, and conservative dosing is recommended.[54]

---

VII. Eating Disorder Medical Risk

Hospitalization Criteria

The AAP/SAHM criteria use percent median BMI (%mBMI) rather than absolute BMI, because absolute BMI varies with age and sex during growth.[60] Any one of the following justifies hospitalization: <=75% mBMI, HR <50 bpm daytime, BP <90/45, temperature <96F, orthostatic HR increase >20 bpm, electrolyte abnormalities, syncope, seizures, or acute food refusal.[60]

Atypical anorexia nervosa (significant weight loss but "normal" weight) now comprises nearly one-third of inpatient eating disorder admissions, with comparably significant medical severity to AN in terms of bradycardia and orthostatic changes.[61][62] Weight alone is a misleading indicator of disease severity.

Refeeding: Paradigm Shift

The landmark STRIPED trial (N = 120, ages 12-24) demonstrated that higher-calorie refeeding (2000 kcal/d, increasing by 200 kcal/d) restored medical stability significantly earlier (HR 1.67), shortened hospital stay by 4.0 days, and saved $19,056 per participant - with no increase in electrolyte abnormalities or adverse events.[61] The APA (2023) now recommends initial calorie prescriptions of 1,500-2,000 kcal/d.[63]

The following survival analysis from the STRIPED trial demonstrates the superiority of higher-calorie refeeding:

Figure 2 Survival Analysis of Primary Outcome, Time to Medical Stability, in Participants Treated With Higher-Calorie Refeeding (HCR) vs Lower-Calorie Refeeding (LCR)

Cardiac Risk

Approximately one-third of deaths in AN are attributed to cardiovascular complications.[64] QTc-prolonging medications and electrolyte abnormalities compound arrhythmic risk.[60] Bupropion is contraindicated in AN and bulimia nervosa due to seizure risk.[63]

Monitoring Protocol

Refeeding monitoring requires serum K, Mg, and phosphorus before initiation and every 12 hours for 3 days in high-risk patients; vital signs every 4 hours for the first 24 hours; daily weights; and thiamine supplementation (2 mg/kg up to 100-200 mg/d in pediatrics) before feeding commences.[65]

---

VIII. Pediatric Agitation Management

Guideline Framework

Three key guidelines anchor management: the AACAP Practice Parameter (2002) on prevention and management of aggressive behavior, the AAEP/AACAP BETA Consensus Statement (2019) recommending a multimodal, etiology-driven approach, and the AAP Clinical Report (2023) reaffirming behavioral de-escalation as first-line.[66][67][9]

De-Escalation First

All guidelines uniformly position verbal de-escalation and environmental modification as first-line.[67][9] Pediatric-specific techniques include: physically lowering oneself to the child's height, asking questions rather than giving commands, providing simple single-step instructions, offering choices and distraction, and minimizing stimulation.[68][69] For ASD, provide soothing sensory items (fidget toys, noise-canceling headphones).[69]

Pharmacologic Management

No medications are FDA-approved specifically for acute agitation in children/adolescents. The PEAChY-O RCT (N = 348, ages 9-17) found no significant difference between oral olanzapine and diazepam (61% vs. 57% successful sedation at 1 hour), with ~40% failure rate for both.[66][70] IM olanzapine in a 10-year pediatric retrospective study (N = 285) showed 17% required additional sedation within 1 hour, with low adverse event rates.[71]

Restraint Time Limits

Regulatory requirements differ critically from adults: 1 hour for children <9 years, 2 hours for ages 9-17, vs. 4 hours for adults >=18.[66] Face-to-face evaluation is required within 1 hour of initiation, and reevaluation every 2 hours for patients <=17.[66] The Joint Commission (2025) eliminated separate "physical holding" standards after finding that 63 of 79 reported restraint fatalities among children/adolescents were from physical holding without mechanical devices.[72]

---

IX. Trauma-Informed Care

Prevalence

Trauma exposure is extremely common: 61.8% of adolescents report at least one lifetime potentially traumatic event, and among youth in a psychiatric ED, 52% reported at least one type of trauma exposure.[73][74] An estimated 50-80% of psychiatric inpatients have a history of trauma.[75]

SAMHSA Framework

The SAMHSA model incorporates the "4 Rs": Realizing the widespread effect of trauma, Recognizing how trauma affects clients and staff, Responding by applying trauma knowledge into practice, and Resisting re-traumatization.[76] Six key principles guide implementation: safety, transparency, peer support, collaboration, empowerment, and cultural sensitivity.[77]

Retraumatization Prevention

Seclusion and restraint can trigger or escalate PTSD symptoms, particularly in youth with prior abuse histories.[75] Involuntary hospitalization negatively impacts trust in 75% of youth studied, with many reporting unwillingness to disclose suicidal feelings post-discharge.[78] The Six Core Strategies (6CS) approach reduced seclusion by 17%, seclusion hours by 19%, and restraint by 30% across 43 inpatient facilities.[79]

Evidence-Based Interventions

TF-CBT is the most evidence-supported intervention for pediatric PTSD (g = 1.06 vs. passive controls in a 2025 network meta-analysis of 70 RCTs).[80] The Child and Family Traumatic Stress Intervention (CFTSI) is a brief (5-8 session) early post-trauma intervention that significantly reduced PTSD diagnoses at 3-month follow-up.[81] No pharmacological treatment is approved for pediatric PTSD; psychotherapy remains first-line.[82]

---

X. Psychotropic Prescribing Differences

Antidepressants

Only fluoxetine (>=8 yr) and escitalopram (>=12 yr) are FDA-approved for pediatric MDD.[31][84] The FDA black box warning (2004, expanded 2007) applies to all antidepressants in patients <25 years, based on a pooled risk ratio of 1.95 for suicidal ideation/behavior.[85] However, the NNH for suicidality is approximately 112, compared to an NNT of 10 for depression response, yielding a benefit-to-risk ratio of approximately 11:1.[86] No completed suicides occurred in any pediatric antidepressant RCT.[87] Tricyclic antidepressants are not effective for adolescent depression (unlike in adults) and carry higher lethality risk in overdose.[88]

Antipsychotic Metabolic Risk

Children and adolescents have higher and faster metabolic adverse effects than adults.[89] Weight gain hierarchy from meta-analysis: ziprasidone (-0.04 kg) < aripiprazole (+0.79 kg) < quetiapine (+1.43 kg) < risperidone (+1.76 kg) < olanzapine (+3.45 kg) vs. placebo.[90] The AACAP recommends BMI and waist circumference monthly for the first 3 months, then at 6 months, then yearly, with fasting glucose, lipid panel, and HbA1c at 3 months then yearly.[12]

The following figure from Nicol et al. (2018) illustrates the differential changes in adiposity across three antipsychotic groups in antipsychotic-naive youth:

Figure 2 Change in Adiposity During Initial Antipsychotic Exposure in the Study Participants

Benzodiazepines

No benzodiazepines have FDA approval for pediatric anxiety disorders, and RCTs do not support their efficacy in this population.[92][93] SSRIs are first-line for pediatric anxiety; duloxetine is the only FDA-approved medication for pediatric GAD (>=7 yr).[94]

Off-Label Prescribing

Off-label prescribing is pervasive: excluding ADHD medications, 95-96% of pediatric psychotropic prescriptions are off-label.[95][96] The most common reason is age (72.2%), followed by indication (23.3%).[95]

XIV. Family Meeting Pearls

1. Structure the meeting deliberately. Begin by identifying all attendees and their relationship to the patient. Clarify the purpose and expected duration. The AACAP recommends starting by identifying family strengths and resources before defining problems.[45]

2. Interview the adolescent alone first. An individual interview is essential - adolescents may not disclose suicidal ideation, substance use, or abuse in front of parents. Establish what is confidential and what will be shared before the family meeting.[45][49]

3. Maintain neutrality. Do not side with parents against the child or vice versa. Conflict that emerges during the session provides powerful clinical data about family dynamics.[45][112]

4. Address confidentiality explicitly. Explain what information will and will not be shared with parents. Adolescents are more likely to engage when confidentiality boundaries are clear. Breach only for danger to self/others, abuse, or severe disorganization.[48][24]

5. Involve families in safety planning. Most adolescent safety planning studies that showed benefit included caregiver involvement.[24][32] Parents need specific guidance on lethal means restriction - 66% of adolescent firearm suicides involve a parent-owned weapon.[38]

6. Provide structured psychoeducation. Use the meeting to deliver diagnosis-specific education. Structured psychoeducation for early-onset psychosis reduced ED visits from 39% to 15%.[42] Parents with higher self-efficacy are more likely to follow through on discharge recommendations.[113]

7. Plan discharge collaboratively. Family involvement in discharge planning is significantly associated with outpatient follow-up within 7 days (OR 2.79).[41] Confirm follow-up appointments, review the safety plan, and identify the highest-risk period (first week post-discharge).

8. Assess family functioning. Screen for parental mental illness, substance use, domestic violence, and adverse childhood experiences. Family dysfunction is both a risk factor for the child's presentation and a barrier to treatment engagement.[45]

9. Use MI spirit with resistant families. Avoid confrontation with parents who are angry, dismissive, or in denial. Reflect their concerns, validate their distress, and elicit their goals for their child. Parental distress is common but does not predict engagement - self-efficacy does.[113]

10. Document the meeting. Record attendees, key discussion points, agreements reached, safety plan review, discharge plan, and any confidentiality decisions. This protects both the patient and the clinician.

XVI. Algorithm: Matching Intervention to Clinical Scenario

Decision Logic:

1. Is the patient medically stable? -> If not, medical stabilization first (eating disorder protocol, intoxication management, medical workup for psychosis)

2. Is the patient safe? -> If not, 1:1 observation, safety plan with family, means restriction counseling, de-escalation for agitation

3. Is there a neurodevelopmental disorder? -> If yes, rule out pain/medical causes, modify environment, use conservative dosing, consult family

4. Is there a family available? -> If yes, involve in safety planning, psychoeducation, and discharge planning; family involvement improves 7-day follow-up (OR 2.79)

5. What is the disposition? -> Confirm follow-up within 7 days; review safety plan at discharge; provide 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline number; consider caring contacts

---

Summary

Adult psychiatrists encountering pediatric patients face a fundamentally different clinical landscape shaped by developmental neurobiology, family systems, legal frameworks, and a narrower evidence base. The most critical differences include: use of %mBMI rather than absolute BMI for eating disorders; parental consent plus child assent for all treatment decisions; shorter restraint time limits and stricter monitoring requirements; higher metabolic vulnerability to antipsychotics with olanzapine explicitly cautioned against as first-line by the FDA; no evidence supporting benzodiazepines for pediatric anxiety; and the finding that standalone safety planning lacks demonstrated efficacy in youth, necessitating family-based adaptations.[32][102][66][92][60] The 2021 joint declaration of a national emergency in child and adolescent mental health underscores the urgency of equipping all psychiatrists - not just child specialists - with the knowledge to safely and effectively care for this population.[5]

## Source: `OPENEVIDENCE RAW FILES TO REVIEW/Consultation-Liaison Psychiatry for Inpatient Psychiatry Residents_ A Comprehensive Evidence Review.docx`

Consultation-Liaison Psychiatry for Inpatient Psychiatry Residents: A Comprehensive Evidence Review

Scope and Framing

This review synthesizes the evidence across twelve core CL psychiatry domains most relevant to residents rotating on adult inpatient psychiatry units. It draws on APA resource documents, SCCM/PADIS guidelines, NEJM and JAMA reviews, Cochrane systematic reviews, FDA drug labels, and landmark trials. The focus is on recognition, acute management, and safe psychopharmacology in medically complex patients.

---

I. Delirium: Prevention and Treatment

Epidemiology and Impact

Delirium affects 14-56% of hospitalized older adults, with incidence as high as 80% in ICU patients.[1] It is independently associated with increased mortality, prolonged hospitalization, cognitive decline, and institutionalization.[1] Despite its prevalence, delirium is unrecognized in up to 70% of cases by treating clinicians.[1]

Screening and Diagnosis

The Confusion Assessment Method (CAM) remains the gold standard bedside tool, requiring (1) acute onset and fluctuating course, (2) inattention, plus either (3) disorganized thinking or (4) altered level of consciousness.[1] Brief adaptations include the 3D-CAM (3-minute assessment) and the 4AT (no training required, validated in ED and general medical settings).[1] The CAM-S scoring system quantifies delirium severity and correlates with clinical outcomes in a direct, graded relationship - measures capturing both intensity and duration correlate best with outcomes.[1]

Prevention: The Strongest Evidence

Multicomponent nonpharmacologic prevention is the most effective strategy and remains the cornerstone of delirium management.[1][2] The Hospital Elder Life Program (HELP) - targeting cognitive stimulation, sleep enhancement, early mobilization, hydration, and sensory optimization - reduced incident delirium by 53% (OR 0.47; 95% CI 0.38-0.58) and falls by 62% in a meta-analysis of 14 studies.[1] The ABCDEF bundle (Awakening, Breathing coordination, Delirium monitoring, Early exercise, Family engagement) in ICU settings is associated with less delirium, reduced mortality, and more ICU days without coma or delirium.[3]

The Cochrane review (2021) confirmed that multicomponent nonpharmacologic interventions probably reduce delirium incidence in non-ICU hospitalized patients.[4] There is currently no evidence to support medication use for delirium prevention in non-ICU settings.[2] In ICU patients, dexmedetomidine is associated with a 23% decrease in delirium compared to benzodiazepines for sedation, but showed no difference compared to propofol with light sedation approaches.[3]

Treatment: Pharmacologic Controversy

The evidence against routine antipsychotic use for delirium treatment has strengthened considerably. The landmark MIND-USA trial (Girard et al., NEJM 2018; N = 566) found that neither haloperidol nor ziprasidone differed from placebo in days alive without delirium or coma in critically ill patients.[5] A 2019 systematic review (16 RCTs, 10 observational studies) concluded that current evidence does not support routine use of haloperidol or SGAs to treat delirium in adult inpatients.[6]

Figure 2 Effects of Haloperidol, Ziprasidone, and Placebo on Days Alive without Delirium or Coma, Days with Delirium, and Days with Coma.

The SCCM PADIS guidelines (2018) suggest not routinely using haloperidol, atypical antipsychotics, or statins to treat delirium (conditional recommendation, low quality evidence).[7] A network meta-analysis (Wu et al., JAMA Psychiatry 2019) found haloperidol plus lorazepam provided the highest response rate among examined therapeutic interventions, and ramelteon appeared optimal for prevention.[8]

Key treatment principles:

- Identify and treat the underlying cause (infection, metabolic derangement, medication effect, pain, urinary retention, constipation)

- Implement nonpharmacologic strategies (reorientation, sleep hygiene, mobilization, sensory aids)

- Avoid benzodiazepines except for alcohol/benzodiazepine withdrawal or severe agitation refractory to other measures[1][9]

- Reserve low-dose antipsychotics for severe agitation posing safety risk - use the lowest effective dose for the shortest duration

- Avoid antipsychotics for hypoactive delirium[1]

---

II. Capacity Assessment

The Four-Component Model

The Appelbaum and Grisso framework defines four abilities necessary for decisional capacity (DC): understanding (grasping basic facts about the condition and proposed treatment), appreciation (recognizing how information applies to one's own situation), reasoning (comparing options and inferring consequences), and expressing a choice (communicating a stable decision).[10][11] This model is endorsed by the APA Resource Document on Decisional Capacity (2019).[12]

Key Principles

Capacity is decision-specific and time-specific - a patient may have capacity for some decisions but not others, and capacity may fluctuate.[3][11] Capacity is not determined by diagnosis or cognitive test scores alone.[10][3] The most common psychiatric diagnoses contributing to incapacity are cognitive disorders (54.1%), substance use disorders (37.2%), and psychotic disorders (25%).[12] Among patients >65, the most common neurologic causes are Alzheimer's disease (39.4%) and delirium (19.0%).[12]

Assessment Approach (APA Resource Document)

The APA recommends an integrated approach including:[12]

1. Ascertain the type of capacity concern (informed consent vs. treatment refusal vs. AMA discharge vs. dispositional capacity)

2. Perform a standardized psychiatric interview including neurocognitive workup (cognitive screening, relevant labs, consider neuroimaging)

3. Formulate a psychiatric diagnosis (or document "no psychiatric illness")

4. Have the patient describe the proposed procedure and its risks/benefits/alternatives in their own words

5. Separately address each of the four Appelbaum-Grisso factors

6. Consider using DC-specific instruments (e.g., MacCAT-T) to supplement clinical judgment - these improve inter-rater reliability but are not required as standard of care[12]

7. Comment on whether treatment could change capacity findings (e.g., treating delirium, psychosis, or depression)

8. Describe differential capacity findings (e.g., patient may be able to choose a surrogate even if unable to consent to surgery)

Any physician can evaluate capacity - psychiatry consultation is helpful but the final determination is made by the treating physician.[11]

---

III. Catatonia in Medically Ill Patients

Recognition

Catatonia is far more common than traditionally recognized, particularly in medical settings. Wilson et al. found that among critically ill patients, 3% had catatonia without delirium and 31% met criteria for both catatonia and delirium.[13] The APA Resource Document (2025) recommends using >=4 catatonic signs for diagnosis in critically ill patients, achieving 91% sensitivity and specificity.[13]

Screening and Diagnosis

The Bush-Francis Catatonia Rating Scale (BFCRS) is the recommended screening and severity instrument.[13] The first 14 items constitute a screening tool encompassing all 12 DSM-5-TR criteria; a score >=2 is considered positive and prompts completion of the full 23-item scale.[13] The BFCRS is the only catatonia scale validated in response to the lorazepam challenge.[13]

The Lorazepam Challenge Test (LCT)

The LCT serves as both diagnostic and therapeutic: lorazepam 2 mg IV (1 mg in elderly, children, or those at respiratory risk) is administered, with a >=50% reduction on the BFCRS considered positive.[13] Response may occur within minutes but can take up to 2 hours with oral administration.[13] Lorazepam is effective in up to 90% of acute catatonia cases.[14] Following a positive IV LCT, continued IV lorazepam for 24-48 hours is recommended before transitioning to oral, with doses sometimes required up to 16 mg/day.[14][13]

Differential Diagnosis

The NEJM review (Heckers & Walther, 2023) provides a clinical framework across settings:[14]

- ED: Differentiate from acute psychosis, intoxication/withdrawal (cannabis, cocaine, alcohol, opioids, benzodiazepines), NMS, serotonin syndrome, and autoimmune encephalitis

- Medical unit: Rule out epilepsy, delirium (may co-occur), autoimmune encephalitis, encephalopathy, focal cerebral lesions, and medications

- All settings: Monitor BFCRS severity, vital signs, and creatine kinase

Treatment Hierarchy

1. Lorazepam (first-line) - dose may be titrated up to 16 mg/day[14]

2. ECT - effective in 60-100% of patients, including after insufficient benzodiazepine response; administered bilaterally with effects expected after 4-6 sessions[14]

3. NMDA receptor antagonists (amantadine, memantine) - second-line[14]

4. Antipsychotics - use with extreme caution; after ruling out NMS, SGAs (particularly clozapine) are preferable to FGAs in patients with catatonia and psychosis[14]

---

IV. Steroid-Induced Psychiatric Syndromes

Incidence and Spectrum

Neuropsychiatric adverse effects occur in 5-20% of patients receiving corticosteroids, with the spectrum including depression, mania, anxiety, psychosis, cognitive deficits, and behavioral disturbances.[15] The risk of suicide and suicide attempts is reportedly 7 times higher in patients receiving glucocorticoid therapy than in non-users.[16] Mania and hypomania are the most common early presentations, while depression predominates with chronic use.[15][17]

Dose-Response Relationship

The classic threshold of prednisone equivalent >40 mg/day is associated with increased psychiatric risk, though this threshold is not rigorously validated.[16] The incidence increases with higher cumulative doses and longer duration.[17] Additional risk factors include female sex, older age, and pre-existing psychiatric illness.[15]

Management

- Dose reduction or discontinuation is the ideal first step but often not feasible due to the underlying medical condition[17][16]

- Antipsychotics (particularly SGAs: risperidone, quetiapine, olanzapine) are commonly used for mania, psychosis, and severe irritability, often as co-administered pulses matching steroid pulses[18]

- Mood stabilizers (lithium, valproic acid) have been used prophylactically in patients with prior steroid-induced episodes[15][18]

- SSRIs are less useful for acute pulsed steroid courses due to delayed onset of action[18]

- Clearly document the indication for any initiated pharmacotherapy to avoid confusion with primary psychiatric disorders[18]

---

V. Parkinson Disease Psychosis

Clinical Approach

Management begins with weaning potentially contributing medications in order: anticholinergics -> amantadine -> dopamine agonists -> MAO-B inhibitors -> levodopa (last resort).[19] Rule out delirium and minimize anticholinergic medication use.[20]

Pharmacotherapy

Three main options exist, with critical differences:[19]

- Pimavanserin (Nuplazid): The only FDA-approved medication for PD psychosis; a selective 5-HT2A inverse agonist/antagonist that does not impair motor function. Should be considered front-line where available. Limitations: safety data beyond 6 weeks are lacking, requires specialty pharmacy, and takes 4-6 weeks for full effect.[21][22][20][19]

- Clozapine: Multiple RCTs demonstrate robust efficacy without worsening motor function. However, requires REMS enrollment and regular neutrophil monitoring. Rarely used despite strongest RCT evidence.[22][19][20]

- Quetiapine: Most commonly prescribed in clinical practice despite multiple studies failing to show benefit over placebo. Associated with significant cognitive impairment (SMD 0.60 vs. placebo). Used due to prescribing convenience.[19][22]

All other antipsychotics should be avoided due to risk of worsening parkinsonism and death.[19] All antipsychotic drugs carry black box warnings regarding use in patients with dementia.[19]

---

VI. Transplant Psychiatry Basics

Psychosocial Evaluation

Both the AASLD/AST (2025) and KDIGO (2020) guidelines recommend psychosocial assessment for all transplant candidates.[23][24] Key domains include: adherence history, caregiver support, cognitive capacity for decision-making, active psychiatric disorders, substance use history, understanding of the transplant process, and financial/insurance coverage.[23][24]

No psychiatric disorder is an absolute contraindication to transplantation - even patients with psychotic disorders or serious SUD can have successful outcomes with proper evaluation, treatment, and support.[23] However, KDIGO recommends against transplanting patients with unstable psychiatric disorders or ongoing SUD that affects decision-making or poses unacceptable post-transplant risk (1C recommendation).[24]

Post-Transplant Psychiatric Considerations

- Depression affects 13-40% of post-transplant patients and is associated with 65% higher mortality.[25]

- Non-adherence to immunosuppressants occurs in 25-30% of patients and increases odds of organ loss after kidney transplant (OR 7.1).[25]

- Psychosocial interventions improve adherence by 10-20% over controls.[25]

- Drug interactions with immunosuppressants are critical: calcineurin inhibitors (tacrolimus, cyclosporine) are CYP3A4 substrates - avoid strong CYP3A4 inhibitors (fluvoxamine, nefazodone) and inducers (carbamazepine, St. John's wort)

Standardized Assessment Tools

The Stanford Integrated Psychosocial Assessment for Transplant (SIPAT) and Psychosocial Assessment of Candidates for Transplantation (PACT) are commonly used instruments, though no single tool should determine eligibility in isolation.[23][24]

---

VII. Serotonin Syndrome

Clinical Triad

Serotonin syndrome is characterized by: (1) neuromuscular excitation (tremor, hyperreflexia, clonus - particularly inducible and ocular clonus), (2) autonomic dysfunction (tachycardia, hypertension/hypotension, hyperthermia, diaphoresis), and (3) altered mental status (agitation, delirium, coma).[26][27][28]

Diagnosis

The Hunter Serotonin Toxicity Criteria are the most specific diagnostic tool, requiring a serotonergic agent plus any of: spontaneous clonus; inducible clonus + agitation or diaphoresis; ocular clonus + agitation or diaphoresis; tremor + hyperreflexia; or muscle rigidity + temperature >38C + ocular or inducible clonus.[27][29]

The following diagnostic algorithm from Boyer & Shannon (NEJM 2005) illustrates the Hunter Criteria decision tree:

Figure 4 Algorithm for Diagnosis.

Management (Tiered by Severity)

- Mild (hyperreflexia, tremor, no fever): Discontinue offending agent, supportive care, benzodiazepines[27]

- Moderate (autonomic instability, fever): Above plus aggressive correction of cardiorespiratory and thermal abnormalities; cyproheptadine 12-32 mg/24h (5-HT2A antagonist)[27]

- Severe (temperature >41.1C): Immediate sedation, neuromuscular paralysis, orotracheal intubation[27]

Physical restraints are contraindicated - they enforce isometric muscle contractions contributing to lactic acidosis and hyperthermia.[27] Most cases resolve within 24 hours of discontinuing serotonergic drugs, but may persist with long-half-life agents.[27]

High-Risk Combinations

The most dangerous combinations involve MAOIs + serotonergic agents - 50% of those ingesting an MAOI with a serotonergic agent in overdose exhibit at least moderately severe serotonin toxicity.[29] Moderate serotonin toxicity occurs in ~14% of SSRI overdoses.[29]

---

VIII. Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome

Clinical Features

NMS is characterized by fever, muscular rigidity ("lead-pipe"), dysautonomia, and altered mental status after exposure to dopamine-blocking agents.[30] It is rare (0.01-0.04% of antipsychotic-treated patients) but carries mortality as high as 10% despite advances in recognition.[31] Most commonly occurs within hours to days of medication initiation or dose increase.[32]

Diagnosis and Workup

- CK is the most common laboratory finding, often >1,000 U/L and sometimes >10,000 U/L[32][30]

- Additional findings: leukocytosis, metabolic acidosis, elevated LDH, transaminases, and lactate

- Monitor for complications: rhabdomyolysis, acute kidney injury, respiratory failure, DIC, cardiac arrhythmias[30]

Treatment

The NEJM review (Wijdicks & Ropper, 2024) outlines a tiered approach:[30]

1. Discontinue the offending agent immediately

2. Supportive care: IV fluids, cooling measures, correction of electrolytes (hypocalcemia, hypomagnesemia, hyperkalemia)

3. Airway management: Intubation may be needed for upper-airway rigidity, respiratory muscle involvement, or aspiration risk

4. Dantrolene: Skeletal muscle relaxant reducing calcium release from sarcoplasmic reticulum - commonly used for hyperthermia and rigidity, though no RCTs have conclusively demonstrated efficacy[31]

5. Bromocriptine: Dopamine agonist for moderate-to-severe cases

6. ECT: Considered for refractory cases

7. Dexmedetomidine: For agitation/delirium management to avoid reintroducing antipsychotics[30]

Rechallenge

There is a low but real risk of recurrence after reexposure to antipsychotics.[30] If rechallenge is necessary, wait at least 2 weeks, use a low-potency agent or agent from a different class, start at the lowest dose, and titrate slowly with close monitoring.

---

IX. Serotonin Syndrome vs. NMS: Differential Diagnosis

[27][30]

The critical distinguishing features are clonus and hyperreflexia (serotonin syndrome) vs. lead-pipe rigidity and bradyreflexia (NMS), and the rapidity of onset (hours vs. days).[27][30][14]

---

X. Lithium Toxicity

Therapeutic Index and Monitoring

Lithium has a narrow therapeutic index - toxic concentrations (>=1.5 mEq/L) are close to therapeutic levels (0.8-1.2 mEq/L for acute episodes, 0.8-1.0 mEq/L for maintenance).[35][36] At concentrations >3.0 mEq/L, patients may progress to seizures, coma, and irreversible brain damage.[35]

Clinical Presentation

Early symptoms are often neurological: coarse tremor, drowsiness, lethargy, weakness, agitation, muscle fasciculation, ataxia, and dysarthria.[36] GI symptoms (vomiting, diarrhea), cardiovascular effects (dizziness, syncope, arrhythmias), and renal symptoms (polyuria, polydipsia) are also common.[36] Symptoms may not correlate with serum levels, particularly in chronic toxicity and in the elderly - monitoring must be guided primarily by symptoms.[36]

Risk Factors for Toxicity

- Reduced renal excretion: Renal disease (including lithium-induced), dehydration, advanced age

- Drug interactions: NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors, ARBs, thiazide diuretics (all reduce lithium clearance); metronidazole, tetracyclines

- Medical illness: Any condition causing dehydration (fever, vomiting, diarrhea, reduced oral intake)

- Elderly patients: Medical comorbidities, polypharmacy, age-related renal changes[36]

Management

- Mild toxicity: Dose reduction or cessation, IV hydration, hold interacting medications[35]

- Severe toxicity: Hemodialysis is the treatment of choice - effective and rapid means of removing lithium. Indications include level >4.0 mEq/L, severe neurological symptoms, renal failure, or hemodynamic instability[35]

- Activated charcoal is NOT effective (does not absorb lithium ions)[35]

- Monitor for rebound in serum levels after dialysis due to delayed diffusion from body tissues[35]

- Protect airway in patients with impaired consciousness; correct volume depletion and electrolyte imbalances[37]

---

XI. QTc Prolongation

Risk Stratification

Drug-induced long QT (QTc >=500 ms) occurred in 0.9% of psychiatric inpatients in a 5-year cross-sectional study, with sudden cardiac death in 5 patients and torsades de pointes in 7.[38] Risk factors that significantly increased drug-induced long QT included hypokalemia, HCV infection, HIV infection, and abnormal T-wave morphology - 85.5% of affected patients had >=2 risk factors.[38]

Antipsychotic QTc Risk Hierarchy

A 2024 safety review stratified antipsychotics by QTc risk:[39]

- Higher risk: Ziprasidone, iloperidone, thioridazine, IV haloperidol

- Moderate risk: Haloperidol (oral), quetiapine, risperidone

- Lower risk: Brexpiprazole, cariprazine, olanzapine, clozapine, aripiprazole, lurasidone

Antidepressant QTc Risk

Citalopram shows dose-dependent QTc prolongation: 7.5 ms at 20 mg/day and 16.7 ms at 60 mg/day.[40] Escitalopram shows similar values. The FDA limits citalopram to 20 mg/day in patients >60 years. Safer alternatives include fluoxetine, sertraline, paroxetine, and fluvoxamine.[40]

Management Principles

- Maintain K+ >4.0 mmol/L and Mg2+ >2.0 mEq/L[41]

- Obtain baseline ECG before initiating QTc-prolonging agents; repeat after dose changes

- QTc >500 ms or increase >60 ms from baseline: Discontinue or switch the offending agent

- Avoid combining multiple QTc-prolonging drugs when possible

- Be aware of pharmacokinetic interactions - CYP2D6 inhibition by SSRIs can increase concentrations of co-administered QTc-prolonging drugs[40]

---

XII. Hepatic and Renal Dosing Considerations

Hepatic Impairment

[42][43]

Antipsychotic Hepatotoxicity Risk

A comprehensive narrative review graded antipsychotics by hepatotoxicity risk:[44]

- Highest risk: Chlorpromazine, clozapine, olanzapine

- Moderate risk: Quetiapine, risperidone

- Low-to-moderate risk: Haloperidol

- Lowest risk: Paliperidone, aripiprazole, lurasidone, loxapine (no reports of liver failure)

Renal Impairment

Most antipsychotics are hepatically metabolized and do not require dose adjustment in renal impairment, with important exceptions:[45][46]

- Risperidone/paliperidone: Reduced clearance in moderate-severe CKD; 9-hydroxyrisperidone (active metabolite) undergoes substantial renal elimination - reduce dose by 50% in CrCl <30 mL/min

- Amisulpride: Primarily renally excreted - reduce dose by 50% in CrCl 30-60, by 67% in CrCl 10-30

- Aripiprazole, quetiapine, ziprasidone, asenapine: No significant pharmacokinetic changes in severe renal impairment; no dose adjustment required[46]

- Lithium: Entirely renally excreted - requires dose reduction proportional to GFR decline; contraindicated in severe renal impairment without close monitoring and dose adjustment

- Gabapentin/pregabalin: Renally excreted - require significant dose reduction

- Benzodiazepines: Hepatically metabolized; prefer lorazepam, oxazepam, temazepam (LOT - no active metabolites, glucuronidation not significantly affected by liver disease)

Psychopharmacology in the Medically Complex Patient: General Principles

- Renal disease affects not only urinary excretion but also protein binding, enterohepatic circulation, and drug-metabolizing enzyme activity - even hepatically metabolized drugs may require monitoring[47]

- In cirrhosis, SSRIs plus neuroleptics or antiepileptics predispose to serotonin syndrome; SSRIs plus antiplatelet/NSAIDs increase GI bleeding risk[42]

- Therapeutic drug monitoring is particularly valuable in renal and hepatic disease for drugs with narrow therapeutic indices (lithium, clozapine, tricyclics)[47]

Sertraline | 70% reduction in clearance; significant half-life prolongation | Reduce dose; use with caution | [2]

Haloperidol | PKs unaffected | No specific dose adjustment | [1]

Diazepam | Half-life increased 2-5 (up to 500 h); clearance decreased 50% | Use with extreme caution | [1]

Consult Question | Key Assessment | First-Line Intervention | Critical Pitfall

"Is this delirium?" | CAM or 4AT; review medications, vitals, labs (CBC, CMP, UA, TSH) | Treat underlying cause; nonpharmacologic strategies; low-dose antipsychotic ONLY for severe agitation | Do not treat hypoactive delirium with antipsychotics; do not use benzodiazepines (except alcohol/benzo withdrawal)

"Does this patient have capacity?" | Assess all 4 Appelbaum-Grisso domains specific to the decision at hand | Document each domain separately; identify reversible causes of incapacity | Capacity = competence (legal term); diagnosis alone does not determine capacity; reassess after treating reversible causes

"Is this catatonia?" | BFCRS screening (14 items); >=2 = positive | Lorazepam challenge (2 mg IV); hold antipsychotics | Do not give antipsychotics before ruling out NMS; catatonia and delirium frequently co-occur (31%)

"Steroid-induced psych symptoms" | Timeline correlation with steroid initiation/dose change; rule out delirium | Dose reduction if possible; SGA for mania/psychosis; pulse dosing to match steroid pulses | Mania is more common early; depression with chronic use; suicide risk 7 higher

"PD patient with hallucinations" | Rule out delirium; review PD medication regimen | Wean anticholinergics -> amantadine -> DA agonists; pimavanserin or clozapine if persistent | NEVER use typical antipsychotics or most SGAs - will worsen parkinsonism; only pimavanserin, clozapine, quetiapine are options

"Pre-transplant psych eval" | SIPAT or PACT; assess adherence, support, cognition, SUD, psychiatric stability | Optimize psychiatric treatment; address SUD; identify caregiver | No psychiatric disorder is an absolute contraindication; avoid CYP3A4 interactions with immunosuppressants

"Is this serotonin syndrome?" | Hunter Criteria; medication review for serotonergic agents | Stop offending agent; benzodiazepines; cyproheptadine for moderate-severe | Look for CLONUS (distinguishes from NMS); do NOT use physical restraints; most resolve in <24h

"Is this NMS?" | Fever + rigidity + AMS + CK elevation after dopamine antagonist exposure | Stop antipsychotic; supportive care; dantrolene  bromocriptine for severe cases | Onset is gradual (days); resolution takes days-weeks (unlike SS); monitor for rhabdomyolysis/AKI

"Lithium level is high" | Serum lithium, BMP, CK; assess hydration, interacting medications | Hold lithium; IV NS; hemodialysis if >4.0 mEq/L or severe neuro symptoms | Symptoms may not correlate with levels (especially chronic toxicity); activated charcoal is ineffective; watch for rebound after dialysis

"QTc is prolonged" | ECG; check K+, Mg2+; review all QTc-prolonging medications | Correct electrolytes (K+ >4.0, Mg2+ >2.0); switch to lower-risk agent | QTc >500 ms or >60 ms = high risk
