## Source: `OPENEVIDENCE RAW FILES TO REVIEW/Discharge Planning from Adult Inpatient Psychiatry_ A Comprehensive Evidence Review.docx`

Discharge Planning from Adult Inpatient Psychiatry: A Comprehensive Evidence Review

Scope and Framing

This review synthesizes evidence on discharge planning interventions from adult inpatient psychiatry units, organized around six critical outcomes: suicide, readmission, ED return, homelessness, medication discontinuation, and loss to follow-up. The review is designed for a residency curriculum and QI project, covering all diagnostic populations. Key sources include the VA/DoD 2024 Clinical Practice Guideline on Suicide Risk, the VA/DoD 2023 Schizophrenia CPG, Joint Commission NPSG 15.01.01, SAMHSA resources, Cochrane reviews, and recent practice-changing trials. The review concludes with an evidence-based discharge checklist, risk-stratified transition algorithm, top 20 references, and recommended QI metrics.

---

1. The Post-Discharge Risk Window

The immediate post-discharge period carries extraordinarily elevated suicide risk. A meta-analysis of 100 studies (17,857 suicides, 4.7 million person-years) found the pooled post-discharge suicide rate was 1,132 per 100,000 person-years within 3 months - approximately 100 times the global suicide rate.[1] A focused meta-analysis found the first-week rate was 2,950 per 100,000 person-years.[2] A Finnish population-based study (193,197 hospitalizations for depression) provided granular temporal data: the incidence rate was 6,062 per 100,000 on days 0-3, declining steeply thereafter, with 8.9% of all suicides within 2 years occurring during the first week.[3] A Norwegian case-crossover study confirmed a causal effect of discharge on short-term suicide risk (IRR 6.32 in the first week).[1]

The figure below from Chung et al. (2017) illustrates the temporal gradient in post-discharge suicide rates, with the highest rates in the first 3 months declining over subsequent years.

Figure 2 Suicide Rates According to Duration of Follow-up

Readmission rates are similarly concentrated early: approximately 12-15% of psychiatric inpatients are readmitted within 30 days, with rates as high as 20-25% for schizophrenia.[1] Only ~50% of patients nationally receive outpatient mental health follow-up within 7 days, and ~two-thirds within 30 days.[5]

---

2. Safety Planning Intervention (SPI)

Evidence Base

The Safety Planning Intervention (Stanley & Brown) is a brief, collaborative intervention consisting of six steps: recognizing warning signs, using internal coping strategies, utilizing social contacts for distraction, contacting family/friends for help, contacting professionals/agencies, and making the environment safe.[6]

Stanley et al. (2018) - the landmark VA cohort comparison across 9 EDs (N = 1,640) - found SPI combined with structured follow-up telephone calls (SPI+) was associated with 45% fewer suicidal behaviors (OR 0.56; 95% CI 0.33-0.95; NNT = 44) and more than double the odds of attending >=1 outpatient mental health visit (OR 2.06; 95% CI 1.57-2.71) over 6 months.[6] Mediation analysis showed the protective effect was not mediated by increased treatment engagement, suggesting the safety plan itself was the active ingredient.[6]

ED-SAFE 2 (Boudreaux et al., 2023) - a stepped-wedge cluster RCT across 8 EDs (N = 2,761) - demonstrated that department-wide implementation of collaborative safety planning yielded a 43% reduction in the suicide composite outcome (OR 0.57; 95% CI 0.43-0.74) during the maintenance phase vs. baseline.[7]

The SPIRIT trial (Weinstock et al., 2025) - the first individual-level RCT of SPI - randomized 800 pretrial jail detainees and found a 42% reduction in composite suicide events (IRR 0.58; 95% CI 0.45-0.78) and a 55% reduction in suicide attempts over 12 months.[8]

A meta-analysis of safety planning-type interventions (Nuij et al., 2021; 6 studies, N = 3,536) found RR 0.57 (95% CI 0.41-0.80; NNT = 16) for suicidal behavior, with no significant effect on suicidal ideation.[9] The Doupnik et al. (2020) meta-analysis of brief acute care suicide prevention interventions (14 studies, N = 4,270) found pooled OR 0.69 (95% CI 0.53-0.89) for subsequent suicide attempts and OR 3.04 (95% CI 1.79-5.17) for linkage to follow-up care.[9]

Figure 2 Forest Plots for 3 Study Outcomes: Depression, Linkage to Follow-up Care, and Subsequent Suicide Attempts

Implementation Quality Matters

VA national data show that while 97.9% of mandated patients complete SPI, only 44.2% of all patients screening positive complete an initial plan within 30 days.[1] Critically, higher whole-plan quality (AHR 0.79; 95% CI 0.66-0.95) and fidelity (AHR 0.84; 95% CI 0.71-0.99) are associated with decreased likelihood of future suicide attempt - warning sign quality (Step 1) was particularly protective (HR 0.48; 95% CI 0.30-0.76).[11] However, qualitative interviews found only 44% of veterans recalled creating a safety plan, highlighting the gap between documentation and patient engagement.[12]

Guideline Positions

The VA/DoD 2024 CPG concluded there is "insufficient evidence to recommend for or against" SPI specifically, rating evidence quality as low - yet acknowledged SPI is "consistent with the standard of care in both VA and DoD" and is recognized by the Joint Commission and CARF.[13] The Joint Commission NPSG 15.01.01 recommends collaborative safety planning as an alternative to no-suicide contracts.[14] A cross-sectional study of 346 Joint Commission-accredited hospitals found that only 4.0% met full criteria for implementing all recommended discharge suicide prevention activities.[15]

---

3. Caring Contacts

Landmark Trials

Motto & Bostrom (2001) - the foundational RCT - randomized 843 patients who refused ongoing follow-up care after psychiatric hospitalization to brief letters >=4 times/year for 5 years vs. no contact. The contact group had a significantly lower suicide rate for the first 2 years (1.8% vs. 3.5%; P = .04), with differences gradually diminishing by year 14.[1] This remains one of the only RCTs demonstrating a reduction in suicide mortality with a brief contact intervention.

WHO SUPRE-MISS (Fleischmann et al., 2008) - randomized 1,867 suicide attempters across 5 countries to a 1-hour psychoeducation session plus 9 follow-up contacts over 18 months vs. TAU. Significantly fewer suicide deaths occurred in the intervention group: 0.2% vs. 2.2% (P < .001).[1] A meta-analysis pooling 3 WHO BIC RCTs found OR 0.20 (95% CI 0.09-0.42) for suicide death - the only intervention class achieving statistical significance for suicide mortality.[16] However, generalizability to high-resource settings is uncertain, as TAU in these countries lacked virtually any psychiatric follow-up.[13]

Comtois et al. (2019) - RCT of 657 active-duty service members randomized to 11 caring text messages over 12 months - found a 48% decrease in odds of suicide attempts (9.0% vs. 14.9%; OR 0.52; 95% CI 0.29-0.92) as a secondary outcome, though primary outcomes were not significant.[17]

Reger et al. (2024) - the largest caring letters evaluation (N = 102,709 veterans contacting the Veterans Crisis Line) - found no association between caring letter receipt and suicide attempt incidence (7.7% vs. 7.8%), though caring letters significantly increased healthcare utilization (outpatient mental health HR 1.19; 95% CI 1.17-1.22).[18] This trial differed from earlier studies by targeting crisis-line callers already engaged in care rather than treatment-refusers.

Guideline Position

The VA/DoD 2024 CPG suggests sending periodic caring communications for 12 months following hospitalization related to suicide risk (moderate-quality evidence), noting that a single contact does not influence outcomes - repeated communication for >=12 months is required.[19]

---

4. Rapid Follow-Up Within 7 Days

Evidence for Suicide Reduction

Che et al. (2023) - Korean population-based cohort (76,462 patients) - found follow-up within 7 days was associated with HR 0.82 (95% CI 0.80-0.83) for suicide compared with no follow-up within 30 days, with a gradient favoring earlier follow-up.[7] Fontanella et al. (2020) - US Medicaid youth (139,694 inpatients) - found 7-day follow-up was associated with adjusted RR 0.44 (95% CI 0.23-0.83) for suicide during days 8-180, a 56% reduction.[5]

Evidence for Readmission Reduction

In a Japanese nationwide cohort (N = 48,579), patients with 30-day follow-up had substantially lower 180-day readmission rates (21.7% vs. 37.5%; adjusted RR 0.54).[1] For schizophrenia and bipolar disorder, 30-day outpatient follow-up was associated with modestly lower readmission during days 31-120 (schizophrenia AOR 0.88; 95% CI 0.81-0.96).[1]

Quality Standards

The NCQA HEDIS FUH measure tracks 7-day and 30-day follow-up rates after psychiatric hospitalization.[1] The Joint Commission NPSG 15.01.01 requires written policies for counseling and follow-up care at discharge for patients identified as at risk for suicide.[14] The UK National Confidential Inquiry has proposed an even more stringent 2-3 day follow-up window, noting many patients who die in the early post-discharge period die before their scheduled appointment.[20]

Critical limitation: No RCTs directly test 7-day outpatient follow-up vs. no follow-up for suicide prevention - the evidence is entirely observational and subject to confounding.[5]

---

5. Bridge Clinics and Transitional Interventions

Overall Meta-Analytic Evidence

A systematic review of 9 RCTs found transitional interventions with bridging components yielded OR 0.76 (95% CI 0.55-1.05) for readmission - a trend favoring intervention but not reaching statistical significance.[1] A 2025 meta-analysis of 12 RCTs (N = 3,663) similarly found no overall significant reduction (pooled RR 0.96; 95% CI 0.86-1.08), though subgroup analyses suggested effectiveness was associated with longer intervention duration.[21] Effective components identified across studies include predischarge and postdischarge psychoeducation, structured needs assessments, medication reconciliation, transition managers, and inpatient/outpatient provider communication, with absolute risk reductions of 13.6-37.0% in individually significant studies.[22]

Critical Time Intervention (CTI)

CTI is the best-studied named transitional model - a time-limited (typically 9-month) care coordination intervention. Among 150 previously homeless individuals with SMI, CTI significantly reduced psychiatric rehospitalization at 18 months (OR 0.11; 95% CI 0.01-0.96).[6] Brief CTI (3 months) among adults with a readmission within 30 days was associated with a 30-day readmission rate of 28% vs. 47% in the comparison cohort (adjusted OR 2.83 for readmission in the comparison group).[23] A 2025 meta-analysis of 8 CTI studies found significant small effects on quality of life, homelessness reduction, and positive symptoms.[24]

---

6. Partial Hospitalization (PHP) and Intensive Outpatient (IOP)

As Alternative to Inpatient Admission

The Cochrane review (Marshall et al., 2011; 10 trials) found approximately 23-38% of patients referred for inpatient admission could be treated in a day hospital, with no significant difference in readmission rates (RR 0.91; 95% CI 0.72-1.15), faster symptom improvement, and 20-50% lower costs.[1] A large European multicenter RCT (N = 1,117) found day hospital care was more effective on social functioning at discharge and at 3- and 12-month follow-up.[1]

As Step-Down After Inpatient Discharge

Direct RCT evidence for PHP/IOP specifically as post-discharge step-down care is surprisingly limited. A Medicaid claims study found intermediate service use within 7 days was associated with longer time to readmission (HR 0.71; P = .04) in unadjusted analysis, but this was not significant in propensity-score matched analysis.[21]

---

7. Assertive Community Treatment (ACT)

ACT has the most robust evidence base among transitional care models, supported by >30 controlled studies. The Cochrane review on intensive case management (Dieterich et al., 2017) found ICM significantly reduced hospitalization, with a meta-regression showing higher fidelity to the ACT model was associated with greater reductions in hospital days (coefficient -0.31; 95% CI -0.59 to -0.03).[25] Baseline hospital use was the strongest moderator - ACT works best when participants have high baseline hospital use.[25]

The ACCESS trial (N = 120, schizophrenia spectrum) showed ACT significantly reduced service disengagement (6.3% vs. 23.2%; P = .004), with sustained improvements at 4-year follow-up.[26][27] However, the UK REACT trial (N = 251) found no significant differences between ACT and well-organized community mental health teams, demonstrating that ACT's benefits are attenuated in well-resourced systems.[28]

The VA/DoD 2023 Schizophrenia CPG recommends ACT based on moderate-quality evidence showing decreased hospitalizations, reduced relapse, and improved functional status.[29]

---

8. Crisis Stabilization Units and Crisis Resolution Teams

The Cochrane review of crisis intervention (Murphy et al., 2015; 8 RCTs, N = 1,144) found crisis intervention may reduce repeat admissions, reduced family burden (RR 0.34; 95% CI 0.20-0.59), and increased patient satisfaction.[30] The landmark North Islington Crisis Study (N = 260) found crisis resolution team patients were significantly less likely to be admitted at 8 weeks (OR 0.19; 95% CI 0.11-0.32).[31] A Swiss RCT (N = 707) found home treatment reduced hospital days by 30.4% over 24 months with comparable clinical outcomes.[32] A peer-staffed crisis respite program found $2,138 lower monthly Medicaid expenditures and 2.9 fewer hospitalizations per year compared to matched controls.[33]

---

9. Peer Support

RCT Evidence Is Mixed

The ENRICH trial (Gillard et al., 2022; N = 590) - the largest and most rigorous RCT - found peer support plus care as usual did not significantly reduce 12-month readmission compared to care as usual alone, with no significant effects on any primary or secondary outcome.[21] Engagement was notably low (mean 6.2 total contacts vs. 14 planned).[21]

The CORE trial (Johnson et al., 2018; N = 441) - testing peer-supported structured self-management - found a significant reduction in readmission to acute care within 1 year: 29% vs. 38% (OR 0.66; 95% CI 0.43-0.99).[27] The key difference was the structured, manualized intervention with a personal recovery workbook including relapse prevention planning.

Meta-analyses consistently show small but significant positive effects on personal recovery (SMD = 0.20; 95% CI 0.11-0.29) and empowerment, but no impact on clinical symptoms or service use.[27][34] The Cochrane review (Chien et al., 2019) found very low-quality evidence overall and concluded no firm conclusions could be drawn.[35]

The VA/DoD 2023 Schizophrenia CPG found insufficient evidence to recommend for or against peer support but considers it a "value-based practice" that should be maintained, with >1,100 Certified Peer Specialists employed across the VA system.[29]

---

10. Family Involvement

Family psychoeducation is among the most efficacious psychosocial interventions for relapse prevention. A network meta-analysis (Rodolico et al., 2022; 90 RCTs, N = 10,340) found family psychoeducation reduced relapse from 37% to 10% (OR 0.18; 95% CI 0.12-0.27) at 12 months - superior to most other psychosocial interventions.[1] The Cochrane review found family interventions may decrease relapse frequency (RR 0.55; 95% CI 0.5-0.6) and hospital admission (RR 0.78; 95% CI 0.63-0.98).[19]

Critically for discharge planning, any involvement between family members and inpatient staff was significantly associated with attending an outpatient appointment within 7 days (OR 2.79; 95% CI 1.28-6.08) and 30 days (OR 3.07; 95% CI 1.29-7.32) after discharge.[1] Despite strong evidence, family intervention remains under-implemented in mental health care.[1]

---

11. Medication Access and Continuity

The Magnitude of the Problem

Approximately 70% of patients discharged from psychiatric hospitals discontinue at least one medication within 3 months.[36] Among schizophrenia patients, 58.2% are nonadherent within 6 months of discharge.[1] Patients who do not fill an antipsychotic prescription within the first week after discharge have a 75% higher risk of early rehospitalization (HR 1.75; 95% CI 1.13-2.72).[37]

Meds-to-Beds Programs

A retrospective cohort across 15 hospital units found participation in a discharge prescription program decreased odds of 7-day readmission by 20% and 30-day readmission by 16%.[38] A psychiatry-specific pharmacy-driven transitional care study found 30-day psychiatric readmission/ED presentations of 15.4% vs. 32.4% in controls (P < .001).[39]

Long-Acting Injectable Antipsychotics (LAIs)

A Finnish nationwide cohort (N = 62,250, up to 20-year follow-up) found olanzapine LAI (aHR 0.46), clozapine (aHR 0.51), and paliperidone LAI (aHR 0.51) had the lowest risk of psychiatric rehospitalization.[40] However, post-discharge LAI adherence is poor - only 37% of patients initiated on LAIs during hospitalization demonstrated primary adherence (received another injection post-discharge).[41]

The figure below from Chen et al. (2024) demonstrates that LAI recipients without early discontinuation had the longest time to readmission, while those with early discontinuation had worse outcomes than patients who never received LAIs - underscoring the importance of ensuring outpatient continuation.

Figure 1 Kaplan-Meier Survival Curves of Patients With Psychotic Readmission Events in the 2004-2017 Cohort and 3 Subcohorts

Prior Authorization Barriers

In a national survey of dual-eligible psychiatric patients, 43.3% were unable to obtain clinically indicated medications because they were not covered or approved, and patients with prior authorization requirements had 2.4-3.4 times increased likelihood of adverse events including ER visits, hospitalizations, and suicidal ideation.[43] A 10-state Medicaid study found patients with medication access problems had 3.6 times greater likelihood of adverse events.[1]

---

12. Lethal Means Counseling

Evidence Base

A quasi-experimental study at Kaiser Permanente Colorado found lethal means assessment reduced the risk of suicide attempt or death within 180 days from 3.3% to 0.83% (P = .034) among patients endorsing suicidal ideation.[44] Firearms are used in ~50% of U.S. suicides and are 85-90% lethal per attempt; most suicidal crises are brief (<1 hour in 30% of cases), and fewer than 10% of attempt survivors ultimately die by suicide - meaning delaying access to lethal means during a crisis can be life-saving.[45][1]

Counseling on Access to Lethal Means (CALM) training significantly increases providers' knowledge, confidence, and comfort in discussing means restriction, with sustained effects at 3-month follow-up and increased client receipt of lethal means counseling.[46] CALM is recommended by SAMHSA, the Joint Commission, and JAMA Psychiatry.[40]

Medication Safety at Discharge

A Danish national cohort found 52.5% of all unnatural deaths post-discharge were fatal poisonings, with the greatest relative risk for fatal poisoning by psychotropic medication (IRR 93.7).[47] Prescribing decisions should account for toxicity in overdose - citalopram and venlafaxine are of most concern among antidepressants, and clozapine is approximately 18 times more likely to result in death when taken in overdose than chlorpromazine.[20]

The VA/DoD 2024 CPG recommends lethal means safety as part of routine care for patients at intermediate or high suicide risk.[1]

---

13. Transitions for Patients Experiencing Homelessness

Homelessness is associated with dramatically elevated suicide rates (males aMRR 2.2; females 3.8), with the combination of psychiatric disorders and homelessness producing an aMRR of 19.9 for males.[47] CTI is the best-studied transitional model for this population - an RCT of 150 previously homeless individuals with SMI found CTI significantly reduced homelessness at 18 months (OR 0.22; 95% CI 0.06-0.88), with effects persisting 9 months after the intervention ended.[1] CTI adapted for homeless veterans showed 19% more days housed per 90-day period (P < .002).[48]

Housing First provides immediate access to permanent housing without preconditions. A Canadian multisite RCT (N = 950) found Housing First with ACT participants spent 71% vs. 29% of time in stable housing (P < .01), with improved quality of life and community functioning.[49] The VA's HUD-VASH program uses a Housing First philosophy with permanent supported housing vouchers.[29]

---

14. Transitions for Patients at Risk of Incarceration

Forensic Assertive Community Treatment (FACT) is recognized as a best practice by SAMHSA. The Rochester FACT RCT (N = 70) found significantly fewer mean days in jail (21.5 vs. 43.5; P = .025), fewer hospital days (4.4 vs. 23.8; P = .025), and more days in outpatient treatment (305.5 vs. 169.4; P < .001), with approximately $1.50 return for every $1 spent.[1][31] Mental health discharge planning from correctional settings is now considered a constitutional right per federal court of appeals ruling.[1]

---

15. Evidence-Based Discharge Checklist

Before Discharge (Begin Day 1 of Admission)

- Assess housing status - identify homelessness or housing instability; initiate CTI or Housing First referral if applicable[1][49]

- Identify family/support persons - engage in discharge planning; any family-staff contact doubles odds of 7-day follow-up[1]

- Complete medication reconciliation - verify all pre-admission medications; resolve discrepancies[1]

- Initiate or optimize psychotropic medications - allow adequate time for dose titration and tolerability assessment

- Begin prior authorization process for discharge medications - 43% of patients unable to obtain medications due to coverage barriers[43]

- Consider LAI initiation for schizophrenia spectrum disorders - ensure outpatient injection appointment is scheduled before discharge[40][41]

- Assess for clozapine - verify REMS registration, ANC monitoring schedule, and outpatient prescriber/pharmacy[1]

- Arrange step-down level of care - PHP/IOP referral if clinically appropriate[1]

- Initiate ACT referral for patients with SMI and high baseline hospital use[25][29]

Suicide Prevention Bundle (All Patients with Suicide Risk)

- Complete collaborative Safety Planning Intervention - all 6 steps, personalized, with high fidelity; ensure patient retains a copy[6][11]

- Conduct lethal means counseling - assess firearm access, medication stockpiles, and other means; develop a specific plan for reducing access; provide locking devices if available[44][45][46]

- Limit medication supply - prescribe <=30-day quantities of medications with overdose potential; avoid prescribing high-lethality agents when alternatives exist[47][20]

- Provide 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline information and local crisis resources[14]

- Initiate caring contacts protocol - plan for >=12 months of periodic contacts (texts, letters, calls) post-discharge[1][19]

Day of Discharge

- Schedule outpatient follow-up within 7 days - confirmed appointment with specific date, time, provider name, and location[5][7]

- Warm handoff to outpatient provider - direct communication (phone call, secure message) between inpatient and outpatient clinician[15][22]

- Medications in hand - meds-to-beds delivery or confirmed pharmacy fill before patient leaves; verify insurance coverage[38][39]

- Provide written discharge summary to patient and outpatient provider - include medication list, safety plan, follow-up appointments, and contingency instructions

- Peer support referral - connect with certified peer specialist for structured self-management support if available[27]

- Family psychoeducation - provide education on illness, warning signs, crisis plan, and medication management; schedule family session if not completed during admission[1]

- Transportation arranged - confirm patient has means to reach follow-up appointment and safe destination; discharge homeless patients during daylight hours[1]

Post-Discharge (First 30 Days)

- Caring contact within 48-72 hours - phone call or text from treatment team[6][19]

- Verify follow-up attendance - if missed, initiate outreach within 24 hours

- Medication adherence check - pharmacy fill verification or patient contact

- Safety plan review at first outpatient visit - update as needed[11]

- Ongoing caring contacts - per protocol for >=12 months[19]

---

16. Risk-Stratified Transition Algorithm

Tier 1: Standard Risk (No Active Suicidality, Stable Housing, Engaged Supports)

- Outpatient follow-up within 7 days

- Safety plan if any history of suicidal ideation

- Medication reconciliation and >=7-day supply

- Written discharge instructions with crisis resources

- Single caring contact at 48-72 hours

Tier 2: Elevated Risk (Recent Suicidal Ideation, Limited Supports, Prior Readmission)

- All Tier 1 interventions PLUS:

- Collaborative SPI with lethal means counseling

- Step-down to PHP/IOP if available

- Warm handoff to outpatient provider (direct clinician-to-clinician communication)

- Meds-to-beds with prior authorization completed

- Caring contacts protocol (>=monthly  12 months)

- Family engagement in discharge planning

- Peer support referral

Tier 3: High Risk (Recent Suicide Attempt, SMI with High Utilization, Homelessness, Justice Involvement)

- All Tier 1 and 2 interventions PLUS:

- Follow-up within 48-72 hours (bridge clinic or home visit)

- ACT team referral for SMI with >=2 hospitalizations in past year

- CTI referral for patients experiencing homelessness

- FACT referral for justice-involved patients with SMI

- LAI initiation during hospitalization with confirmed outpatient injection appointment

- Housing First/HUD-VASH referral

- Caring contacts protocol (weekly  4 weeks, then monthly  12 months)

- Consider crisis stabilization unit as step-down if available

- Coordinate with probation/parole if applicable

Escalation Triggers (Any Tier -> Higher Tier)

- Missed first follow-up appointment -> immediate outreach + escalate to Tier 2 or 3

- Medication non-fill within 7 days -> pharmacy outreach + clinician notification

- New suicidal ideation reported on caring contact -> same-day clinical assessment

- Loss of housing -> CTI/Housing First referral

- Arrest/incarceration -> coordinate with jail mental health services

18. Metrics a Residency Program Should Track

Process Metrics (Discharge Quality)

Outcome Metrics

Balancing Metrics (To Detect Unintended Consequences)

Recommended Reporting Cadence

- Monthly: Process metrics (safety plan completion, lethal means counseling, 7-day appointment scheduling, medications in hand)

- Quarterly: Outcome metrics (readmission rates, follow-up attendance, medication fill rates)

- Annually: Suicide attempts/deaths, trend analysis, comparison to national benchmarks

- Per event: Root cause analysis for any post-discharge suicide death within 30 days; sentinel event review per Joint Commission requirements

## Source: `OPENEVIDENCE RAW FILES TO REVIEW/Family Involvement and Family Interventions in Adult Inpatient Psychiatry_ A Comprehensive Evidence Review.docx`

Family Involvement and Family Interventions in Adult Inpatient Psychiatry: A Comprehensive Evidence Review

---

1. Scope and Framing

This review synthesizes the evidence base for family involvement in adult inpatient psychiatric care, spanning landmark randomized controlled trials, Cochrane reviews, network meta-analyses, and major guideline recommendations. The focus is on schizophrenia spectrum disorders and bipolar disorder - the two conditions with the deepest evidence base for family interventions - though principles apply broadly across serious mental illness (SMI). The review covers family psychoeducation, structured family meetings, relapse prevention, caregiver burden, expressed emotion, confidentiality frameworks, communication strategies, discharge planning, and brief interventions feasible during short admissions. It concludes with practical tools for clinical implementation: a top-20 paper list, a family meeting structure, resident scripts, teaching pearls, and a suggested family handout.

---

2. The Evidence Base: Landmark Trials and Foundational Research

2.1 Expressed Emotion - The Theoretical Foundation

The entire field of family intervention in psychiatry rests on the expressed emotion (EE) construct, first described by Brown and colleagues in 1962, who demonstrated that the emotional climate of the family environment predicted schizophrenia relapse.[1] The Butzlaff & Hooley (1998) meta-analysis of 27 studies confirmed that EE is a significant and robust predictor of relapse, with the relationship strongest for patients with chronic illness and extending transdiagnostically to mood disorders and eating disorders.[2] A p-curve analysis later verified the integrity of this literature, confirming no evidence of publication bias.[3]

The Bebbington & Kuipers (1994) aggregate analysis of 25 studies (1,346 cases) worldwide found the EE-relapse association was "overwhelming" and maintained regardless of geography, with high contact with a high-EE relative increasing relapse risk while medication and EE operated as independent predictors.[4] An updated 2021 meta-analysis (33 prospective cohort studies, 2,284 patients) quantified the effect: global high-EE predicted early relapse with OR 4.87 (95% CI 3.22-7.36), while higher warmth was protective (OR 0.35, 95% CI 0.15-0.85).[5] Critical comments are the strongest predictor of relapse, associated with higher rehospitalization rates and intensification of positive symptoms over 20-year follow-up.[6]

2.2 Landmark RCTs in Schizophrenia

The first generation of family intervention trials in the 1980s established the evidence base that has since been replicated over 100 times worldwide:

Falloon et al. (1982, NEJM) - This landmark RCT (N=36) compared at-home behavioral family therapy (psychoeducation + problem-solving skills training) with clinic-based individual supportive care. At 9 months, 6% of family-treated patients relapsed versus 44% in the individual treatment group, with family-treated patients averaging 0.83 hospital days versus 8.39 days for controls.[7]

Leff et al. (1982) - This RCT (N=24 families) selected high-risk patients in high contact with high-EE relatives. The experimental group received education about schizophrenia, a relatives' group, and family sessions. Relapse rate was 9% in the experimental group versus 50% in controls (P=0.04). In families where therapeutic aims were achieved (73%), no patient relapsed.[8] Two-year follow-up combining data from a subsequent trial showed patients receiving any social intervention had a relapse rate of 40% versus 75% for controls.[9][10]

Anderson, Hogarty & Reiss (1980/1986) - Developed the psychoeducational model aimed at diminishing relapse by de-intensifying the family environment, reflecting the vulnerability-stress framework. The Strachan (1986) review confirmed that this program, along with Falloon, Goldstein, and Leff, all demonstrated "very significant decreases in relapse rates" when combined with neuroleptic medication.[11][12]

Tarrier et al. (1988, Salford Trial) - This RCT allocated high-EE families to behavioral intervention, education only, or routine treatment. Relapse rates over 9 months were significantly lower in the behavioral intervention groups, with reduction of hostility occurring only in those groups.[13]

McFarlane et al. (1995) - Multifamily Groups (MFGs) - This three-way comparison RCT found psychoeducational MFGs averaged 12.5-14% relapse per year and were significantly more effective than single-family format in extending remission.[14] McFarlane's subsequent review summarized that across >100 outcome studies, meta-analyses put relapse rate reduction at 50-60% over treatment as usual, and MFGs were endorsed by SAMHSA/CMHS as one of six evidence-based practices for chronic mental illness.[15][16]

2.3 Bipolar Disorder: Family-Focused Therapy (FFT)

Miklowitz et al. (2000) - The first major FFT RCT (N=101) randomized bipolar patients to 21 sessions of FFT (9 months) versus 2-session crisis management, all on mood stabilizers. FFT patients had fewer relapses and longer delays before relapse, with effects most dramatic among patients from high-EE families.[17]

Rea et al. (2003) - N=53 recently hospitalized bipolar manic patients randomized to 9-month FFT versus individually focused treatment. Over 2 years, FFT patients were less likely to be rehospitalized and experienced fewer mood disorder relapses.[18]

Miklowitz et al. (2003, Arch Gen Psychiatry) - Two-year follow-up RCT showing FFT significantly prolonged time to relapse compared with crisis management plus medication.[19]

Miklowitz et al. (2021, JAMA Psychiatry NMA) - This network meta-analysis of 39 RCTs (3,863 participants) found adjunctive manualized psychotherapies reduced recurrence vs. control (OR 0.56, 95% CI 0.43-0.74); family/group-format psychoeducation was the standout for recurrence (OR 0.12, 0.02-0.94), and family/conjoint therapy improved treatment retention (OR 0.46, 0.26-0.82) and helped stabilize depressive symptoms (SMD -0.46, not significant).[20]

---

3. Cochrane Reviews and Major Meta-Analyses

3.1 Cochrane Reviews

[21][22][1][23]

3.2 Network Meta-Analyses

The Rodolico et al. (2022, Lancet Psychiatry) network meta-analysis - the first to compare 11 different family intervention models across 90 RCTs (10,340 participants) - represents the most comprehensive evidence synthesis to date. Family psychoeducation alone achieved a 10% relapse rate at 12 months versus 37% with treatment as usual (OR 0.18, 95% CI 0.12-0.27), ranking first in most sensitivity analyses. Critically, interventions comprising <=2 sessions were ineffective, establishing a minimum dose threshold.[24]

The Bighelli et al. (2021, Lancet Psychiatry) NMA of 72 RCTs (10,364 participants) examining all psychosocial interventions for relapse prevention found family interventions among the most efficacious (OR 0.35, 95% CI 0.24-0.52), but notably only after 12 months - not at 6 months - suggesting these interventions need time to take effect.[25]

For first-episode psychosis, the Camacho-Gomez & Castellvi (2020) meta-analysis of 11 RCTs (1,360 patients) found family intervention reduced relapse (RR=0.42, 95% CI 0.29-0.61), hospitalization days (MD=-3.31 days), psychotic symptoms (SMD=-0.68), and increased functionality (SMD=1.36).[26]

---

4. Caregiver Burden

4.1 Prevalence and Impact

Caregiver burden in SMI is pervasive: approximately 51% of caregivers experience mild-to-moderate burden and 34% experience high or severe burden, with nearly half showing psychological distress.[27] Caregivers of schizophrenia patients report mean Zarit Burden Interview scores of 49.68 (15.03), indicating moderate-to-severe burden.[28] Approximately 37% of SMI caregivers show post-traumatic stress symptoms, and 15% meet full PTSD diagnostic criteria - compared to 0% among caregivers of patients with chronic medical illness.[29] A systematic review of 28 studies (6,166 caregivers) found that burden and psychological functioning were comparable across schizophrenia and bipolar disorder; symptoms and functional difficulties affected caregivers more than diagnosis per se.[30]

4.2 Interventions That Reduce Caregiver Burden

The Chien et al. (2024) Cochrane review found family-based interventions reduced short-term caregiver burden with moderate-certainty evidence (MD -5.84, 95% CI -6.77 to -4.92; 8 studies, 563 participants).[22] The Gleeson et al. (2025) meta-analysis of 36 RCTs in early psychosis found significant effects for carer burden (Hedges g = -0.68), critical comments (g = -0.81), and emotional overinvolvement (g = -0.92).[31] A meta-analysis of psychoeducation for carers (32 RCTs, 2,858 carers) found psychoeducation reduced perceived burden (SMD -0.434) and global morbidities (SMD -0.230).[32]

The figure below from the Perlick et al. (2018) RCT illustrates the trajectory of caregiver depression and mental health functioning scores, showing sustained between-group differences favoring Family-Focused Treatment for Health Promoting Intervention (FFT-HPI) at post-treatment and 6-month follow-up.

Figure 2 Mean caregiver depression and mental health scores over time. CES D, Center for Epidemiologic Studies Depression Scale; SF  MCS , SF 36 Mental Component Summary. a Higher scores indicate poorer symptoms/functioning. b Higher scores indicate better health status

4.3 Measurement Tools

The Zarit Burden Interview (ZBI) is the most widely used caregiver burden instrument globally, with excellent internal consistency (Cronbach's  = 0.89-0.91).[28][34] The 22-item version uses a 5-point Likert scale (total 0-88), with thresholds of 8-17 (moderate), 18-32 (high), and >32 (severe burden).[35] The Caregiver Burden Inventory (CBI) is a 24-item, five-subscale multidimensional instrument capturing time-dependence, developmental, physical, social, and emotional burden.[36][37]

5. Guideline Recommendations

5.1 Summary of Major Guidelines

[38][39][40][41][42][43]

5.2 The Implementation Gap

Despite this strong evidence base and universal guideline endorsement, family involvement remains dramatically under-implemented, with implementation rates varying from 0% to 53% across settings.[44][38] A scoping review of 46 articles identified key barriers: organizational culture not supportive of family work, clinician uncertainty about confidentiality, absence of standardized procedures, patients declining involvement due to privacy concerns, and staff time constraints.[44] Facilitators include whole-team coordinated effort, training and ongoing supervision, standardization of family involvement practices, and proactively recommending family services as standard care rather than opt-in.[45][46]

---

6. Confidentiality and Consent

6.1 HIPAA Framework

Under HIPAA, covered entities may disclose limited health information to a relative, friend, or designated person without written authorization, provided the patient is informed in advance and has the opportunity to agree or object. Disclosable information is limited to information directly relevant to the person's involvement in care or payment, or notification of location, general condition, or death.[47] If the patient is incapacitated or in an emergency, the entity may disclose information directly relevant to the person's involvement if it reasonably believes disclosure is in the patient's best interests.[47] Psychotherapy notes receive heightened protection and cannot be disclosed without specific authorization.[48]

6.2 Practical Framework: Listening vs. Disclosing

A critical practical distinction: clinicians can receive information from families without violating confidentiality - listening is not disclosing. The distinction between sharing information with families (requires consent or HIPAA exception) and receiving information from families (generally permissible) is the most important practical framework for navigating this tension.[49][50] A scoping review identified four categories of ethical challenges, including the phenomenon of clinicians using confidentiality as a "smokescreen" to avoid the complexity of family involvement.[50] When professionals gained competence in family involvement through training, this led to vital changes in how they interpreted and practiced confidentiality.[49]

---

7. Communication Frameworks

7.1 Motivational Interviewing with Families

Motivational Interviewing for Loved Ones (MILO) - A pilot RCT (N=40 caregivers of early psychosis patients) tested a brief 5-hour psychoeducational MI training for caregivers, showing large effect sizes (d=1.08-1.43) for caregiver wellbeing, self-efficacy, family conflict, and expressed emotion.[51] Teaching MI to parents of young adults with schizophrenia and cannabis use was feasible, with parents showing significantly greater MI adherence, competence, and empathy expression.[52] The VA/DoD guidelines recommend MI techniques to engage patients in family services by exploring the role they want their family to play in recovery.[40]

7.2 Open Dialogue

The Finnish family-oriented crisis intervention approach emphasizing immediate response, social network involvement, and dialogical practice has shown promising observational results. A 19-year register-based cohort study (N=108 OD patients vs. N=1,763 controls) found significantly lower durations of hospital treatment, disability allowances, and neuroleptic use in the OD group, though the observational design limits causal inference.[53] The ODDESSI multi-site cluster RCT in England is currently testing OD versus TAU.[54]

7.3 LEAP (Listen, Empathize, Agree, Partner)

The LEAP method by Amador is widely used clinically for engaging patients with anosognosia, building on research showing that 32.7% of schizophrenia patients lack awareness of illness.[55] However, formal RCT evidence specifically evaluating LEAP as a standalone communication intervention was not identified in the literature. It remains a clinical practice framework rather than an evidence-based intervention per se.

8. Brief Family Interventions Feasible During Short Admissions

Given average inpatient psychiatric stays of 5-7 days, several brief models have evidence supporting feasibility:

Veteran-Centered Brief Family Consultation (VCBFC) - A 1-3 session intervention (maximum 5 sessions) designed to integrate family/chosen supports into the recovery process, endorsed by the VA/DoD 2023 guidelines as a first step in assessment or treatment planning and a bridge to more intensive family therapies.[40]

Short Therapeutic Conversation Intervention (Calgary Model-based) - A controlled before-and-after study (N=136 intervention, N=148 control) found that 2-5 therapeutic conversations delivered by trained nurses during acute psychiatric admission led to significantly higher perceived cognitive and emotional support from nurses.[57]

Brief Family Strengths-Oriented Therapeutic Conversation (FAM-SOTC) - A quasi-experimental study (N=61 dyads) showed this brief intervention for inpatients with schizophrenia and their caregivers produced statistically significant improvements in symptom severity, family coping, and caregiver burden at 1- and 3-month follow-up.[58]

Carer Involvement Intervention (East London) - A feasibility study found structured carer involvement could be delivered within the first week of admission in 53% of consenting patients, facilitating a three-way collaborative approach. Main barriers included staff/carer unavailability, consent withdrawal, and early discharge.[59]

Important caveat: The Cochrane review of brief family intervention for schizophrenia (Okpokoro et al., 2014) found only 4 RCTs (N=163) with very low quality evidence, and results were inconclusive for relapse and hospitalization outcomes.[1] The Rodolico et al. (2022) NMA confirmed that interventions comprising <=2 sessions were ineffective for relapse prevention.[24] This suggests that inpatient family meetings should be conceptualized as the initiation of a longer-term family intervention rather than a standalone treatment.

---

9. Discharge Planning with Families

Family involvement in discharge planning is strongly associated with improved post-discharge outcomes. Haselden et al. (2019) found that any family-staff involvement during psychiatric hospitalization was associated with attending an outpatient appointment within 7 days (OR 2.79, 95% CI 1.28-6.08) and 30 days (OR 3.07, 95% CI 1.29-7.32) after discharge.[60] An earlier study found family involvement more than tripled the odds of successful linkage to outpatient care.[61]

The VA/DoD guidelines recommend the following target areas when collaborating with families for discharge: (1) understanding the diagnosis, (2) setting realistic goals, (3) supporting recovery, and (4) preparing for crisis - including recognizing early symptoms/triggers, developing a Wellness Recovery Action Plan, and planning for mental health emergencies.[41]

A multi-country qualitative study (55 service users, 6 European countries) emphasized that discharge planning should include structured plans, coping strategies, self-monitoring techniques, and close contact with community services, with support from peers and family members considered critical.[62]

---

10. Peer Family Support: NAMI Programs

NAMI Family-to-Family (FTF) - A free, 8-session peer-taught educational program designated an evidence-based practice by the National Registry of Evidence-Based Practices.[63] An RCT (N=318) found FTF participants had significantly greater improvements in problem-focused coping, empowerment, and illness knowledge.[64] Earlier studies found reduced subjective burden (p<0.01) and increased empowerment (p<0.01), with benefits sustained at 6-month follow-up.[65][66] The VA/DoD guidelines list NAMI FTF, NAMI Homefront, and the Support and Family Education Model (SAFE) as recommended resources.[41][40]

12. Family Meeting Structure for Inpatient Psychiatry

Recommended Structure: The 30-Minute Inpatient Family Meeting

Pre-Meeting (5 minutes)

- Review chart for consent status, safety concerns, and contraindications (abuse, trauma, custody disputes, financial exploitation)[40]

- Confirm patient has agreed to family participation and clarify what may/may not be shared

- Identify attendees and their relationship to the patient

- Review the "listening vs. disclosing" framework with the team

Opening Phase (5 minutes)

- Introductions and role clarification

- Set the agenda collaboratively: "We have about 30 minutes. What is most important for us to discuss today?"

- Establish ground rules: one person speaks at a time; the goal is understanding, not blame

Information Gathering Phase (10 minutes)

- Elicit the family's perspective on the current crisis and timeline of events

- Ask about prior episodes, what has helped before, and what has not

- Assess the home environment, stressors, and support systems

- Screen for expressed emotion patterns (criticism, hostility, emotional overinvolvement) without labeling them

Psychoeducation and Planning Phase (10 minutes)

- Provide brief, jargon-free illness education tailored to the family's knowledge level

- Discuss the treatment plan, medications, and expected course

- Introduce relapse prevention concepts: early warning signs, triggers, action plan

- Discuss discharge plan: outpatient appointments, medication management, crisis contacts

- Provide written materials (see handout below)

Closing Phase (5 minutes)

- Summarize key points and action items

- Ask: "What questions do you still have?"

- Provide family resources: NAMI Family-to-Family, NAMI helpline (1-800-950-NAMI), local support groups

- Schedule follow-up meeting if admission continues

- Document the meeting in the chart

---

13. Resident Scripts

Script 1: Opening the Family Meeting

> "Thank you for coming in today. I'm Dr. [Name], one of the physicians caring for [Patient]. Before we begin, I want to acknowledge that having a loved one in the hospital is stressful, and your perspective is important to us. I'd like to hear from you about what's been happening, share some information about [Patient]'s treatment plan, and talk about next steps together. [Patient] has agreed to this meeting and to our discussing [specify scope]. Is there anything specific you'd like to make sure we cover today?"

Script 2: Navigating Confidentiality

> "I want to be transparent about how confidentiality works. [Patient] has given permission for us to discuss [specific topics]. For anything outside that scope, I'm not able to share details - but I want you to know that I can always listen. Anything you want to tell me about what you've observed or what concerns you - I welcome that information, and it helps us provide better care. You don't need anyone's permission to share your observations with us."

Script 3: Addressing Expressed Emotion (Without Labeling)

> "Caring for someone with [diagnosis] is incredibly demanding, and it's natural to feel frustrated, worried, or even angry at times. Research shows that the emotional climate at home - how much stress and tension there is - actually affects recovery. That's not about blame; it's about understanding that everyone in the family is affected, and everyone deserves support. Let's talk about what's been hardest for you and what might help."

Script 4: Psychoeducation (Schizophrenia)

> "[Diagnosis] is a brain-based illness - it's not caused by bad parenting or personal weakness. It affects how the brain processes information, which is why [Patient] may experience [symptoms]. The good news is that with the right combination of medication and support, most people improve significantly. Research shows that when families are involved in treatment and learn about the illness, relapse rates drop by about half. Your involvement matters enormously."

Script 5: Psychoeducation (Bipolar Disorder)

> "Bipolar disorder involves episodes of mood changes - sometimes highs, sometimes lows - that go beyond normal mood variation. It's a medical condition with a strong genetic component. Medication is the foundation of treatment, but research shows that family-focused therapy - where families learn communication skills and problem-solving together - is one of the most effective additions to medication. The strongest evidence we have shows it can reduce the chance of another episode by about 70%."

Script 6: Discharge Planning with Family

> "As we prepare for discharge, I want to make sure we have a solid plan together. Let's talk about three things: First, the outpatient appointments and medications. Second, early warning signs to watch for - what would tell you that [Patient] might be heading toward another episode? And third, what to do if that happens - who to call, where to go. Having this plan in place before discharge makes a real difference in preventing rehospitalization."

Script 7: When the Patient Declines Family Involvement

> "I understand [Patient] has asked that we not involve family at this time, and we respect that decision. I do want you to know that you can still reach out to us - you can share information or concerns, and we'll listen. I'd also encourage you to seek support for yourself. NAMI's Family-to-Family program is free and peer-led, and many families find it helpful. Here's the number: 1-800-950-NAMI."

---

14. Teaching Pearls

1. The NNT=7 pearl: Family intervention for schizophrenia has an NNT of 7 for relapse prevention - comparable to statins for cardiovascular events. This is one of the most effective interventions in all of psychiatry.[21]

2. The 50% rule: Across >100 RCTs, family interventions reduce relapse rates by approximately 50% compared to treatment as usual.[15][67]

3. The dose threshold: Interventions with <=2 sessions are ineffective. The minimum effective dose appears to be approximately 6-10 sessions over >=3 months. Simple psychoeducation paradoxically outperforms more complex interventions, possibly because complexity creates barriers to implementation.[24]

4. The 12-month lag: Family interventions typically do not show significant relapse prevention effects at 6 months - only after 12 months. This means the inpatient meeting is planting a seed, not harvesting a crop.[25]

5. Listening is not disclosing: The single most important confidentiality concept. Clinicians can always receive information from families without violating HIPAA. This reframe transforms the confidentiality barrier from a wall into a one-way door.[49][50]

6. EE is modifiable: High expressed emotion is not a fixed trait. Family interventions can shift families from high to low EE (RR 3.90 for shift to low EE with intervention).[22][5]

7. Bipolar family work matters: In the Miklowitz 2021 NMA, adjunctive psychotherapies cut recurrence overall (OR 0.56, 0.43-0.74); family/group-format psychoeducation was strongest for recurrence (OR 0.12), and family/conjoint therapy improved treatment retention (OR 0.46) - family involvement is a high-value adjunct alongside medication.[20]

8. Family involvement triples outpatient follow-up: Any family-staff contact during hospitalization is associated with 3 the odds of attending outpatient appointments within 7 and 30 days post-discharge.[60]

9. Caregivers are hidden patients: 37% of SMI caregivers show PTSD symptoms; 15% meet full diagnostic criteria. Caregiver burden is comparable across schizophrenia and bipolar disorder.[29][30]

10. The implementation paradox: Despite being one of the most evidence-based interventions in psychiatry, family involvement rates range from 0-53%. The most common barrier is not patient refusal - it is clinician avoidance, often rationalized through confidentiality concerns.[44][49]

---

15. Suggested Family Handout

Understanding Your Loved One's Illness: A Guide for Families

What is happening?

Your family member has been admitted to the hospital for treatment of a psychiatric illness. This can be a frightening and confusing time. This handout provides basic information to help you understand what is happening and how you can help.

Key facts about serious mental illness:

- Mental illnesses like schizophrenia and bipolar disorder are brain-based medical conditions - they are not caused by bad parenting, personal weakness, or moral failing

- These conditions are treatable. With the right combination of medication and support, most people improve significantly

- Research consistently shows that family involvement in treatment reduces the chance of relapse by about 50%

- Your involvement matters - it is one of the most powerful factors in your loved one's recovery

What you can do right now:

- [yes] Attend family meetings when offered - ask the treatment team when the next one is scheduled

- [yes] Share your observations with the treatment team - you know your loved one best

- [yes] Ask questions - there are no bad questions

- [yes] Take care of yourself - caregiver stress is real and deserves attention

Warning signs to watch for after discharge:

- Changes in sleep patterns (sleeping much more or much less)

- Social withdrawal or isolation

- Stopping medications

- Increased irritability, suspiciousness, or unusual beliefs

- Neglecting self-care (hygiene, eating)

- Increased substance use

If you notice warning signs:

1. Contact the outpatient treatment team: ___________

2. Call the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline (call or text 988)

3. Go to the nearest emergency department if there is immediate danger

Resources for families:

- NAMI Helpline: 1-800-950-NAMI (6264) - free support, information, and referrals

- NAMI Family-to-Family: Free 8-session course taught by trained family members - ask about local classes

- NAMI Support Groups: Free peer-led groups for family members - find one at nami.org

- Crisis Text Line: Text HOME to 741741

Communication tips:

- Use calm, clear, simple language

- Avoid arguing about delusions or hallucinations - instead, acknowledge the person's feelings

- Express concern without criticism: "I'm worried about you" rather than "You're not taking care of yourself"

- Set realistic expectations - recovery is a process, not an event

- Celebrate small steps forward

Your outpatient appointment: Date: Time: Location: ___

Medications at discharge: ___

Emergency contact: ___

---

Remember: You are not alone. Millions of families navigate these challenges, and support is available.

---

16. Evidence Gaps and Emerging Directions

Several important uncertainties remain. Most landmark RCTs initiated family interventions during or shortly after hospitalization but measured outcomes in the community/outpatient phase; evidence specifically designed for 5-7 day inpatient stays is limited.[1][59] The quality of evidence across the field is generally low to moderate, with no studies in the Rodolico NMA having low risk of bias.[24][21] Long-term durability of relapse prevention effects is uncertain - the Chien 2024 Cochrane review found the effect may not extend beyond short-term follow-up.[22] Cultural variation in EE interpretation complicates universal application, with some evidence that high EE may paradoxically be associated with better outcomes in African-American families.[69] The ODDESSI multi-site cluster RCT testing Open Dialogue versus TAU is ongoing and may reshape the evidence landscape for family-oriented acute care.[54]

The most promising emerging direction is the integration of brief family consultation models (such as VCBFC) as standard inpatient practice, serving as a bridge to longer-term family psychoeducation programs - aligning the strong evidence for sustained family intervention with the reality of short hospital stays.[40]

## Source: `OPENEVIDENCE RAW FILES TO REVIEW/Inpatient Psychiatric Management of Borderline Personality Disorder and Severe Personality Pathology_ A Comprehensive Evidence Review (1).docx`

Inpatient Psychiatric Management of Borderline Personality Disorder and Severe Personality Pathology: A Comprehensive Evidence Review

---

1. Scope and Framing

This review synthesizes the evidence base for managing patients with borderline personality disorder (BPD) and other severe personality pathology on inpatient psychiatric units. The focus is on practical inpatient management - when to admit, how to structure the admission, what to do (and not do) pharmacologically and psychotherapeutically, and how to discharge safely. The evidence draws from Cochrane systematic reviews, major guideline statements (NICE CG78, APA 2001/2010, Lancet 2021 seminar, JAMA 2023 review), landmark RCTs, and consensus frameworks. BPD constitutes approximately 20% of psychiatric hospital admissions and outpatient referrals, making competent management a core skill for every inpatient psychiatrist.[1]

---

2. Indications and Contraindications for Hospitalization

When to Admit

All major guidelines converge on a narrow set of indications for inpatient admission:[2][3]

- Confirmed suicidal intent with a plan and inability to contract for safety in the community

- Life-threatening self-injury or serious suicide attempt requiring medical stabilization

- Acute psychotic episodes (transient, stress-related paranoid ideation or severe dissociation) that impair reality testing

- Extreme agitation or anxiety unmanageable in outpatient settings

- Serious attacks on others or imminent danger to third parties

- Inability to access or tolerate outpatient treatment when day-hospital or residential alternatives are unavailable[4]

The critical clinical distinction is between suicide attempts, non-suicidal self-injury (NSSI), and high-risk behaviors - these must be differentiated before any admission decision.[2]

When Not to Admit

Expert consensus and guideline recommendations are equally clear about contraindications:[2][3][5]

- NSSI without suicidal intent - inpatient crisis intervention should not be initiated for non-life-threatening self-injury

- Chronic suicidality without acute escalation - recurrent suicidal ideation in the context of ongoing outpatient treatment is generally better managed with crisis planning and outpatient intensification

- Repeated serial hospitalizations - inconsistent treatment histories are associated with suicide attempts and completed suicides; frequent admissions can disrupt longer-term outpatient therapies[2]

- Behavioral escalation aimed at obtaining admission - admitting in response to escalating threats without genuine acute risk reinforces maladaptive contingencies

Outpatient crisis management is the preferred default whenever feasible. The Lancet 2021 seminar explicitly states: "Offer crisis intervention on an outpatient basis whenever possible".[2]

---

3. The Risk of Iatrogenic Harm

The Widely Held Concern

The belief that hospitalization causes regression, reinforces maladaptive behaviors, and creates institutional dependency in BPD patients is pervasive in psychiatric training. This concern has shaped decades of clinical practice, but the empirical evidence directly testing this hypothesis is surprisingly thin.[6]

What the Evidence Actually Shows

The most direct empirical examination is the Fowler et al. (2018) naturalistic longitudinal study comparing 245 BPD inpatients with 220 matched reference inpatients during extended treatment. Large effect-size improvements were observed in depression, anxiety, suicidal ideation, and functional disability (Cohen's d >= 1.0). Clinical deterioration was rare (<=1.1% on any outcome), with no difference from the non-BPD cohort. The authors concluded there was "no empirical support" for the assertion that extended inpatient care leads to deterioration in BPD.[6]

Chen et al. (2025) found that BPD-positive patients on an acute inpatient unit reported significantly greater improvements in anxiety, depression, and general psychiatric severity compared to BPD-negative patients during short-term hospitalization.[7]

Where Iatrogenic Harm Is Documented

The most tangible iatrogenic risk is medication escalation during hospitalization. A study of 569 BPD patients at a tertiary care unit found that the odds of being prescribed antidepressants, antipsychotics, mood stabilizers, hypnotics, or anxiolytics were all higher at discharge than at admission (incidence rate ratio 1.9 for total psychotropic prescriptions).[8] This is particularly concerning given that no medication class has been consistently effective for BPD core symptoms.[3][9]

A meta-synthesis of patient experiences (Stapleton & Wright, 2019) identified negative elements including lack of staff contact, negative staff attitudes, staff's lack of BPD knowledge, coercive involuntary admission, and poor discharge planning.[10] These process failures - rather than hospitalization per se - appear to drive negative outcomes.

---

4. Brief Admissions vs. Prolonged Admissions

Guideline Consensus: Brief, Goal-Directed Admissions

The dominant position across all major guidelines favors brief crisis admissions with discharge planning beginning on day one.[2][5] The Goal-Oriented Limited-Duration (GOLD) approach (Siefert, 2012) provides a structured framework: a preadmission treatment agreement with a planned discharge date, clear treatment goals, and specified staff roles. Setting a discharge date early allows the team to immediately begin working with feelings of rejection and abandonment rather than avoiding them.[5]

Evidence on Structured Brief Admission Models

The Brief Admission Skane (BASRCT) model allows self-referral admissions of up to 3 days, maximum 3 times per month, integrated into existing treatment plans before crises occur.[11] However, the 2022 Cochrane review of crisis interventions for BPD found only two RCTs total and no clear evidence of benefit for either joint crisis plans or brief admission over treatment as usual.[12]

The Gold Card SA initiative in South Australia - a 4-session structured psychological intervention after acute crisis - demonstrated 63% reduction in ED presentations, 65% reduction in mental health admissions, and 82% reduction in bed days in an uncontrolled pre-post design (n=332).[13] A specialized short-term crisis track in Basel was associated with significantly shorter median length of stay and stable low rates of coercive measures over 8 years.[14]

Extended Treatment: Not Necessarily Harmful

The Fowler et al. data challenge the assumption that longer stays are inherently harmful.[6] Bartak et al. (2011) compared outpatient, day hospital, and inpatient psychotherapeutic treatment for Cluster B personality disorders (n=207) and found the inpatient group showed the largest improvements, with a marginally significant advantage over outpatient treatment for psychiatric symptoms (p=0.057).[15] Kujovic et al. (2024) compared 8-week vs. 12-week adapted inpatient DBT (n=175) and found both durations produced large effect sizes (BSL-23 d=1.29 and d=1.16 respectively) with no significant between-group differences.[16]

The key variable is not length of stay but structure of stay. Unstructured, open-ended admissions without clear goals are the problem - not duration per se.

---

5. Managing Core Inpatient Challenges

Splitting and Staff Conflict

Splitting - the tendency to view some clinicians as "all good" and others as "all bad" - is among the most disruptive dynamics on inpatient units. The JAMA review explicitly recommends that clinicians "facilitate open communication and agreement on a consistent approach with all treating clinicians" to prevent this dynamic.[3] Practical strategies include:

- Daily team huddles with explicit discussion of the patient's interpersonal patterns

- Single treatment plan communicated identically by all staff

- Rotating primary contacts to prevent exclusive attachment to one clinician

- Normalizing the dynamic in team formulation: splitting reflects the patient's internal experience of relationships, not staff failure

- Therapist consultation meetings - identified as one of five common elements across all effective BPD treatments ("therapists discuss cases, including personal reactions, with others")[1]

A quasi-experimental study on a psychiatric intensive care unit demonstrated that implementing a schema-informed case formulation for a patient with emotionally unstable personality disorder resulted in complete extinction of incidents requiring seclusion, restraint, and rapid tranquilization.[17]

Recurrent Self-Harm

The critical first step is functional behavioral analysis: identifying the exact problem behavior, triggering parameters, maintenance parameters, and vulnerability factors (sleep problems, substance misuse, social problems).[2] Interventions should be based on this analysis rather than reflexive escalation of observation levels. The Lancet seminar recommends teaching distress tolerance skills as the primary intervention for reducing high levels of distress.[2]

Chronic Suicidality

Chronic suicidality in BPD must be distinguished from acute suicidal crises. Gunderson's NEJM review recommends that when suicidal intent is denied, outpatient crisis management with concerned attention and safety planning is preferred over hospitalization.[18] The VA/DoD clinical practice guideline supports crisis response planning - a collaborative, step-by-step document including crisis signs, self-management skills, social supports, and crisis resources - which significantly reduced suicide attempts compared to treatment as usual.[19][20]

Affective Instability

Short-term symptoms of depression or anxiety that are part of BPD emotional instability and can be related to specific triggering situations (e.g., interpersonal problems) should not be misinterpreted as comorbid disorders and should be treated solely with psychotherapy.[3] This is one of the most common errors on inpatient units - treating BPD-related affective storms as if they were independent mood or anxiety disorders, leading to inappropriate medication escalation.

---

6. DBT-Informed Inpatient Approaches

Evidence Base

The systematic review by Bloom et al. (2012) evaluated 11 studies of DBT in inpatient settings and found considerable variation in implementation but consistent reductions in suicidal ideation, self-injurious behaviors, depression, and anxiety. Results for anger and violent behaviors were mixed.[21]

Bohus et al. (2004) conducted a controlled trial of 3-month inpatient DBT (n=50) showing significant improvements on 10 of 11 psychopathological variables, with 42% meeting criteria for clinically relevant recovery.[22] Tebbett-Mock et al. (2020) found that acute-care adolescent inpatient DBT (n=425) produced significantly fewer constant observation hours, fewer suicide attempts and self-injury incidents, fewer restraints, and fewer days hospitalized compared to historical TAU, saving $251,609 in staff time for constant observation.[23]

A dismantling RCT by Linehan et al. (2015) demonstrated that better and faster treatment effects occurred when group skills training was involved, supporting the value of skills groups as a core component even when full DBT cannot be delivered.[24] The McMain et al. (2017) RCT showed that brief DBT skills training produced superior reductions in self-harm, with the DBT group reaching near-zero rates by 32-week follow-up and lower hospitalization probability during treatment.[25]

Figure 2 Outcomes for dialectical behaviour therapy ( N = 42) and waitlist ( N = 42) groups over 32 weeks after randomization. Estimated marginal means and 95% confidence intervals over specific outcomes. DSHI , Deliberate SelfHarm Inventory; LSASI , Lifetime Suicide Attempt SelfInjury. Estimates of the marginal means were derived from multilevel generalized linear models. Estimates are incident rate ratios for the selfharm measures and probabilities for the occurrence of Emergency Room Visits and Hospitalizations.

Practical Inpatient DBT Adaptation

On acute units where full DBT is not feasible, the following DBT-informed elements can be incorporated:

- Daily distress tolerance skills groups (TIPP skills: Temperature, Intense exercise, Paced breathing, Progressive relaxation)

- Chain analysis of self-harm episodes as a structured alternative to punitive responses

- Diary cards tracking emotions, urges, and skill use

- Validation strategies balanced with change-oriented interventions

- Behavioral targets hierarchy: life-threatening behaviors -> therapy-interfering behaviors -> quality-of-life-interfering behaviors

---

7. Safety Planning

The Safety Planning Intervention (SPI) is a cognitive-behavioral intervention with six components: (1) identifying personalized warning signs, (2) internal coping strategies, (3) social contacts and settings for distraction, (4) individuals who can provide support, (5) professional and crisis resources, and (6) lethal means counseling.[26] In combination with follow-up contacts, SPI is associated with reduction in suicidality.[27] The VA/DoD guideline recommends SPI for any patient at intermediate or high acute or chronic suicide risk.[20]

No-suicide contracts are explicitly not recommended - they lack evidence of effectiveness, may feel coercive, and do not include personalized coping mechanisms.[27] Safety plans should be living documents, updated during the admission and reviewed at discharge.

---

8. Team-Based Behavioral Plans

Structure

Effective behavioral plans for BPD inpatients share common elements derived from expert consensus and the common factors literature:[1][3]

1. Formulation-driven: Based on a shared understanding of the patient's interpersonal patterns, triggers, and maintaining factors

2. Consistent across all staff: Every team member responds identically to target behaviors

3. Explicit contingencies: Clear "if-then" statements for predictable scenarios

4. Validation + limits: Acknowledging the patient's distress while maintaining boundaries

5. Regular review: Updated at least weekly in team meetings

Staff Training

Even brief training interventions produce meaningful shifts in staff attitudes. A one-day interactive training session significantly reduced stigmatizing attitudes (all measures p < 0.001).[28] A one-day Good Psychiatric Management (GPM) training improved attitudes on 11 of 13 items, with changes persisting at 6-month follow-up.[29] A one-day STEPPS workshop (n=271) produced significantly greater empathy, increased competency, and reduced dislike toward BPD patients.[30] Key effective training elements include co-production with people with lived experience, communicating a psychological model, and teaching clinical skills for practice.[31]

---

9. Medication Use and Overuse

The Evidence-Practice Gap

No medication has been approved by any regulatory agency for BPD, and no class of psychoactive medication has been consistently effective in RCTs for core BPD symptoms.[3][32] Yet approximately 80% of BPD patients take standing psychotropic medications, with 28.6% taking four or more simultaneously.[9][18] Among European BPD inpatients, approximately 70% receive antidepressants and 70% receive antipsychotics.[9] Out of 87 medications used in clinical practice for BPD, RCT data exist for only 9.[33]

What the Evidence Shows by Drug Class

The forest plot from the Lieslehto et al. (2023) Swedish nationwide cohort study illustrates the comparative suicide risk across pharmacotherapy classes, demonstrating that benzodiazepines carried the highest risk elevation while ADHD medications were uniquely protective.

Figure 1 Risk of Attempted or Completed Suicide During Use of Pharmacotherapy Compared With Nonuse of the Medication Class in Within-Individual Analyses

NICE Crisis Pharmacotherapy Recommendations

For acute crisis management, NICE recommends a single drug at minimum effective dose for no longer than 1 week.[3] Preferred agents are sedative antihistamines (e.g., promethazine) or low-potency antipsychotics (e.g., quetiapine) for agitation or sleep problems.[2] Benzodiazepines and tricyclic antidepressants should be avoided.[2]

Deprescription as a Therapeutic Intervention

Soler et al. (2022) demonstrated that DBT skills training significantly reduced polypharmacy, with substantial decreases in the number of medications, medication load index, and sedation load index compared to controls.[39] This supports the principle that teaching coping skills can replace medications rather than the reverse.

Figure 1 Differences between groups in prescription changes prepost intervention

---

10. Discharge Planning and Transitions of Care

Core Principles

- Begin discharge planning on day one - this is a consistent recommendation across all major guidelines[2][5]

- Set a discharge date at admission (GOLD approach) - this allows the team to work with abandonment fears proactively rather than reactively[5]

- Make binding agreements about further treatment between the patient and their therapeutic team, reviewed after crisis intervention[2]

- Coordinate across providers - all involved service providers should be informed about medication changes and treatment plan modifications[2]

- Ensure outpatient follow-up is scheduled before discharge - not merely "recommended"

- Update the safety plan at discharge with current triggers, coping strategies, and crisis contacts

Stepped Care and Continuity

Inconsistent treatment histories are associated with suicide attempts and completed suicides.[2] Stepped care models - where intensity of treatment is matched to clinical staging - can reduce the need for severe crisis interventions.[2] Inpatient DBT may function as an "intensive orientation" to outpatient DBT services, making the transition from inpatient to outpatient a therapeutic bridge rather than a cliff.[21]

Family Involvement

Family members of individuals with BPD have elevated levels of grief and burden compared with relatives of individuals with other severe mental disorders.[2] An RCT of group psychoeducation for 68 family members reduced emotional stress compared with wait-list control.[3] The Family Connections program (12 sessions, DBT-based) showed that patients of caregivers who received the intervention showed significant improvements in stress, depression, and anxiety.[40] Highest-rated sessions in family psychoeducation programs covered communication skills and coping with crises.[41]

12. Practical Inpatient Management Principles

The 15 Principles

1. Admit only for acute safety - confirmed suicidal intent, life-threatening self-injury, acute psychosis, or danger to others. NSSI without suicidal intent is not an indication for admission.[2]

2. Set a discharge date at admission. Communicate it clearly and begin discharge planning on day one.[5][2]

3. Conduct a functional behavioral analysis of the crisis behavior within the first 24 hours - identify triggers, maintaining factors, and vulnerability factors.[2]

4. Differentiate BPD affective instability from comorbid mood disorders. Short-term depression or anxiety related to interpersonal triggers should not be treated as independent disorders.[3]

5. Minimize medication changes. Resist the pressure to "do something" pharmacologically. If medications are used in crisis, use a single agent at minimum dose for <=1 week. Never prescribe benzodiazepines.[3][2]

6. Deprescribe before prescribing. Discontinue medications with unclear benefit before adding new ones.[18]

7. Maintain team consistency. Hold daily huddles. Ensure every staff member communicates the same plan. Document the behavioral plan prominently.[3]

8. Validate distress while holding limits. The therapeutic relationship should balance appreciation of the patient's subjective needs with clear orientation toward problem-solving.[2]

9. Teach at least one distress tolerance skill during every admission (e.g., TIPP, ice diving, paced breathing).

10. Complete a safety plan (Stanley-Brown model) collaboratively before discharge. Update it if one already exists.[26]

11. Name the diagnosis. Psychoeducation about BPD is therapeutic - most patients experience relief upon learning their experiences constitute a coherent, treatable syndrome.[2]

12. Schedule outpatient follow-up before discharge - do not discharge with "follow up with your outpatient provider."

13. Involve family/supports with psychoeducation about the disorder, communication strategies, and crisis management.[3][40]

14. Use team formulation to understand splitting and countertransference. Discuss personal reactions to the patient in structured team meetings.[1]

15. Document the rationale for not admitting as carefully as the rationale for admitting. Both decisions carry risk.
