## Source: `OPENEVIDENCE RAW FILES TO REVIEW/OPENEVIDENCE REVIEWS INPATIENT.docx`

I'll conduct a comprehensive review across these 13 domains of adult inpatient psychiatry. Let me launch parallel research agents to cover this breadth efficiently.

Now let me launch the remaining research agents for the topics not yet covered.

Comprehensive Review: Evidence-Based Adult Inpatient Psychiatry - Admission Through Discharge

---

1. Suicide Assessment

Strongest Evidence

The Columbia-Suicide Severity Rating Scale (C-SSRS) is the most widely endorsed tool. A 2025 meta-analysis found prior suicidal behavior predicted future attempts (pooled OR 3.14, 95% CI 1.86-5.31), and in an inpatient cohort of 1,055 adults, the C-SSRS demonstrated AUC = 0.757 for post-discharge suicide-related behavior.[1][2] The Joint Commission (NPSG 15.01.01) and the VA/DoD 2024 Clinical Practice Guideline endorse the C-SSRS for screening.[3][4] However, a systematic review using GRADE found that no instrument fulfilled requirements for sufficient diagnostic accuracy (sensitivity >80% and specificity >50%).[5]

The SAD PERSONS scale should not be used: multiple studies demonstrate it performs no better than chance (AUC 0.55-0.59), with sensitivity as low as 1% for repeat self-harm.[6][7][8] The VA/DoD 2024 guideline explicitly excludes it.[4]

Environmental safety has the strongest single-intervention evidence. The VHA Mental Health Environment of Care Checklist (MHEOCC) produced an 82% reduction in inpatient suicide rate (from 2.64 to 0.87 per 100,000 admissions, P < .001), sustained over 7 years.[9][10] Hanging accounts for 71% of inpatient suicide deaths, and ligature point removal was associated with significant reductions in suicide by hanging in a UK national study.[11][12]

Landmark Studies

The Diefenbach et al. (2024) RCT in JAMA Psychiatry (n=200) is the largest inpatient suicide prevention trial: up to 4 sessions of Brief Cognitive Behavioral Therapy produced a 60% reduction in post-discharge suicide attempts (OR 0.40, 95% CI 0.20-0.80; NNT = 7) and a 71% reduction in readmissions among patients without substance use disorders.[13]

The Doupnik et al. (2020) meta-analysis of 14 studies found brief inpatient/acute-care suicide prevention interventions reduced subsequent attempts (pooled OR 0.69) and increased linkage to follow-up (OR 2.74).[14] The following figure summarizes these outcomes:

Figure 2 Forest Plots for 3 Study Outcomes: Depression, Linkage to Follow-up Care, and Subsequent Suicide Attempts

Current Controversies

A major paradigm shift is underway: prediction versus prevention. Hawton et al. (2022, Lancet Psychiatry) argue for shifting from risk prediction to therapeutic assessment, formulation, and risk management.[15] UK/NICE and Australian/New Zealand guidelines now advise against using risk scales for prediction and treatment allocation, while US and European guidelines still endorse structured tools as adjuncts.[16][17] Nearly 90% of UK mental health patients who died by suicide were rated as no/low risk at their last clinical contact.[16]

Practical Recommendations

- Use the C-SSRS to structure comprehensive assessments and trigger interventions, not to predict individual suicide[4][17]

- Implement environmental safety checklists (MHEOCC) with systematic ligature point removal[9][12]

- Deliver brief CBT for suicide prevention (up to 4 sessions) during hospitalization[13]

- Complete a Safety Planning Intervention before discharge[18][19]

- Ensure follow-up within 7 days of discharge - associated with reduced suicide risk (RR 0.44 in youth)[20]

- Send caring contacts for 12 months post-discharge[4]

---

2. Violence Risk Assessment

Strongest Evidence

For imminent (24-hour) risk, the Brset Violence Checklist (BVC) and Dynamic Appraisal of Situational Aggression (DASA) have the best evidence. A meta-analysis of 31 studies (282,238 assessments) found pooled effect sizes of Hedges' g = 1.35 (95% CI 1.15-1.56) for the BVC and g = 1.04 (95% CI 0.69-1.39) for the DASA.[21] Both are rated as having acceptable utility and feasibility.[21][22]

For medium/long-term risk, the HCR-20v3 is the most globally used structured professional judgment tool, with pooled AUC of 0.69 (95% CI 0.65-0.72) for violent recidivism in forensic populations.[23] An international study found HCR-20v3 performance deteriorated after 6 months, suggesting reassessment every 6 months is needed to maintain predictive validity.[24]

Current Controversies

A narrative review found that 67% of HCR-20 studies focused on predictive validity rather than whether its use actually reduced violence - only one study tested whether using the HCR-20 affected violence rates.[25] The critical question remains whether risk assessment tools improve outcomes or merely classify patients.

Practical Recommendations

- Use the BVC or DASA for daily shift-level violence risk screening[21][22]

- Use the HCR-20v3 for medium-term risk assessment with reassessment every 6 months[23][24]

- Combine structured tools with clinical judgment rather than relying on either alone[26]

---

3. Agitation Management

Strongest Evidence

Verbal de-escalation is first-line treatment per APA and AAEP Project BETA guidelines, effective for a majority of patients within 5 minutes.[27][28] A cluster randomized study across all Slovenian psychiatric hospitals found de-escalation training reduced aggressive events by 73% (IRR 0.268) and physical restraints by 70% (IRR 0.304).[29] However, Cochrane reviews found no RCTs of de-escalation techniques for psychosis-induced aggression.[30][31]

When pharmacotherapy is needed, a landmark individual participant data network meta-analysis (Lancet Psychiatry, 2026; 2,705 participants, 13 RCTs) provides the most comprehensive comparison:[32]

Landmark Studies

The TREC trials established haloperidol + promethazine as superior to haloperidol alone (NNT = 6 for tranquility at 20 min), with all 10 dystonia cases occurring in the haloperidol-alone group - the trial was stopped early.[35] The TREC-India trial found IM olanzapine and IM haloperidol + promethazine were similarly effective at 15 minutes, but olanzapine required significantly more additional drugs (43% vs. 21%).[36]

Inhaled loxapine achieves peak plasma concentration in ~2 minutes and was significantly faster than IM aripiprazole in the PLACID trial (median 50 vs. 60 min to response; P = 0.0005), but carries a black box warning for bronchospasm and requires REMS enrollment.[37][38]

Practical Recommendations

- Always attempt verbal de-escalation first[27][28]

- For mild-moderate agitation: offer oral medications (olanzapine 10 mg, lorazepam 2 mg, or haloperidol 5 mg + lorazepam 2 mg)[39]

- For severe agitation requiring IM: haloperidol 5 mg + promethazine 25-50 mg IM, or olanzapine 10 mg IM (never combine IM olanzapine with IM benzodiazepines)[35][36]

- Midazolam 5 mg IM is the fastest-acting agent but carries respiratory depression risk[33][40]

- Avoid haloperidol monotherapy - it is the least effective option with the highest EPS risk[32]

---

4. Rapid Tranquilization

Key Evidence Summary

The 2026 network meta-analysis confirmed that treatment effect differences between agents are smaller in severe agitation than moderate agitation (ratio of ORs 0.38, 95% CI 0.17-0.80), meaning agent selection matters more for moderately agitated patients.[32] Confidence in all estimates was low to very low.[32]

For methamphetamine-related agitation, IV midazolam 5 mg + droperidol 5 mg achieved adequate sedation at 10 min in 85% vs. 47% (droperidol alone) and 50% (olanzapine alone).[41]

Current Controversies

- Ketamine for agitation is emerging but limited to ACEP Level C consensus recommendations; a network meta-analysis ranked it highest for effectiveness (SUCRA 93%) but with very low confidence[42][43]

- IV vs. IM route: IV combinations may be faster but carry greater hemodynamic risks; most guidelines recommend avoiding IV treatments[44]

- Droperidol availability varies by country, limiting generalizability of evidence favoring it[34]

---

5. Seclusion and Restraint

Seclusion/restraint (S/R) may only be used as last-resort interventions per APA and Joint Commission standards.[28][45] PTSD incidence after S/R ranges from 25-47%.[46] Mechanical restraints have been associated with asphyxiation, cardiac arrest, and pulmonary embolism.[28]

The Six Core Strategies (6CS) for S/R reduction have the strongest implementation evidence: a multisite study of 43 facilities found the stabilized implementation group reduced seclusion hours by 19% and proportion restrained by 30%.[47] CMS public reporting reduced restraint duration by 49% and seclusion by 54%.[48] Pennsylvania State hospitals achieved near-cessation of S/R through continuous 6CS adherence.[49]

---

6. Delirium

Strongest Evidence

The Confusion Assessment Method (CAM) remains the gold standard for delirium detection, with sensitivity 94-100%, specificity 90-95%, and interrater reliability  = 0.92.[50] A 2023 meta-analysis confirmed the CAM has the highest specificity (0.98) among bedside tools.[51] Only 12-35% of delirium cases are recognized through routine clinical documentation.[52]

Multicomponent non-pharmacological prevention is the cornerstone of management. A meta-analysis of 14 HELP-based studies showed a 53% reduction in incident delirium (OR 0.47, 95% CI 0.38-0.58).[50] The SCCM PADIS guidelines conditionally recommend these interventions.[53]

Antipsychotics do not improve delirium outcomes. The MIND-USA trial (n=566) found no difference in days alive without delirium or coma with haloperidol or ziprasidone vs. placebo.[54] The AID-ICU trial (n=1,000) similarly found no significant difference in the primary outcome.[55] Long-term MIND-USA follow-up showed no benefit at 3 or 12 months.[56] The PADIS guidelines recommend against routine antipsychotic use for delirium.[53]

Dexmedetomidine has the strongest pharmacological evidence: a meta-analysis of 77 RCTs found it reduced delirium risk (RR 0.67, 95% CI 0.55-0.81) compared to other sedatives, though with increased bradycardia and hypotension.[57]

Practical Recommendations

- Screen all at-risk patients using the CAM, 3D-CAM, or 4AT[50][51]

- Implement multicomponent non-pharmacological bundles (reorientation, mobilization, sleep hygiene, sensory optimization)[50][53]

- Reserve antipsychotics for severe hyperactive delirium with behavioral disturbance refractory to non-pharmacological measures[58][59]

- Use benzodiazepines only for alcohol/benzodiazepine withdrawal delirium[52][60]

- Prefer dexmedetomidine over benzodiazepines for ICU sedation[57][53]

---

7. Catatonia

Strongest Evidence

Catatonia prevalence in acute psychiatric inpatient settings is 9-20%, with mood disorders (not schizophrenia) being the most common underlying condition.[61][62][63] The Bush-Francis Catatonia Rating Scale (BFCRS) is the most widely used and recommended instrument, with a screening cutoff of >=2 items.[61][64] Notably, the BFCRS identifies substantially more cases than DSM-5 criteria alone (18.3% vs. 6.6% prevalence in one study).[65]

Lorazepam is effective in up to 90% of acute catatonia cases.[66] A 2026 meta-analysis found an overall remission rate of 55% and response rate of 77%, with a mean BFCRS reduction of 11.88 points (Cohen's d = -3.15).[67] The lorazepam challenge test (2 mg IV) is both diagnostic and therapeutic.[61]

ECT is the definitive treatment, with response rates of 80-100%, including up to 60% of benzodiazepine non-responders.[61][68] The FDA reclassified ECT devices in 2018 as indicated for catatonia.[69] Effects can be expected after 4-6 sessions; bitemporal placement is generally preferred.[61][68]

Differentiating Catatonia from NMS

Many experts consider NMS a type of malignant catatonia precipitated by dopamine-blocking agents.[61][70] Key differentiating features favoring NMS include fever (OR 7.3), diaphoresis (OR 10.0), and lead-pipe rigidity (OR 9.6); features favoring catatonia include stupor, stereotypy, waxy flexibility, and negativism.[71]

Current Controversies

The evidence base consists primarily of case series and open studies - no high-quality RCTs exist for either benzodiazepines or ECT in catatonia.[72][73] The Cochrane review found insufficient trial-derived evidence.[72] DSM-5-TR states catatonic disorder due to another medical condition cannot be separately diagnosed during delirium, but research shows approximately one-third of ICU patients may have both conditions simultaneously.[74][63]

Practical Recommendations

- Screen with the BFCRS (>=2 items positive) in any patient with unexplained motor abnormalities, mutism, or negativism[61]

- Perform a lorazepam challenge test (2 mg IV; 1 mg in elderly)[61]

- If positive, continue scheduled lorazepam (minimum TID; typical maintenance 8-24 mg/day)[61][75]

- If benzodiazepines insufficient or malignant features present, initiate ECT urgently[61]

- Avoid high-potency first-generation antipsychotics - they can worsen catatonia and precipitate NMS[61]

- Consider NMDA antagonists (amantadine, memantine) when delirium co-occurs, as benzodiazepines may worsen delirium[61][76]

---

8. Capacity Evaluation

Strongest Evidence

Appelbaum's four abilities model - understanding, appreciation, reasoning, and expressing a choice - is the foundational framework, endorsed by the APA Resource Document on Decisional Capacity (2019).[77][78] Capacity is always decision-specific and not determined solely by diagnosis.[78][79]

The MacArthur Competence Assessment Tool for Treatment (MacCAT-T) is the most widely used structured instrument, with excellent interrater reliability (ICC 0.92-0.98 across validations) and strong construct validity.[80][81][82][83] A critical finding is that clinical assessment alone frequently overestimates capacity: in one study, 53.5% of schizophrenia patients were classified as impaired by MacCAT-T vs. only 18.4% by clinical assessment.[84][85]

Practical Recommendations

- Assess all four Appelbaum criteria for every capacity determination[77]

- Use the MacCAT-T for difficult cases or those likely to involve legal proceedings[78]

- MMSE scores <19 are highly likely to be associated with incompetence; scores >=23-26 strongly suggest competence[78]

- Document the specific decision, the information disclosed, and the patient's responses to each of the four criteria

- Remember that capacity can fluctuate - reassess when clinical status changes

---

9. Involuntary Treatment

Legal Framework

Three landmark U.S. Supreme Court cases define the legal landscape: Washington v. Harper (1990) allows administrative review for involuntary medication of dangerous/gravely disabled prisoners; Sell v. United States (2003) requires judicial authorization for competency restoration with four specific criteria; and Riggins v. Nevada (1992) extends protections to pretrial detainees.[86][87] A retrospective review found that 79% of federal defendants involuntarily treated under Sell were successfully restored to competency.[88]

Outcomes Evidence

A systematic review of 41 studies found involuntary patients had equal or longer length of stay, equal or greater readmission risk, and lower social functioning compared to voluntary patients.[89] A pooled analysis of 2,790 involuntary patients across 11 countries showed significant reductions in suicidality (13.9% -> 5.0% at 1 month) and hostility (46.1% -> 14.5%).[90] However, a systematic review of 10 studies found no consistent trend toward improved long-term medication adherence after involuntary hospitalization.[91]

Current Controversies

The UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (CRPD) Committee holds that all persons have legal capacity at all times and that involuntary detention/treatment violates the Convention - a position not universally accepted within the UN system and strongly criticized by some academics.[92][93] The WHO's 2023 guidance fundamentally rejects coercion, representing a decisive shift from its 2006 position.[94][95] International involuntary hospitalization rates vary nearly 20-fold (14.5 to 282 per 100,000), driven by legislative, cultural, and systemic factors.[96]

Advance statements are the only intervention category showing a statistically significant reduction in compulsory admissions in meta-analysis.[97] The following figure from de Jong et al. (2016) illustrates this finding:

Figure 2 Relative Risk of Compulsory Admission per Subgroup of Intervention

Practical Recommendations

- Use the least restrictive alternative consistent with patient safety

- Document the specific legal criteria met for involuntary treatment

- Involve patients in decision-making to the greatest extent possible - perceived fairness partially mediates the relationship between involuntary status and perceived coercion[98]

- Discuss psychiatric advance directives with all patients, particularly those with recurrent involuntary admissions[97]

---

10. Family Meetings

Strongest Evidence

Family psychoeducation (FPE) has the most robust evidence base, supported by over 100 RCTs.[99] A Lancet Psychiatry network meta-analysis (2022) comparing 11 family intervention models found FPE was the most efficacious for relapse prevention in schizophrenia at 12 months: OR 0.18 (95% CI 0.12-0.27), with only 10% relapsing vs. 37% with treatment as usual.[100] Even the simplest form of family psychoeducation was ranked among the most efficacious, suggesting that informing families about illness, symptoms, and treatment options has a protective role.[100]

An RCT of 83 hospitalized patients with major depression found that at 15 months, treatment response rates were 49% (multi-family group therapy), 24% (single-family therapy), and 9% (TAU).[101]

Family involvement in discharge planning is significantly associated with outpatient follow-up: any family involvement with inpatient staff was associated with follow-up within 7 days (OR 2.79) and 30 days (OR 3.07).[102]

Current Controversies

The Open Dialogue approach has generated substantial interest but no completed RCT exists; the ODDESSI trial is ongoing.[103] Non-randomized Finnish studies reported impressive outcomes (82% with no/mild psychotic symptoms at 2 years, only 35% needing neuroleptics), but these cannot be attributed to the intervention without controlled data.[104]

Implementation remains poor despite strong guideline recommendations. Key barriers include confidentiality concerns, organizational culture, and clinician uncertainty about family involvement.[105][106]

Practical Recommendations

- Offer family psychoeducation to all patients with psychotic disorders and their families - even brief, simple formats are effective[100]

- Involve families in discharge planning - it significantly increases follow-up attendance[102]

- Address confidentiality proactively with patients and families[106]

- For mood disorders, consider multi-family group therapy during hospitalization[101]

---

11. Discharge Planning

Strongest Evidence

The 2022 Cochrane review (33 RCTs, 12,242 participants) found individualized discharge planning reduced readmissions (RR 0.89, 95% CI 0.81-0.97) and shortened length of stay (MD -0.73 days), though evidence for psychiatric populations specifically was limited.[107] Effective components include pre- and post-discharge psychoeducation, structured needs assessments, medication reconciliation, transition managers, and inpatient-outpatient provider communication.[108]

Scheduling an outpatient appointment at discharge is significantly associated with attending follow-up, regardless of pre-admission engagement level. Patients with no prior outpatient care were three times more likely to follow up within 7 days when an appointment was scheduled.[109]

Post-Discharge Suicide Risk

The post-discharge period carries the highest risk for suicide: pooled rates of 2,950 per 100,000 person-years in the first week and approximately 100 times the global suicide rate during the first 3 months.[110][111] Follow-up within 7 days is a HEDIS quality indicator and is associated with reduced suicide risk and greater medication adherence.[112][113]

Practical Recommendations

- Schedule a specific outpatient appointment before discharge - do not simply provide a phone number[109]

- Complete a Safety Planning Intervention with all patients at suicide risk[19]

- Ensure medication reconciliation and patient/family education about medications

- Communicate directly with outpatient providers (warm handoff)[114]

- Target follow-up within 7 days for all psychiatric discharges[112][113]

---

12. Readmission Reduction

Strongest Evidence

Thirty-day psychiatric readmission rates range from 7-17% across studies.[115][116][117] The strongest and most consistent predictor is previous psychiatric hospitalizations.[115][116][118][119] Other predictors include homelessness, schizophrenia/bipolar/personality disorder diagnoses, medical comorbidity, and co-occurring substance use disorders.[115][120][119]

Critical Time Intervention (CTI) has the strongest RCT evidence for readmission reduction. The landmark Herman et al. trial (n=150, formerly homeless with SMI) found CTI significantly reduced rehospitalization (OR 0.11, 95% CI 0.01-0.96) and homelessness (OR 0.22).[121][122] Brief CTI reduced 30-day readmission from 47% to 28% (P < .001).[123]

However, meta-analyses of transitional interventions overall show modest, often non-significant effects on readmission (pooled OR 0.76, 95% CI 0.55-1.05).[124] The ENRICH trial (n=590), the definitive RCT of peer support for psychiatric discharge, found no significant effect on readmission (RR 0.97, 95% CI 0.82-1.14).[118]

Practical Recommendations

- Implement CTI or Brief CTI for high-risk patients (homeless, recurrent admissions)[121][123]

- Address social determinants - housing instability is a major readmission driver[115][125]

- Use the READMIT index to identify high-risk patients for targeted intervention[119]

- Combine case management with CBT and psychoeducation - this combination shows the most consistent improvements[124]

---

13. Follow-Up Interventions and Collaborative Care

Post-Discharge Follow-Up

The Safety Planning Intervention with structured telephone follow-up (SPI+) was associated with ~50% fewer suicidal behaviors over 6 months and more than double the odds of engaging in outpatient care.[19] The VA/DoD 2024 guideline recommends periodic caring communications for 12 months post-discharge, with moderate-quality evidence showing a 43% reduction in suicide attempts at 1 year.[4]

Telehealth follow-up shows promise: the ATTEND pilot reduced wait times by 18.6 days and showed lower readmission rates (5% vs. 19%).[126] Telehealth partial hospitalization was as effective as in-person treatment with higher completion rates (72.9% vs. 62.3%).[127]

Collaborative Care

The Collaborative Care Model (CoCM) has one of the strongest evidence bases of any complex intervention in psychiatry, supported by over 90 RCTs.[128][129] The 2012 Cochrane review (79 RCTs, 24,308 participants) demonstrated significantly greater improvement in depression outcomes (SMD -0.34, 95% CI -0.41 to -0.27).[130] A 2025 individual participant data meta-analysis in JAMA Psychiatry (35 datasets, N = 20,046) identified the therapeutic treatment strategy component - particularly manual-based psychotherapy and family involvement - as the most effective driver.[131]

The IMPACT trial (n=1,801) is the landmark CoCM study: 45% of intervention patients had >=50% reduction in depressive symptoms vs. 19% of usual care (OR 3.45, P < .001), with benefits persisting one year after resources were withdrawn.[132][133]

Measurement-Based Care

MBC can improve remission rates by up to 75% compared to usual care.[134] The Joint Commission requires MBC in all accredited behavioral health programs since 2018.[135] However, less than 20% of practitioners engage in MBC, and the VA/DoD 2022 guideline rated the overall evidence as weak.[136][137]

Current Controversies

The DIAMOND initiative highlights the implementation gap: despite increased collaborative care services and higher patient satisfaction, depression remission rates were not significantly different from comparison groups in real-world implementation across 75 clinics.[138] The most important implementation factors were an engaged psychiatrist (r = 0.62) and face-to-face warm handoffs (r = 0.54).[114]

Practical Recommendations

- Implement SPI+ (safety planning + structured telephone follow-up within 72 hours) for all patients at suicide risk[19]

- Send caring contacts (text, mail) for 12 months post-discharge[4]

- Use collaborative care models for depression management in primary care settings[130][132]

- Implement measurement-based care using validated tools (PHQ-9, GAD-7) at every encounter[134][135]

- Leverage telehealth to bridge the gap between discharge and first outpatient appointment[126][127]

---

Summary: Evidence Hierarchy Across Domains

---

Would you like to explore any of these domains in greater depth - for example, specific pharmacological protocols for rapid tranquilization by clinical scenario, or implementation strategies for the Zero Suicide framework in inpatient settings?

The 20 Most Important Papers in Psychopharmacology: A Ranked Curriculum by Medication Class

---

Rank 1. Cipriani et al. - Comparative Efficacy of 21 Antidepressants (SSRIs/SNRIs/Others)

Cipriani A, Furukawa TA, Salanti G, et al. "Comparative Efficacy and Acceptability of 21 Antidepressant Drugs for the Acute Treatment of Adults with Major Depressive Disorder." Lancet. 2018;391(10128):1357-1366. doi:10.1016/S0140-6736(17)32802-7. PubMed: 29477251

Class: SSRIs, SNRIs, TCAs, atypicals | Seminal trial: Yes - the definitive antidepressant comparison

Why #1: This network meta-analysis (522 RCTs, 116,477 participants) settled the public debate about whether antidepressants work and provided the definitive comparative efficacy and tolerability data. All 21 antidepressants were more effective than placebo (ORs 1.37-2.13; overall SMD 0.30). Amitriptyline was most efficacious; reboxetine least. For the critical balance of efficacy and tolerability, escitalopram and sertraline emerged as optimal first-line choices. A "novelty effect" was identified: drugs appeared 1.18 more effective when they were the experimental agent.[1]

Controversy: The mean drug-placebo difference (~2 HDRS points) falls below the NICE 3-point clinical significance threshold, though response/remission rate differences are clinically meaningful (~50% vs. ~30%). A reanalysis argued certainty of evidence should be rated "very low" by GRADE.[2][3]

Current best practice: Start escitalopram or sertraline as first-line for MDD. All antidepressants are effective; selection should be guided by side-effect profile, drug interactions, cost, and patient preference.[1][4]

Educational importance:  Essential | Difficulty: Intermediate | Still practice-changing? Yes

---

Rank 2. STARD - The Reality of Antidepressant Treatment (SSRIs/Switching/Augmentation)

Rush AJ, Trivedi MH, Wisniewski SR, et al. "Acute and Longer-Term Outcomes in Depressed Outpatients Requiring One or Several Treatment Steps: A STARD Report." American Journal of Psychiatry. 2006;163(11):1905-1917. doi:10.1176/ajp.2006.163.11.1905. PubMed: 17074942

Class: SSRIs, SNRIs, bupropion, buspirone, lithium, TCAs | Seminal trial: Yes - the largest depression effectiveness trial

Why #2: STARD (N=4,041, 41 US sites) revealed the gap between efficacy trials and real-world practice. Step 1 citalopram remission was 36.8%; cumulative remission after 4 steps was originally reported as 67% but a 2023 reanalysis using protocol-stipulated blinded measures found it was approximately 35%. No antidepressant switch strategy was superior to another. Relapse rates increased with each step: 34% after step 1 remission vs. 59% for response-without-remission. This trial established measurement-based care as the standard approach and defined treatment-resistant depression as failure of >=2 adequate trials.[5][6][7][8]

Controversy: The 2023 reanalysis (Pigott et al., BMJ Open) challenged the widely cited 67% cumulative remission rate, finding it was inflated by use of unblinded clinician ratings rather than protocol-stipulated blinded HRSD assessments.[7]

Current best practice: Use PHQ-9 at every visit to guide treatment decisions. After 2 failed adequate trials, consider augmentation (lithium, aripiprazole, bupropion) or switch to a different class before declaring treatment resistance.[5][6]

Educational importance:  Essential | Difficulty: Intermediate | Still practice-changing? Yes

---

Rank 3. CATIE - The End of the FGA/SGA Myth (Antipsychotics)

Lieberman JA, Stroup TS, McEvoy JP, et al. "Effectiveness of Antipsychotic Drugs in Patients with Chronic Schizophrenia." NEJM. 2005;353(12):1209-1223. doi:10.1056/NEJMoa051688. PubMed: 16172203

Class: FGAs, SGAs | Seminal trial: Yes - the largest antipsychotic effectiveness trial

Why #3: This NIMH-funded pragmatic trial (N=1,493, 57 US sites) shattered the marketing-driven assumption that SGAs were categorically superior. 74% discontinued before 18 months. Perphenazine (FGA) performed comparably to quetiapine, risperidone, and ziprasidone. Olanzapine had modestly longer time to discontinuation but the worst metabolic profile. In Phase 2, clozapine was superior to other SGAs for patients who failed Phase 1.[9][10]

Controversy: The open-label design and high discontinuation rates limit interpretation. Some argue olanzapine's modest superiority was clinically meaningful despite metabolic costs.

Current best practice: Choose antipsychotics by individual side-effect profile, not class. Reserve clozapine for treatment resistance (after 2 adequate trials).[9]

Educational importance:  Essential | Difficulty: Intermediate | Still practice-changing? Yes

---

Rank 4. Kane et al. - Clozapine for Treatment-Resistant Schizophrenia (Clozapine)

Kane J, Honigfeld G, Singer J, Meltzer H. "Clozapine for the Treatment-Resistant Schizophrenic." Archives of General Psychiatry. 1988;45(9):789-796. doi:10.1001/archpsyc.1988.01800330013001. PubMed: 3046553

Class: Clozapine | Seminal trial: Yes - established clozapine's unique superiority

Why #4: After a rigorous haloperidol lead-in to confirm treatment resistance, 30% of clozapine patients responded vs. 4% on chlorpromazine (p<0.001; SMD -0.88) - an effect size never replicated. Approximately 40% of TRS patients respond to clozapine, yet mean delay to initiation remains ~4 years. Clozapine is the only antipsychotic with two FDA-approved indications: treatment-resistant schizophrenia and suicidality reduction (InterSePT, 2003).[11][12][13]

Modern comparison: The Huhn 2019 NMA (402 RCTs, 53,463 participants) confirmed clozapine's largest effect size (SMD -0.89) among 32 antipsychotics.[14]

Current best practice: Initiate clozapine after 2 failed adequate antipsychotic trials. ANC monitoring: weekly  6 months -> biweekly  6 months -> monthly. Use lower ANC threshold (>=1,000) for benign ethnic neutropenia.[11][15]

Educational importance:  Essential | Difficulty: Intermediate | Still practice-changing? Yes

---

Rank 5. BALANCE Trial - Lithium vs. Valproate for Bipolar Maintenance (Lithium)

BALANCE Investigators, Geddes JR, Goodwin GM, et al. "Lithium Plus Valproate Combination Therapy Versus Monotherapy for Relapse Prevention in Bipolar I Disorder." Lancet. 2010;375(9712):385-395. doi:10.1016/S0140-6736(09)61828-6. PubMed: 20092882

Class: Lithium, valproate | Seminal trial: Yes - the definitive lithium vs. valproate comparison

Why #5: This multicenter RCT (N=330, 41 sites, up to 24 months) demonstrated that lithium monotherapy was significantly superior to valproate monotherapy for preventing relapse (HR 0.71, 95% CI 0.51-1.00; NNT=10). Combination therapy was superior to valproate monotherapy (NNT=7) but not significantly better than lithium monotherapy (NNT=19). This trial re-established lithium's primacy after decades of valproate overtaking it in prescribing patterns.[16]

Modern meta-analysis: Geddes et al. (2004) meta-analysis of 5 RCTs (N=770) confirmed lithium reduces all relapses (RR 0.65) and manic relapses (RR 0.62) vs. placebo.[17]

Current best practice: Lithium should be the default first-line maintenance agent for bipolar I disorder. Valproate monotherapy should not be substituted without reason. Maintenance levels: 0.6-0.8 mmol/L.[16][18]

Educational importance:  Essential | Difficulty: Intermediate | Still practice-changing? Yes

---

Rank 6. Cipriani et al. - Lithium and Suicide Prevention (Lithium)

Cipriani A, Hawton K, Stockton S, Geddes JR. "Lithium in the Prevention of Suicide in Mood Disorders: Updated Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis." BMJ. 2013;346:f3646. doi:10.1136/bmj.f3646. PubMed: 23814104

Class: Lithium | Meta-analysis: Yes - the definitive lithium-suicide analysis

Why #6: This meta-analysis of 48 RCTs (N=6,674) found lithium reduced completed suicides by 87% (OR 0.13, 95% CI 0.03-0.66) and all-cause mortality by 62% (OR 0.38). No other psychiatric medication has comparable anti-suicide evidence. However, the Katz et al. 2022 VA RCT (N=519) was stopped for futility, possibly due to subtherapeutic levels (mean 0.42 mEq/L). Observational data remain strongly supportive: a Swedish within-individual study (N=51,535) found 14% reduction in suicide-related events during lithium treatment.[19][20][21]

Controversy: The tension between the dramatic meta-analytic effect (OR 0.13) and the negative VA RCT remains unresolved. The VA/DoD 2024 guideline notes mixed evidence.[22][23]

Current best practice: Preferentially consider lithium in patients with mood disorders and suicidal history. Ensure therapeutic levels (0.6-1.0 mEq/L).[19][18]

Educational importance:  Essential | Difficulty: Intermediate | Still practice-changing? Yes

---

Rank 7. UK ECT Review Group - Definitive ECT Efficacy (ECT)

UK ECT Review Group. "Efficacy and Safety of Electroconvulsive Therapy in Depressive Disorders." Lancet. 2003;361(9360):799-808. doi:10.1016/S0140-6736(03)12705-5. PubMed: 12642045

Class: ECT | Meta-analysis: Yes - the definitive ECT efficacy review

Why #7: This systematic review established ECT's superiority over both sham ECT (SES -0.91, 6 trials) and pharmacotherapy (SES -0.80, 18 trials). Bilateral ECT was moderately more effective than unilateral (SES -0.32). These effect sizes are among the largest in all of psychiatry. ECT achieves 60-80% response rates in treatment-resistant depression.[24][25]

Modern comparison: The ELEKT-D trial (Anand et al., NEJM 2023; N=403) showed ketamine was noninferior to ECT for nonpsychotic TRD (55.4% vs. 41.2% response), with less cognitive impact, though ECT may remain superior for psychotic and late-life depression.[26]

The following figure from the ELEKT-D trial shows response rates and longitudinal depression scores, demonstrating ketamine's noninferiority to ECT.

Figure 1 Response to Ketamine and ECT According to the QIDS-SR-16 and MADRS during the Initial 3-Week Treatment Phase.

Current best practice: ECT remains first-line for psychotic depression, catatonia, severe suicidality, and treatment resistance. Always plan continuation treatment - 84% relapse on placebo at 24 weeks (Sackeim 2001).[27]

Educational importance:  Essential | Difficulty: Intermediate | Still practice-changing? Yes

Rank 8. Sackeim et al. - Post-ECT Relapse Prevention (ECT + Pharmacotherapy)

Sackeim HA, Haskett RF, Mulsant BH, et al. "Continuation Pharmacotherapy in the Prevention of Relapse Following Electroconvulsive Therapy." JAMA. 2001;285(10):1299-1307. doi:10.1001/jama.285.10.1299. PubMed: 11255384

Class: ECT, TCAs, lithium | Seminal trial: Yes - first post-ECT relapse prevention RCT

Why #8: This double-blind RCT (N=84 remitters) revealed the critical problem of post-ECT relapse: placebo 84%, nortriptyline alone 60%, nortriptyline + lithium 39% at 24 weeks. Even the best regimen left substantial relapse risk, particularly in the first month. The CORE study (2006) subsequently showed continuation ECT was equivalent to nortriptyline-lithium (~46% sustained remission both arms), and the PRIDE study (2016) demonstrated that continuation ECT + medication achieved >80% sustained response in geriatric depression.[27][28][29]

The following figure shows the Kaplan-Meier survival curves for all three arms, with the placebo curve declining precipitously.

Figure 2

Current best practice: Never discharge a patient after ECT without a continuation plan. Nortriptyline-lithium or continuation ECT are the evidence-based options. A 2026 Delphi consensus recommends lithium + antidepressant for all post-ECT patients.[30]

Educational importance:  Essential | Difficulty: Intermediate | Still practice-changing? Yes

---

Rank 9. Zarate et al. - Ketamine for Treatment-Resistant Depression (Ketamine)

Zarate CA, Singh JB, Carlson PJ, et al. "A Randomized Trial of an N-Methyl-D-Aspartate Antagonist in Treatment-Resistant Major Depression." Archives of General Psychiatry. 2006;63(8):856-864. doi:10.1001/archpsyc.63.8.856. PubMed: 16894061

Class: Ketamine (NMDA antagonist) | Seminal trial: Yes - launched the glutamatergic antidepressant era

Why #9: This crossover RCT (N=18) demonstrated that a single IV ketamine infusion (0.5 mg/kg over 40 min) produced antidepressant effects within 2 hours, with 71% response at 24 hours (Hedges' g ~1.0). Effects peaked at 24 hours and waned by 7 days. This paradigm shift - onset in hours rather than weeks - catalyzed the entire field of rapid-acting antidepressants and led to esketamine's FDA approval (2019).[31][32][33]

Modern trials: ELEKT-D (2023) showed ketamine noninferior to ECT.[26] SUSTAIN-1 showed esketamine reduced relapse by 51% in remitters (HR 0.49, NNT=6).[34] However, an IPD meta-analysis found esketamine's effect vs. placebo was only 2.94 MADRS points - below the clinical significance threshold.[35]

The following figure from the SUSTAIN-1 trial shows clear separation in time to relapse between continued esketamine and placebo groups.

Figure 2 Kaplan-Meier Estimates of Time to Relapse

Controversy: Blinding is problematic (dissociative effects); saline-controlled trials show larger effects (d ~1.8) than midazolam-controlled trials (d ~0.7). The FDA label states effectiveness in preventing suicide has not been established.[36][37][38]

Current best practice: Reserve ketamine/esketamine for patients who have failed multiple adequate pharmacologic trials. It is a bridge intervention, not a standalone treatment.[39]

Educational importance:  Essential | Difficulty: Intermediate | Still practice-changing? Yes

Rank 10. Tiihonen et al. - Real-World Antipsychotic Effectiveness and LAIs (LAIs)

Tiihonen J, Mittendorfer-Rutz E, Majak M, et al. "Real-World Effectiveness of Antipsychotic Treatments in a Nationwide Cohort of 29,823 Patients with Schizophrenia." JAMA Psychiatry. 2017;74(7):686-693. doi:10.1001/jamapsychiatry.2017.0899. PubMed: 28493348

Class: LAIs, oral antipsychotics | Seminal trial: Yes - the definitive real-world LAI study

Why #10: This within-individual analysis (N=29,823, Sweden) showed clozapine and LAI formulations are the most effective treatments in real-world settings. LAIs were associated with 22% lower rehospitalization than equivalent oral formulations (HR 0.78); in newly diagnosed patients, the advantage was 32% (HR 0.68). The Kishimoto 2013 mirror-image meta-analysis (N=5,940) found an even larger 57% reduction (RR 0.43).[40][41]

The following figure shows the treatment failure hierarchy, with clozapine and LAIs clustering well below oral alternatives.

Figure 3 Adjusted Hazard Ratios (HRs) and 95% CIs for Treatment Failure During Each Monotherapy Compared With Oral Olanzapine Use

Controversy: RCTs consistently show no LAI advantage over oral formulations - the consensus explanation is that RCTs select adherent patients, masking LAI benefits. The EULAST trial (2023, N=511) found no significant difference in early-phase schizophrenia, except in patients with comorbid substance use disorder (36% lower discontinuation with LAIs).[42][43]

Current best practice: Offer LAIs early - not as a "last resort" for "noncompliant" patients. The greatest benefit occurs in early-phase illness.[40][44]

Educational importance:  Essential | Difficulty: Intermediate | Still practice-changing? Yes

---

Rank 11. MTA Cooperative Group - Multimodal Treatment of ADHD (Stimulants)

MTA Cooperative Group. "A 14-Month Randomized Clinical Trial of Treatment Strategies for Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder." Archives of General Psychiatry. 1999;56(12):1073-1086. doi:10.1001/archpsyc.56.12.1073. PubMed: 10591283

Class: Stimulants (methylphenidate) | Seminal trial: Yes - the landmark ADHD treatment study

Why #11: The largest and longest ADHD RCT (N=579, 14 months) showed carefully managed medication was substantially superior to behavioral treatment alone and community care for core ADHD symptoms. Combined treatment (medication + behavioral) was not significantly superior to medication alone for core symptoms but offered advantages in non-ADHD domains (academic performance, parent-child relations). Success rates: combined 68%, medication 56%, behavioral 34%, community care 25%.[45][46]

Modern comparison: The Cortese 2018 NMA (133 RCTs) confirmed methylphenidate as first-choice in children (SMD -0.78, best tolerability) and amphetamines in adults (SMD -0.79, most efficacious).[47]

Controversy: The 3-year follow-up showed the medication advantage was no longer apparent, possibly due to convergence in medication use across groups. Growth suppression of 1-2 cm from predicted adult height was identified.[48][49]

Current best practice: Stimulants are first-line for ADHD in children >=6 years and adults. Careful titration and monthly follow-up are essential - the MTA's superiority over community care was attributed to systematic dose optimization.[49]

Educational importance:  Essential | Difficulty: Introductory | Still practice-changing? Yes

---

Rank 12. Turner et al. - Publication Bias in Antidepressant Trials (SSRIs)

Turner EH, Matthews AM, Linardatos E, Tell RA, Rosenthal R. "Selective Publication of Antidepressant Trials and Its Influence on Apparent Efficacy." NEJM. 2008;358(3):252-260. doi:10.1056/NEJMsa065779. PubMed: 18199864

Class: SSRIs, SNRIs, atypicals | Seminal study: Yes - exposed systematic publication bias

Why #12: By comparing 74 FDA-registered trials with their published counterparts, Turner revealed that 94% of published trials appeared positive vs. only 51% per FDA analysis. Twenty-two negative studies were never published; 11 were published as positive. Published literature inflated effect sizes by 32% overall. A 2022 follow-up found reporting bias has diminished but persists for newer antidepressants.[50][51]

Why it matters for trainees: This paper teaches critical appraisal - the published literature systematically overestimates antidepressant efficacy. Every trainee should understand that the evidence base they read is filtered through publication bias.

Educational importance:  Essential | Difficulty: Introductory | Still practice-changing? Yes - foundational for evidence-based medicine

---

Rank 13. Leucht et al. - Maintenance Antipsychotic Treatment, NNT=3 (Antipsychotics)

Leucht S, Tardy M, Komossa K, et al. "Antipsychotic Drugs Versus Placebo for Relapse Prevention in Schizophrenia." Lancet. 2012;379(9831):2063-2071. doi:10.1016/S0140-6736(12)60239-6. PubMed: 22560607

Class: All antipsychotics | Meta-analysis: Yes - the definitive maintenance evidence

Why #13: This meta-analysis of 65 RCTs (N=6,493) showed maintenance antipsychotics reduce 1-year relapse from 64% to 27% (NNT=3) - among the strongest treatment effects in all of medicine. LAI formulations reduced relapse more than oral medications (RR 0.31 vs. 0.46). The updated Cochrane review (75 RCTs, N=9,145) confirmed these findings.[52][53]

Current best practice: Maintenance antipsychotic treatment is essential for relapse prevention. The NNT of 3 should be shared with patients during shared decision-making discussions.[52]

Educational importance:  Essential | Difficulty: Introductory | Still practice-changing? Yes

---

Rank 14. Fudala et al. - Buprenorphine/Naloxone for Opioid Use Disorder (Buprenorphine)

Fudala PJ, Bridge TP, Herbert S, et al. "Office-Based Treatment of Opiate Addiction with a Sublingual-Tablet Formulation of Buprenorphine and Naloxone." NEJM. 2003;348(1):24-32. doi:10.1056/NEJMoa022164. PubMed: 12510039

Class: Buprenorphine/naloxone (partial opioid agonist) | Seminal trial: Yes - enabled office-based OUD treatment

Why #14: This pivotal 4-week RCT (N=326) demonstrated that buprenorphine/naloxone was significantly superior to placebo for opioid-negative urines (17.8% vs. 5.8%) and treatment retention. This trial led to FDA approval and, combined with the DATA 2000 Act, enabled office-based OUD treatment for the first time - moving addiction treatment from methadone clinics to primary care. The X-waiver requirement was eliminated in January 2023, further expanding access.[54]

Modern challenge: Fentanyl's lipophilicity complicates standard buprenorphine induction. Alternative approaches include micro-dosing (Bernese method: start <=0.5 mg while continuing full agonist) and high-dose induction (8-32 mg on day 1).[55][56][57]

Current best practice: Any DEA-licensed prescriber can now prescribe buprenorphine for OUD. Standard induction: wait for COWS >=8-12, then 2-4 mg SL, titrate to 8-16 mg on day 1. For fentanyl users, consider micro-dosing or high-dose protocols.[58][56]

Educational importance:  Essential | Difficulty: Intermediate | Still practice-changing? Yes

---

Rank 15. Saitz et al. - Symptom-Triggered Benzodiazepine Dosing for Alcohol Withdrawal (Benzodiazepines)

Saitz R, Mayo-Smith MF, Roberts MS, et al. "Individualized Treatment for Alcohol Withdrawal: A Randomized Double-Blind Controlled Trial." JAMA. 1994;272(7):519-523. doi:10.1001/jama.1994.03520070039035. PubMed: 8046805

Class: Benzodiazepines (chlordiazepoxide) | Seminal trial: Yes - established symptom-triggered dosing

Why #15: This double-blind RCT (N=101) demonstrated that CIWA-Ar-guided symptom-triggered dosing reduced treatment duration from 68 to 9 hours (p<0.001) and total benzodiazepine dose from 425 to 100 mg chlordiazepoxide (p<0.001), with no differences in withdrawal severity, seizures, or delirium tremens. A meta-analysis (6 RCTs, N=664) confirmed 60-hour reduction in treatment duration. This trial fundamentally changed alcohol withdrawal management worldwide.[59][60]

Current best practice: ASAM 2020 recommends symptom-triggered dosing as preferred. Use long-acting agents (diazepam, chlordiazepoxide) except in liver disease (use lorazepam/oxazepam). Front-load for severe withdrawal (CIWA-Ar >=19).[61]

Educational importance:  Essential | Difficulty: Introductory | Still practice-changing? Yes

---

Rank 16. Pillinger et al. - Metabolic Effects of 18 Antipsychotics (Antipsychotics)

Pillinger T, McCutcheon RA, Vano L, et al. "Comparative Effects of 18 Antipsychotics on Metabolic Function in Patients with Schizophrenia." Lancet Psychiatry. 2020;7(1):64-77. doi:10.1016/S2215-0366(19)30416-X. PubMed: 31860457

Class: All antipsychotics | Meta-analysis: Yes - the definitive metabolic risk hierarchy

Why #16: This NMA of 100 RCTs (N=25,952) provided the definitive metabolic risk ranking: clozapine (+3.01 kg) and olanzapine (+2.78 kg) worst; ziprasidone, haloperidol, aripiprazole, lurasidone, and cariprazine cause no significant weight gain. A novel finding was that improvements in psychopathology correlated with metabolic worsening (r=0.36), suggesting shared neurobiological pathways. This operationalizes the ADA/APA metabolic monitoring consensus.[62]

Current best practice: Baseline and follow-up monitoring of weight, BMI, fasting glucose, and lipids for every patient on antipsychotics. Consider metformin co-initiation with olanzapine or clozapine (-3.32 kg weight gain reduction).[63][64][65]

Educational importance:  Essential | Difficulty: Introductory | Still practice-changing? Yes

---

Rank 17. Kaul et al. - Xanomeline-Trospium: The First Non-Dopaminergic Antipsychotic (Novel Mechanism)

Kaul I, Sawchak S, Correll CU, et al. "Efficacy and Safety of the Muscarinic Receptor Agonist KarXT (Xanomeline-Trospium) in Schizophrenia (EMERGENT-2)." Lancet. 2024;403(10422):160-170. PubMed: 38104575

Kaul I, Sawchak S, Walling DP, et al. "Efficacy and Safety of Xanomeline-Trospium Chloride in Schizophrenia (EMERGENT-3)." JAMA Psychiatry. 2024;81(8):749-756. PubMed: 38691388

Class: Muscarinic agonist (M1/M4) + peripheral antagonist | Seminal trial: Yes - first non-D2 antipsychotic

Why #17: The EMERGENT trials broke the 70-year monopoly of D2 receptor blockade. Xanomeline-trospium achieved PANSS reductions of -9.6 (d=0.61) and -8.4 (d=0.60) vs. placebo - exceeding the median effect size of 0.42 across 105 antipsychotic trials. Critically, EPS rates were 0%, weight gain 0%, and no prolactin elevation. FDA approved September 2024. Main side effects are cholinergic: nausea, vomiting, constipation.[66][67][68]

Current best practice: Xanomeline-trospium is a new option for patients who cannot tolerate D2-blocking antipsychotics due to EPS, weight gain, or hyperprolactinemia. Long-term data and head-to-head comparisons are still needed.[68]

Educational importance:  Very Important | Difficulty: Intermediate | Still practice-changing? Yes - the first new antipsychotic mechanism in 70 years

---

Rank 18. Hammad et al. / Bridge et al. - The FDA Black Box Warning (Antidepressants in Youth)

Hammad TA, Laughren T, Racoosin J. "Suicidality in Pediatric Patients Treated with Antidepressant Drugs." Archives of General Psychiatry. 2006;63(3):332-339. PubMed: 16520440

Bridge JA, Iyengar S, Salary CB, et al. "Clinical Response and Risk for Reported Suicidal Ideation and Suicide Attempts in Pediatric Antidepressant Treatment." JAMA. 2007;298(15):1801-1812. PubMed: 17940236

Class: SSRIs, SNRIs, TCAs | Meta-analyses: Yes - the evidence behind the black box warning

Why #18: Hammad's FDA meta-analysis (24 pediatric trials, >4,400 patients) found antidepressants doubled suicidal ideation/behavior (4% vs. 2%, RR 1.95), with no completed suicides. Bridge's counterpoint showed NNH=143 for suicidality vs. NNT=10 for MDD response - benefits far outweigh risks. Stone et al. (2009, 372 adult RCTs, N=99,231) extended the analysis: risk increased in patients <25 (OR 2.30), was neutral at 25-64, and protective at >=65 (OR 0.06). The warning's unintended consequence: antidepressant prescribing dropped 31% in adolescents while suicide attempts increased 21.7%.[69][70][71][72]

Controversy: A 2024 systematic review found the warning's intended effect (increased monitoring) was not achieved, while unintended reductions in mental health care occurred.[73]

Current best practice: Fluoxetine is the only antidepressant with robust efficacy evidence in youth (Cipriani 2016 pediatric NMA). Monitor at weeks 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, and 12. Combine with CBT when possible.[74][75]

Educational importance:  Essential | Difficulty: Introductory | Still practice-changing? Yes - shapes every youth prescription

---

Rank 19. Furukawa et al. - Optimal SSRI Dosing (SSRIs)

Furukawa TA, Cipriani A, Cowen PJ, et al. "Optimal Dose of Selective Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitors, Venlafaxine, and Mirtazapine in Major Depression." Lancet Psychiatry. 2019;6(7):601-609. doi:10.1016/S2215-0366(19)30217-2. PubMed: 31178367

Class: SSRIs, venlafaxine, mirtazapine | Meta-analysis: Yes - the definitive dose-response analysis

Why #19: This dose-response meta-analysis (77 studies, 19,364 participants) demonstrated that SSRI efficacy plateaus at 20-40 mg fluoxetine equivalents - the minimum effective dose is generally optimal. Above this range, no further efficacy gain occurred, but dropouts due to adverse effects increased exponentially (RR 1.94 at 40 mg, 3.73 at 80 mg fluoxetine equivalents). For venlafaxine, efficacy increased up to 75-150 mg; for mirtazapine, up to ~30 mg.[76]

Current best practice: Start SSRIs at the minimum effective dose (e.g., sertraline 50 mg, escitalopram 10 mg). Higher doses add side effects without efficacy for most patients. The exception is OCD, which requires higher doses (fluoxetine 60-80 mg) and longer trials (8-12 weeks).[76]

Educational importance:  Very Important | Difficulty: Introductory | Still practice-changing? Yes

---

Rank 20. Lichtenstein et al. - ADHD Medication Reduces Criminality (Stimulants)

Lichtenstein P, Halldner L, Zetterqvist J, et al. "Medication for Attention Deficit-Hyperactivity Disorder and Criminality." NEJM. 2012;367(21):2006-2014. doi:10.1056/NEJMoa1203241. PubMed: 23171097

Class: Stimulants | Landmark cohort study: Yes - the definitive real-world outcomes study

Why #20: This Swedish national register study (N=25,656) used within-individual comparisons to show that ADHD medication was associated with a 32% reduction in criminality for men (HR 0.68) and 41% for women (HR 0.59) during medicated vs. non-medicated periods. Companion studies showed 58% reduction in serious transport accidents (Chang 2014) and reduced suicidal behaviors, substance misuse, and transport accidents (Zhang 2025 target trial emulation, N=148,581).[77][78][79]

Why it matters for trainees: This paper demonstrates that ADHD treatment benefits extend far beyond symptom control - to criminal justice involvement, motor vehicle safety, and mortality. It provides the strongest argument for treating ADHD as a public health priority.

Educational importance:  Very Important | Difficulty: Introductory | Still practice-changing? Yes

Notable Papers That Narrowly Missed the Top 20

Suggested Reading Order by Training Phase

Phase 1 - Foundations (Weeks 1-2): Turner (#12) for critical appraisal, then Cipriani (#1) and STARD (#2) for the antidepressant evidence base. Add Furukawa (#19) for practical dosing and Hammad/Bridge (#18) for the black box warning.

Phase 2 - Antipsychotics & Mood Stabilizers (Weeks 3-4): CATIE (#3), Kane/Clozapine (#4), Leucht/Maintenance (#13), and Pillinger (#16) as a block. Then BALANCE (#5) and Cipriani/Suicide (#6) for lithium. Add KarXT (#17) for the frontier.

Phase 3 - Somatic Treatments & Special Populations (Weeks 5-6): UK ECT Review (#7), Sackeim (#8), and Zarate (#9) for ECT and ketamine. Tiihonen (#10) for LAIs. MTA (#11) and Lichtenstein (#20) for ADHD. Fudala (#14) for buprenorphine and Saitz (#15) for alcohol withdrawal.

Would you like to explore the evidence for any specific medication class in greater depth - such as the comparative cardiovascular safety data for ADHD medications, the emerging evidence for psilocybin, or the detailed clozapine monitoring protocols?

## Source: `OPENEVIDENCE RAW FILES TO REVIEW/OPENEVIDENCE TOP 200.docx`

OPENEVIDENCE TOP 200

This is a massive undertaking. Let me plan the approach and begin systematic research across all major psychiatric subdomains.

Now let me research the remaining subdomains.

Now let me research the remaining subdomains - child/adolescent psychiatry, suicide, personality disorders, eating disorders, geriatric psychiatry, and psychiatric epidemiology/nosology.

Now I have comprehensive research across all major subdomains. Let me compile the definitive ranked list.

---

The Psychiatry Canon: 200 Papers Every Graduating Psychiatrist Should Know

Format and Methodology

This list was compiled by systematically surveying the evidence landscape across all major psychiatric subdomains, identifying papers that meet one or more of the following criteria: (1) changed clinical practice, (2) established a new treatment paradigm, (3) provided definitive evidence on a contested question, (4) introduced a foundational concept or framework, or (5) represent the best available synthesis of a critical topic. The list is weighted toward the modern era (2000-present) while including classic landmarks that remain essential knowledge. Papers are ranked #1-25 overall, then organized by subdomain with internal ranking.

---

TOP 25: THE ESSENTIAL CANON

These are the 25 papers that, taken together, define the intellectual foundation of modern psychiatry. A graduating resident who deeply understands these 25 papers possesses the conceptual scaffolding for the entire field.

**1. STARD - Rush et al., "STARD: Revising Conventional Wisdom," CNS Drugs 2009 (summary of all phases)**

The largest and most influential effectiveness trial in psychiatry. Enrolled 4,041 outpatients with MDD across sequential treatment steps. Demonstrated ~33% remission with initial citalopram, declining rates with each subsequent step, and a cumulative remission of ~35-67% (depending on analytic method).[1][2] Established that no single antidepressant is clearly superior, both switching and augmentation are reasonable strategies, and measurement-based care is feasible. Every treatment algorithm in depression traces back to STARD.

**2. CATIE - Lieberman et al., "Effectiveness of Antipsychotic Drugs in Patients with Chronic Schizophrenia," NEJM 2005**

The landmark NIMH-funded trial (N=1,460) that shattered the assumption of second-generation antipsychotic superiority. Found 74% discontinuation before 18 months, perphenazine comparable to most SGAs, and olanzapine modestly superior but with significant metabolic costs.[3][4][5] Phase 2 demonstrated clozapine's superiority for treatment-resistant cases.[6] Fundamentally changed how psychiatrists think about antipsychotic selection.

**3. Cipriani et al., "Comparative Efficacy and Acceptability of 21 Antidepressant Drugs," Lancet 2018**

The definitive network meta-analysis (522 RCTs, 116,477 participants) establishing that all 21 antidepressants are more effective than placebo, with agomelatine, escitalopram, mirtazapine, and venlafaxine among the most efficacious.[7] The single most cited reference for antidepressant comparative effectiveness.

**4. Felitti et al., "Relationship of Childhood Abuse and Household Dysfunction to Many of the Leading Causes of Death in Adults: The ACE Study," Am J Prev Med 1998**

Surveyed 9,508 adults and demonstrated a graded dose-response relationship between adverse childhood experiences and adult disease, with >=4 ACEs conferring 4-12 increased risk for depression, suicide attempt, alcoholism, and drug abuse.[8][9] Transformed understanding of the developmental origins of psychiatric illness.

**5. Kessler et al., "Lifetime Prevalence and Age-of-Onset Distributions of DSM-IV Disorders in the NCS-R," Arch Gen Psychiatry 2005**

The NCS-R (N=9,282) established that 46.4% of Americans meet criteria for a mental disorder in their lifetime, with half of all cases beginning by age 14 and three-quarters by age 24.[10] Defined the epidemiological landscape of psychiatry and underscored the critical importance of early intervention.

**6. Kane et al., "Clozapine for the Treatment-Refractory Schizophrenic," Arch Gen Psychiatry 1988**

The pivotal trial (N=268) demonstrating clozapine's 30% response rate vs. 4% for chlorpromazine in treatment-resistant schizophrenia.[11] Led to FDA approval and established clozapine as the gold standard for TRS - a position it has held for nearly four decades.

**7. Turner et al., "Selective Publication of Antidepressant Trials and Its Influence on Apparent Efficacy," NEJM 2008**

Compared 74 FDA-registered antidepressant trials with their published counterparts, finding that 94% of published trials appeared positive vs. 51% per FDA assessment, with 32% effect size inflation.[12] Essential for understanding publication bias and critical appraisal of the psychiatric literature.

**8. Caspi et al., "Influence of Life Stress on Depression: Moderation by a Polymorphism in the 5-HTT Gene," Science 2003 - paired with Border et al., "No Support for Historical Candidate Gene Hypotheses for Major Depression," AJP 2019**

These two papers together tell the story of psychiatric genetics' evolution. Caspi's landmark GxE study launched a decade of candidate gene research; Border's definitive refutation (N=62,138-443,264) effectively ended the candidate gene era.[13][14] Together they illustrate both the promise and the pitfalls of genetic research in psychiatry.

**9. Sachs et al., "Effectiveness of Adjunctive Antidepressant Treatment for Bipolar Depression," NEJM 2007 (STEP-BD)**

The STEP-BD antidepressant trial (N=366) found no benefit of adjunctive antidepressants for bipolar depression - durable recovery 23.5% vs. 27.3% with placebo.[15] Changed clinical practice and guideline recommendations regarding antidepressant use in bipolar disorder.

**10. Linehan et al., "Two-Year Randomized Controlled Trial of DBT vs Therapy by Experts for Suicidal Behaviors and BPD," Arch Gen Psychiatry 2006**

The definitive DBT trial (N=101) demonstrating that DBT halved suicide attempts compared to expert community therapy in women with BPD.[16] Established DBT as the first empirically validated treatment for BPD and the model for manualized psychotherapy research.

**11. Schizophrenia Working Group of the PGC, "Biological Insights from 108 Schizophrenia-Associated Genetic Loci," Nature 2014**

The landmark GWAS (36,989 cases, 113,075 controls) identifying 128 independent associations across 108 loci, including DRD2 and glutamatergic genes.[17] Among the top 10 most cited NIMH-funded papers, this study validated the polygenic architecture of schizophrenia and opened the era of large-scale psychiatric genomics.

**12. Howes & Kapur, "The Dopamine Hypothesis of Schizophrenia: Version III - The Final Common Pathway," Schizophr Bull 2009**

The most cited modern formulation of the dopamine hypothesis, synthesizing >6,700 articles to propose that multiple risk factors converge on increased presynaptic striatal dopaminergic function, leading to psychosis via aberrant salience.[18] Essential conceptual framework for understanding psychosis.

**13. Mann et al., "Suicide Prevention Strategies: A Systematic Review," JAMA 2005**

The foundational systematic review establishing that physician education in depression recognition and restricting access to lethal means are the only strategies with clear evidence of reducing suicide rates.[19] The starting point for all evidence-based suicide prevention.

**14. Elkin et al., "NIMH Treatment of Depression Collaborative Research Program," J Consult Clin Psychol 1989**

The most influential comparative psychotherapy trial (N=239), comparing IPT, CBT, imipramine, and placebo.[20][21] Established the template for psychotherapy research and sparked decades of debate about the relative efficacy of psychotherapy and pharmacotherapy.

**15. Hollon et al., "Prevention of Relapse Following Cognitive Therapy vs Medications," Arch Gen Psychiatry 2005**

Demonstrated that patients withdrawn from prior CT had 31% relapse vs. 76% for medication withdrawal, establishing the enduring effect of cognitive therapy.[22] One of the most important findings in psychotherapy research - that psychotherapy teaches skills providing lasting protection.

**16. UK ECT Review Group, "Efficacy and Safety of ECT in Depressive Disorders," Lancet 2003**

The definitive meta-analysis establishing ECT's superiority over sham (SES -0.91) and pharmacotherapy (SES -0.80).[23] The evidence base for psychiatry's most effective acute treatment for severe depression.

**17. Cipriani et al., "Lithium in the Prevention of Suicide in Mood Disorders," BMJ 2013**

Meta-analysis of 48 RCTs (6,674 participants) demonstrating lithium reduces completed suicides (OR 0.13) and deaths from any cause (OR 0.38).[24] The strongest evidence for any pharmacological anti-suicide intervention.

**18. BALANCE Trial - Geddes et al., "Lithium Plus Valproate Combination Therapy vs Monotherapy for Bipolar I Disorder," Lancet 2010**

The definitive lithium vs. valproate comparison (N=330), establishing lithium's superiority over valproate monotherapy and supporting combination therapy.[25] Anchors bipolar maintenance treatment guidelines worldwide.

**19. Moncrieff et al., "The Serotonin Theory of Depression: A Systematic Umbrella Review," Mol Psychiatry 2022**

The most influential recent challenge to the serotonin hypothesis, finding no consistent evidence that depression is associated with lowered serotonin.[26] Essential for understanding the limitations of monoamine theories and the shift toward neuroplasticity frameworks.

**20. Rosenhan, "On Being Sane in Insane Places," Science 1973**

Eight pseudopatients admitted to psychiatric hospitals despite normal behavior after admission.[27][28] Despite serious methodological concerns and allegations of fraud, this paper accelerated the development of DSM-III's operationalized criteria and remains essential for understanding diagnostic validity, labeling, and the history of psychiatric nosology.[29]

**21. March et al., "Fluoxetine, CBT, and Their Combination for Adolescents with Depression (TADS)," JAMA 2004**

The landmark adolescent depression trial (N=439) establishing combination treatment (71% response) as superior to either monotherapy.[30][31] The foundational reference for child/adolescent depression treatment.

**22. Whiteford et al., "Global Burden of Disease Attributable to Mental and Substance Use Disorders," Lancet 2013**

GBD 2010 data establishing mental disorders as the leading cause of years lived with disability worldwide (22.9% of all YLDs).[32] Transformed the global health policy conversation about mental illness.

**23. Caspi et al., "Longitudinal Assessment of Mental Health Disorders Across 4 Decades (Dunedin Study)," JAMA Network Open 2020**

Across 4 decades, 86% of cohort members met criteria for a disorder at some point, with 692 unique life-history patterns among 1,037 participants.[33] Introduced the p-factor concept and demonstrated that mental disorders are far more common, comorbid, and fluid than categorical diagnosis suggests.

**24. Anton et al., "Combined Pharmacotherapies and Behavioral Interventions for Alcohol Dependence (COMBINE)," JAMA 2006**

The definitive AUD pharmacotherapy trial (N=1,383) establishing naltrexone's efficacy and, surprisingly, acamprosate's lack of efficacy in a US population.[34][35] The reference point for all AUD treatment decisions.

**25. Stanley et al., "Safety Planning Intervention With Follow-up vs Usual Care," JAMA Psychiatry 2018**

Demonstrated that the Safety Planning Intervention reduced suicidal behaviors by ~50% over 6 months.[36] The most impactful brief intervention in suicide prevention and now standard of care.

B. PSYCHOPHARMACOLOGY - SCHIZOPHRENIA (Papers 46-65)

46. Huhn et al., "Comparative Efficacy and Tolerability of 32 Oral Antipsychotics," Lancet 2019 - Updated NMA (53,463 participants): clozapine, amisulpride, olanzapine, risperidone most efficacious[58]

47. Leucht et al., "Second-Generation vs First-Generation Antipsychotic Drugs," Lancet 2009 - Only clozapine, amisulpride, olanzapine, risperidone superior to FGAs[59]

48. Leucht et al., "Antipsychotic Drugs vs Placebo for Relapse Prevention," Lancet 2012 - Relapse reduced from 64% to 27% (NNT=3); depot > oral[60]

51. Taipale et al., "20-Year Follow-Up of Physical Morbidity and Mortality (FIN20)," World Psychiatry 2020 - Antipsychotic use halves mortality; clozapine most protective (aHR 0.39)[63]

53. Meltzer et al., "Clozapine Treatment for Suicidality (InterSePT)," Arch Gen Psychiatry 2003 - Clozapine reduced suicidal behavior vs. olanzapine (HR 0.76)[65][66]

54. Kane et al., "Comprehensive vs Usual Care for First-Episode Psychosis (RAISE-ETP)," AJP 2016 - NAVIGATE improved quality of life and symptoms; effects stronger with shorter DUP[67][68]

56. Kahn et al., "Amisulpride and Olanzapine Followed by Clozapine (OPTiMiSE)," Lancet Psychiatry 2018 - 56% remit on first antipsychotic; no benefit of switching; 28% remit on clozapine[70]

65. Efthimiou et al., "Combining RCT and Real-World Data for Antipsychotic Effectiveness," Lancet Psychiatry 2024 - Clozapine most effective; drug effectiveness 40% larger in RCT-eligible patients[81]

73. Yildiz et al., "Pharmacological Interventions for Acute Bipolar Depression (NMA)," Lancet Psychiatry 2023 - OFC, quetiapine, lurasidone, cariprazine effective; lithium not[89]

A Note on Scope

This list necessarily omits important papers in several areas that a comprehensive curriculum would also address, including: sleep medicine and psychiatry, consultation-liaison psychiatry (delirium management), forensic psychiatry, cultural psychiatry, telepsychiatry, and the social determinants of mental health. Several classic texts (Kraepelin's nosology, Freud's foundational works, Jaspers' General Psychopathology) are better assigned as book chapters than individual papers. The list also does not include the many excellent NEJM, JAMA, and Lancet review articles that serve as outstanding teaching tools for each disorder - these are better curated at the rotation level.

Would you like to explore any specific subdomain in greater depth, or discuss how this curriculum might be structured across the four years of residency training?
