## Source: `OPENEVIDENCE RAW FILES TO REVIEW/Perinatal and Reproductive Psychiatry_ A Comprehensive Evidence Review for Adult Inpatient Psychiatry.docx`

Perinatal and Reproductive Psychiatry: A Comprehensive Evidence Review for Adult Inpatient Psychiatry

Scope and Framing

This review synthesizes the evidence landscape on psychiatric medication safety and management during pregnancy, postpartum, and lactation - organized for use as both a clinical quick-reference on inpatient psychiatry units and a resident teaching resource. Coverage spans psychiatric hospitalization indications, postpartum psychosis, bipolar disorder management, psychotropic medication safety (antidepressants, antipsychotics, mood stabilizers, benzodiazepines), ECT, lactation, novel FDA-approved therapies, and contraception counseling. Guideline positions from ACOG (2023), APA, NICE, AAN/AES/SMFM (2024), and VA/DoD (2023) are integrated throughout.

---

1. Psychiatric Hospitalization During Pregnancy and Postpartum

Epidemiology and Indications

Postpartum psychiatric admissions occur at a rate of approximately 4 per 1,000 deliveries, with the most common indications being substance-related disorders (28.8%) and depression (28.7%).[1] Hospitalizations are generally short (median 3 days) and occur later than expected (median 5.5 months postpartum).[1] Key risk factors include age <20 (aOR 5.01), treatment for schizophrenia during pregnancy (aOR 4.21), and any psychiatric diagnosis during pregnancy (aOR 3.58).[1]

Indications for emergent psychiatric hospitalization in the perinatal period include active suicidal ideation with plan or intent, postpartum psychosis (a psychiatric emergency), severe mood decompensation with inability to care for self or infant, command hallucinations or delusions involving the infant, and acute agitation or grossly disorganized behavior.[2][3][4] ACOG 2023 guidelines state that patients with psychosis, active suicidal thoughts, or thoughts of harming their newborns should receive same-day psychiatric consultation and referral for possible inpatient treatment.[5]

Specialized Perinatal Units

NICE guidelines recommend mother and baby units (MBUs) as the preferred setting for inpatient psychiatric care of postpartum women, allowing co-admission of mother and infant.[6][7] MBUs provide perinatally-focused, family-centered care; women and clinicians prefer MBUs over general psychiatric wards, where separation of mothers and babies is experienced as traumatic.[7] A quasi-experimental study across 42 UK healthcare organizations found no significant difference in 12-month readmission rates between MBU and non-MBU care (aOR 0.95, 95% CI 0.86-1.04), but service satisfaction was significantly higher among MBU patients.[8] The first US Perinatal Psychiatry Inpatient Unit (PPIU) at UNC Chapel Hill demonstrated significant improvements in depression, anxiety, suicidal ideation, and functioning between admission and discharge (all p < 0.0001).[6]

---

2. Postpartum Psychosis

Epidemiology and Clinical Features

Postpartum psychosis occurs in approximately 1-2 per 1,000 births, with onset typically within the first 1-4 weeks after delivery (median ~10 days).[4][9][10] The DSM-5 classifies it under mood episodes with the "peripartum onset" specifier rather than as a distinct diagnosis, though expert consensus now recommends reclassification within the bipolar disorders chapter based on shared genetic architecture and treatment response.[11][12]

Earliest symptoms include feeling excited/elated/high (52%), inability to sleep (48%), increased energy (37%), and increased talkativeness (31%).[13] Core features include mood fluctuation, delusions (87.6%), persecutory delusions (75.2%), visual hallucinations (52.3%), auditory hallucinations (48.1%), and cognitive confusion.[14] Bipolar I disorder is the strongest risk factor, with a recurrence risk of 30-50% per subsequent delivery in women with a prior episode.[12]

Differential Diagnosis

Organic causes must be excluded: autoimmune thyroiditis, infections, anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis, and inborn errors of metabolism.[4] Postpartum delirium (fluctuating level of awareness/attention) must be differentiated from postpartum psychosis.[12] Thyroid function should be assessed in all cases.[12]

Treatment

The largest treatment study (N = 64) used a structured sequential algorithm - benzodiazepines -> antipsychotics -> lithium -> ECT - achieving complete remission in 98.4% within the first three steps; none required ECT.[7] Lithium maintenance was associated with significantly lower relapse rates than antipsychotic monotherapy.[7] ECT response rates are higher in the postpartum period (87.0%) than outside it (73.5%, p = 0.001).[7] Lithium has an NNT of 3 for prevention of postpartum mood episode relapse.[14]

---

3. Bipolar Disorder in Pregnancy and Postpartum

Relapse Risk

Pregnancy itself appears to be a relatively low-risk period for new bipolar episodes (~5.2% episode risk during pregnancy in BD-I).[15] However, postpartum relapse risk is substantial: a meta-analysis across 5,700 deliveries found a pooled relapse rate of 35% (95% CI 29-41), rising to 39% (95% CI 29-49) for any mood episode in BD-I specifically.[16][17] The risk is six times higher after delivery compared to during pregnancy.[15] Mania/psychosis within 6 weeks postpartum occurs in 23% of BD-I patients versus 4% in BD-II.[18]

Medication status profoundly affects relapse risk: medication-free during pregnancy carries a 66% relapse rate (95% CI 57-75) versus 23% (95% CI 14-37) with prophylactic medication - a more than twofold reduction.[16] Abrupt discontinuation increases relapse risk significantly.[19]

Prophylaxis Strategy

For women with history of postpartum psychosis only (no bipolar disorder outside the perinatal period), lithium prophylaxis initiated immediately postpartum avoids in utero exposure; in one study, 0% of women who used postpartum prophylaxis relapsed versus 44.4% who declined.[20] For women with established bipolar disorder, prophylaxis should continue throughout pregnancy and postpartum, with the understanding that 24.4% may still relapse during pregnancy.[20] A written perinatal bipolar relapse prevention plan covering maintenance treatment, delivery planning, postpartum medication, feeding plan, sleep/circadian strategies, and early symptom recognition is recommended.[21]

---

4. Antidepressants in Pregnancy

Teratogenicity: SSRIs as a Class

Overall risk is small and substantially attenuated by confounding by indication. A meta-analysis of 29 cohort studies (>9 million births) found SSRIs associated with a modest increase in major congenital anomalies (RR 1.11, 95% CI 1.03-1.19), but when restricted to women with a psychiatric diagnosis, neither association remained significant (RR 1.04, 95% CI 0.95-1.13).[22] The landmark Huybrechts et al. NEJM cohort (949,504 pregnancies) showed that associations between SSRIs and cardiac defects were progressively attenuated with increasing confounding adjustment, with a fully adjusted RR of 1.06 (95% CI 0.93-1.22) among women with depression.[23] A 2025 umbrella review found no convincing or highly suggestive evidence of adverse health outcomes associated with psychotropic medication use in pregnant people with mental disorders.[24]

The following figure from the Huybrechts et al. NEJM study demonstrates how associations between antidepressants and specific cardiac malformations progressively attenuate with increasing confounding adjustment.

Figure 2 Risk of Specific Cardiac Malformation in Infants, According to Maternal Exposure to Antidepressants.

Individual SSRI Profiles

Sertraline and escitalopram are recommended as first-line by ACOG 2023 for treatment-naive patients with perinatal depression.[26] Escitalopram showed no elevated adjusted ORs with any examined birth defects in the National Birth Defects Prevention Study (NBDPS).[27] Paroxetine carries the highest concern among SSRIs: a meta-analysis of 23 studies found first-trimester exposure associated with major cardiac malformations (pooled OR 1.28, 95% CI 1.11-1.47), specifically atrial septal defects (OR 2.38) and right ventricular outflow tract defects (OR 2.29).[28] The FDA label states paroxetine should be "initiated only after consideration of the other available treatment options" in women in the first trimester.[29] Fluoxetine has been associated with right ventricular outflow tract obstruction (OR 2.0) and craniosynostosis (OR 1.9) in Bayesian analysis, though these attenuate after confounding adjustment.[17]

SNRIs

SNRIs show higher point estimates for congenital malformations than SSRIs. A 2023 meta-analysis found SNRIs associated with cardiovascular abnormalities (OR 1.64, 95% CI 1.36-1.97) and nervous system malformations (OR 2.28, 95% CI 1.50-3.45).[30] Venlafaxine had the highest proportion of elevated birth defect associations among all antidepressants in the NBDPS, including anencephaly (aOR 9.14, 95% CI 1.91-43.83).[31] Duloxetine appears unlikely to be a major teratogen (PS-matched OR 0.98, 95% CI 0.74-1.30 for major malformations in a Danish-Swedish cohort of >2 million births), but duloxetine-exposed infants had the highest rates of NICU admission (39.6%) among individual antidepressants studied.[28][32]

Persistent Pulmonary Hypertension of the Newborn (PPHN)

A meta-analysis found SSRI/SNRI exposure associated with PPHN (OR 2.08, 95% CI 1.44-3.01 for exposure >20 weeks), with an incidence of 2.9 per 1,000 and NNH ~1,000.[33] However, the largest US study (3.8 million pregnancies) found the association substantially attenuated after high-dimensional propensity-score adjustment (OR 1.10, 95% CI 0.94-1.29 for SSRIs), suggesting much of the observed risk may be due to confounding.[34]

Neonatal Adaptation Syndrome (PNAS)

This is the most consistently documented adverse effect of late-pregnancy SSRI/SNRI exposure, occurring in 20-30% of exposed neonates.[35][36] Symptoms include irritability, tachypnea, temperature instability, jitteriness, and tremor. Severe syndrome (seizures, intubation) is rare (~1/313 cases); no neonatal deaths have been attributed to SRI exposure.[35] Symptoms are typically self-limited, resolving within 2 weeks.[35] Discontinuation of SSRIs in the third trimester does not improve neonatal outcomes.[37]

Long-Term Neurodevelopmental Outcomes

Converging evidence from sibling-design studies suggests that observed associations between prenatal antidepressant exposure and neurodevelopmental problems (ASD, ADHD) are largely due to confounding by maternal condition rather than direct drug effects. The Suarez et al. JAMA Internal Medicine study (2022) using Medicaid data found that sibling analyses showed hazard ratios very close to 1.0 for all neurodevelopmental outcomes.[7] A 2026 Lancet Psychiatry meta-analysis of 37 studies confirmed that associations were largely attenuated in sensitivity analyses, and pre-conception antidepressant use showed similar risk elevations, arguing against causation.[38]

Risks of Untreated Depression

Untreated antenatal depression carries its own risks: preterm birth (OR 1.56), low birth weight (OR 1.96), intrauterine growth restriction (RR 4.39), and decreased breastfeeding initiation (OR 0.68).[39][40][41]

---

5. Antipsychotics in Pregnancy

Antipsychotics do not appear to be major teratogens. A meta-analysis of 12 studies (>10 million pregnancies) found borderline evidence of association with congenital malformations (OR 1.27, 95% CI 0.996-1.624, p = 0.054), with no significant association when limited to SGAs (OR 1.16, 95% CI 0.78-1.72).[42] Aripiprazole, olanzapine, and quetiapine are not associated with increased risk of major congenital malformations, whereas risperidone and paliperidone may carry a very minor increased risk.[43]

Gestational diabetes risk is the primary metabolic concern. The most recent meta-analysis (2025) found an overall OR of 1.33 (95% CI 1.22-1.44) for antipsychotic use and GDM, driven by SGAs (1.4 higher risk) with no increased risk for FGAs.[44] Drug-specific data show adjusted RRs of 1.61 for olanzapine and 1.28 for quetiapine, with no significant increase for aripiprazole, ziprasidone, or risperidone.[45]

The FDA drug label for all antipsychotics warns of neonatal extrapyramidal and/or withdrawal symptoms in neonates exposed during the third trimester.[46] Approximately 32.6% of SGA-exposed infants experience at least one PNAS sign, comparable to the 34.6% rate in SSRI/SNRI-exposed infants.[47] A 2025 systematic review found transient motor delays but no persistent increased risk of neurodevelopmental disorders after adjusting for confounders.[48]

---

6. Mood Stabilizers in Pregnancy

Lithium

Teratogenicity. The Patorno et al. NEJM 2017 study (N = 1,325,563 pregnancies, 663 lithium-exposed) found cardiac malformations in 2.41% of lithium-exposed infants versus 1.15% of unexposed (adjusted RR 1.65, 95% CI 1.02-2.68).[17] The risk is dose-dependent: RR 1.11 for <=600 mg/day, 1.60 for 601-900 mg/day, and 3.22 (95% CI 1.47-7.02) for >900 mg/day.[17] The historical 400-fold increase in Ebstein anomaly risk from the 1970s International Register of Lithium Babies is now considered a major overestimate based on methodologic limitations.[17] Modern absolute risk of any congenital malformation is approximately 4.2%, and cardiac malformations ~1.2%.[2] Fetal echocardiography between 16-20 weeks gestation is recommended for first-trimester lithium exposure.[17]

The following figure from the Patorno et al. NEJM study illustrates the dose-dependent relationship between lithium exposure and cardiac malformation risk.

Figure 2 Absolute and Relative Risk of Cardiac Malformations among Lithium-Exposed and Lamotrigine-Exposed Infants as Compared with Unexposed Infants, Stratified According to the Mother's Dose of the Drug.

Pharmacokinetic changes. Lithium blood levels decrease by 24% in the first trimester, 36% in the second trimester (nadir), and 21% in the third trimester, with a 9% increase postpartum.[2] Lithium elimination clearance increases an average of 63.5% by the third trimester.[50] The FDA label recommends decreasing or discontinuing lithium 2-3 days before expected delivery to reduce risk of maternal/neonatal toxicity, then restarting at preconception dose when medically stable postpartum.[17][25] Monitoring should include lithium levels every 2-4 weeks until 34 weeks, then weekly until delivery, and twice weekly for the first 2 weeks postpartum.[51]

Risk-benefit balance: Lithium has an NNT of 3 for prevention of mood episode relapse versus NNH of 33 for any congenital anomaly.[2]

Valproate - Contraindicated

Valproate carries the highest teratogenic risk among all psychotropic medications. The overall malformation rate is ~9.3% (vs. 2.1% for lamotrigine), increasing to 25.2% at doses >=1,450 mg/day.[52][53] The risk of spina bifida is 1-2% (vs. background 0.06-0.07%).[54] The NEAD study found age-6 IQ was significantly lower after valproate exposure: mean IQ 97 versus lamotrigine 108, carbamazepine 105, and phenytoin 108, with a dose-dependent effect (r = -0.56, p < 0.0001).[53] Valproate exposure is associated with a 2.9-fold increased risk of ASD.[54]

The FDA contraindicated valproate in pregnancy for migraine prophylaxis (2013) and states it "should not be used" for epilepsy or bipolar disorder unless other medications have failed.[54][55] The AAN/AES/SMFM 2024 guideline states valproate must be avoided if clinically feasible (Level A recommendation).[56] The VA/DoD 2023 guideline recommends against valproate in individuals of childbearing potential.[53]

Carbamazepine

The overall malformation rate is approximately 3.3-5.5%, with spina bifida risk of ~0.5-1% (lower than valproate).[57][58] Neurodevelopmental outcomes appear relatively safe: the NEAD study found no significant IQ difference between carbamazepine and lamotrigine or phenytoin.[53] Carbamazepine is an enzyme-inducing AED; routine neonatal vitamin K is standard, though evidence for antenatal maternal supplementation is insufficient per the AAN 2009 guideline.[25]

Lamotrigine - Preferred

Lamotrigine has the lowest malformation rate among mood stabilizers/ASMs: 2.0-2.9% across major registries, similar to the general population background rate of 2-4%.[59] An initial signal of increased oral cleft risk has not been replicated in multiple large registries and is now considered most likely a chance finding.[35] Neurodevelopmental data are the most reassuring among all ASMs: mean IQ of 108 at age 6 in the NEAD study.[53]

Pharmacokinetic changes are dramatic. Estrogen-induced enhancement of UGT-mediated glucuronidation increases clearance by up to 230% above prepregnancy baseline at 32 weeks.[2] The MONEAD study showed clearance changes begin as early as 3-5 weeks gestation, with a 50% increase by end of the first trimester.[25] PBPK modeling suggests doses need to increase by 1.3-fold in the first trimester, 2.4-fold in the second, and 2.7-fold in the third.[60] In MONEAD, 87.7% of participants had at least 1 dose change, with doses increased by a median of 100 mg/day at 4-6 week intervals.[60] Postpartum, clearance returns to pre-pregnancy values within weeks; dose should be reduced by ~25% weekly for 3 weeks to avoid toxicity.[60]

The following figure from the MONEAD study illustrates the progressive decline in dose-normalized lamotrigine concentrations across trimesters with restoration postpartum.

Figure 1 Lamotrigine and Levetiracetam Dose-Normalized Concentrations During Pregnancy and the Postpartum Period

---

7. Benzodiazepines in Pregnancy

The historical concern about oral clefts originated from 1970s case-control studies. A 2019 meta-analysis of 8 prospective cohort studies found no significant association with overall congenital malformations (OR 1.13, 95% CI 0.99-1.30).[60] However, the largest recent population-based study (South Korea, N = 3,094,227 pregnancies) found a small but significant dose-dependent increased risk: adjusted RR 1.09 (95% CI 1.05-1.13) for overall malformations and 1.15 (95% CI 1.10-1.21) for heart defects, rising to RR 1.26 for >2.5 mg/day lorazepam-equivalent.[62]

Neonatal effects include floppy infant syndrome (hypotonia, lethargy, sucking difficulties, apnea) from third-trimester exposure and neonatal withdrawal in 20-40% of exposed neonates.[63] Guidelines recommend prescribing at the lowest effective dose, preferring lorazepam due to its lack of active metabolites, and optimizing non-pharmacologic alternatives.[63]

---

8. ECT in Pregnancy

ECT is effective for severe depression, suicidal ideation, psychosis, and catatonia during pregnancy, with at least partial remission in 78% of cases.[64] A 2025 scoping review of >1,300 pregnancies confirmed rapid benefit with a manageable safety profile.[65] No associations with congenital anomalies or neurocognitive disturbances in children have been identified.[66]

Pregnancy-specific modifications include: left lateral tilt positioning after ~20 weeks to prevent aortocaval compression; fetal heart rate monitoring before and after ECT in the second and third trimesters; aspiration precautions (consider endotracheal intubation in later trimesters); and multidisciplinary team involvement (obstetrics, MFM, psychiatry, anesthesiology).[66][67] The APA supports ECT use for severe postpartum depressive disorders and states ECT is generally safe in pregnancy.[67]

---

9. Brexanolone and Zuranolone: Novel Therapies for Postpartum Depression

Brexanolone (Zulresso)

FDA-approved March 2019 as the first drug specifically for PPD; no longer commercially available in the US as of January 2025 (FDA approval withdrawn April 2025 at manufacturer's request).[68] Administered as a 60-hour continuous IV infusion requiring REMS-certified facility with continuous monitoring.[69] Phase 2 trial showed a mean HAM-D reduction of 21.0 versus 8.8 for placebo (difference -12.2, p = 0.0075).[70] Phase 3 trials confirmed significant reductions with durable response through day 30.[67]

Zuranolone (Zurzuvae)

FDA-approved August 2023 as the first oral medication specifically for PPD.[71] Dosed at 50 mg orally once daily in the evening with fat-containing food for 14 days.[72] Two phase 3 trials showed significant improvement: HAMD-17 change at day 15 of -15.6 versus -11.6 (difference -4.0, p = 0.001) in Study 1, and -17.8 versus -13.6 (difference -4.2, p = 0.003) in the ROBIN trial.[73][74] Significant improvement was observed from day 3 through day 45.[73] The AAFP notes the mean between-group difference of ~4 points is of borderline clinical significance (MID for HAMD-17 is 3-5 points).[75]

A 2025 Cochrane review of 6 RCTs (674 women) found moderate-certainty evidence that zuranolone probably improves depression response (RR 1.26, 95% CI 1.03-1.55) and remission (RR 1.65, 95% CI 1.22-2.22) at day 45, but low-certainty evidence for brexanolone.[76] All studies were industry-sponsored, and no active-comparator trials exist.[68][76]

Key safety considerations: Zuranolone is a Schedule IV controlled substance; patients must avoid driving or caring for infant alone for >=12 hours after each dose.[68] Animal studies show embryo-fetal toxicity; effective contraception is required during treatment and for 1 week after the final dose.[72] Phase 1 lactation data showed RID <1%, suggesting likely compatibility with breastfeeding, though direct infant data are lacking.[77]

---

10. Lactation Safety

General Principles

A relative infant dose (RID) <10% is the widely accepted threshold below which drug exposure via breast milk is considered clinically unimportant.[78] LactMed (National Library of Medicine) is the authoritative, free resource for lactation safety data.[79] The general clinical principle is to continue the medication that was effective during pregnancy rather than switching for lactation.[80]

Key Drug-Specific Data

Sertraline is the first-line antidepressant for new-onset postpartum depression during lactation: RID ~0.4-2.2%, with 87.4% of infant sertraline levels below the limit of detection.[81][82] Paroxetine is undetectable in infant serum in all studied cases and is preferred during lactation despite pregnancy concerns.[83] Fluoxetine should be avoided if possible during lactation due to higher RID (4-12%) and the highest infant plasma concentrations among SSRIs.[83] Quetiapine (RID <1%) and olanzapine (RID ~1%) are the preferred antipsychotics during breastfeeding.[84][85]

Lithium is the most controversial: RID ~12-30%, with infant serum concentrations averaging ~21% of maternal levels.[84][86] The FDA label states breastfeeding is "not recommended," but more recent evidence supports lithium as a "possible treatment option" during breastfeeding with close monitoring of infant serum lithium, creatinine, and thyroid function.[84][87] Lamotrigine has a relatively high infant-to-maternal serum ratio (~29%) but rare adverse events and reassuring neurodevelopmental data up to 6 years.[88][89] Valproate and carbamazepine have very low milk transfer (RID ~3-5%) and are considered relatively safe during breastfeeding.[78][90]

Lorazepam is the preferred benzodiazepine during lactation due to its lack of active metabolites and low RID.[63][83] A 2025 JAMA Network Open study found no adverse cognitive effects in preschool-aged children exposed to SSRIs through breast milk.[83]

The following figure from the MONEAD/Birnbaum et al. JAMA Neurology study shows infant-to-maternal plasma concentration percentages for antiepileptic drugs, demonstrating that lamotrigine has the highest median transfer (~29%) with wide variability.

11. Contraception Counseling for Teratogenic Medications

Regulatory Framework

No REMS exists for valproate in the US, a major regulatory gap given that valproate is among the most teratogenic drugs in the neuropsychiatric pharmacopeia.[72][33] The US approach relies on boxed warnings, medication guides, and drug safety communications. The European Medicines Agency (EMA) implemented substantially more stringent measures in 2018, including a Pregnancy Prevention Programme requiring highly reliable contraception (IUD or implant), monthly pregnancy tests if not using such contraception, and annual signed risk-acknowledgment forms.[92][72]

Real-World Compliance Gaps

Compliance is alarmingly low across all settings. In the US, only 14.1% of females of reproductive age using valproate were also using contraception (2017-2022).[72] Documentation of teratogenicity discussion occurred in only 13.2% of charts at one US academic medical center.[49] Even in Europe, the monthly proportion of compliant valproate prescriptions with contraceptive coverage was <25% across 5 countries after the 2018 PPP.[49] Pregnancy rates during valproate use in the US did not decrease despite enhanced FDA safety communications.[49]

Contraceptive Method Selection

For women on enzyme-inducing AEDs (carbamazepine, phenytoin, phenobarbital), combined hormonal contraceptives have reduced efficacy (USMEC Category 3).[49] Preferred methods include the LNG-IUD (52 mg), copper IUD, and DMPA (all USMEC Category 1).[49][17] Valproate and lithium do not induce hepatic enzymes and do not reduce hormonal contraceptive efficacy.[93] Lamotrigine has a unique bidirectional interaction with combined oral contraceptives: COCs reduce lamotrigine concentrations by 40-60%, potentially causing breakthrough seizures.[94]

The APA Resource Document on the Post-Roe Era (2024) states that psychiatrists caring for individuals of childbearing age should play a crucial role in discussing and facilitating family planning goals, including contraception access.[95] A comprehensive review in the American Journal of Psychiatry emphasized that long-acting reversible contraceptives (LARCs) have low failure rates and favorable safety profiles, yet are chosen by only 14% of women; all contraceptive methods are acceptable for women with depression (USMEC Category 1).[96]

Medication Safety Summary Table

---

Postpartum Psychosis Emergency Algorithm

Step 1: Recognition and Safety (Hours 0-4)

- Identify red flags: new-onset insomnia, elation, confusion, paranoia, disorganized behavior within 1-4 weeks postpartum

- Assess safety: suicidal ideation, infanticidal ideation, command hallucinations

- Ensure infant safety; do not leave mother alone with infant

- Rule out organic causes: CBC, CMP, TSH, urinalysis, urine drug screen, consider anti-NMDA receptor antibodies

- Admit to inpatient psychiatry (MBU if available)

Step 2: Acute Stabilization (Hours 4-24)

- Lorazepam 1-2 mg PO/IM q4-6h PRN for agitation and insomnia (max 6 mg/day)

- Ensure sleep: treat insomnia aggressively - sleep deprivation worsens psychosis

- If breastfeeding, discuss risks/benefits; lorazepam is preferred BZD

Step 3: Antipsychotic Initiation (Days 1-3)

- If symptoms persist beyond benzodiazepine management:

- Olanzapine 5-10 mg/day PO (preferred if breastfeeding; monitor metabolic effects) OR

- Quetiapine 100-400 mg/day PO (lowest breast milk transfer)

- Haloperidol 2-5 mg PO/IM if rapid control needed (avoid during lactation per FDA)

Step 4: Lithium Initiation (Days 3-7)

- If inadequate response to antipsychotic, or if history of bipolar disorder:

- Lithium carbonate 300 mg BID-TID, titrate to therapeutic level (0.6-1.0 mEq/L)

- Check baseline: Cr, TSH, ECG, pregnancy test

- If breastfeeding: shared decision-making; monitor infant Li, TSH, Cr

- 98.4% achieve remission by this step[7]

Step 5: ECT (If Refractory)

- If inadequate response to Steps 2-4, or if catatonic features present:

- ECT - response rate 87% in postpartum psychosis[7]

- Typically 1-6 sessions for improvement, 5-11 for remission

- Can be administered during lactation

Step 6: Maintenance and Discharge Planning

- Continue lithium for >=9 months minimum (relapse rate 20% vs. 60% without maintenance)

- Written relapse prevention plan: sleep hygiene, early warning signs, emergency contacts

- Outpatient follow-up within 1 week of discharge

- Counsel on 30-50% recurrence risk with future pregnancies[12]

---

Lactation Quick-Reference

Key monitoring for lithium during lactation: Infant serum lithium, creatinine, and thyroid function at baseline and periodically. Infant serum concentrations average ~21% of maternal levels and decrease up to 60% by the third month postpartum.[84][86]

---

Resident Counseling Language

For Antidepressants in Pregnancy

"The evidence shows that SSRIs like sertraline and escitalopram have a very reassuring safety profile in pregnancy. While early studies raised concerns about heart defects, the largest and best-designed studies show that when we account for the depression itself, there is no meaningful increase in risk. The absolute risk of any birth defect is very similar to the general population. On the other hand, untreated depression during pregnancy is associated with preterm birth, low birth weight, and difficulty bonding with your baby. We recommend continuing your antidepressant because the benefits of treating your depression outweigh the small, uncertain risks."

For Lithium in Pregnancy

"Lithium is one of the most effective medications for preventing mood episodes, and it's especially important after delivery when the risk of relapse is highest. There is a small increased risk of heart defects - about 2.4% compared to 1.2% in the general population - and this risk goes up with higher doses. We will get a specialized heart ultrasound of the baby between 16 and 20 weeks. We'll also need to check your lithium levels more frequently during pregnancy because your kidneys clear the drug faster, and we may need to adjust your dose near delivery. The risk of stopping lithium - a 66% chance of relapse - is much higher than the small risk to the baby."

For Valproate

"Valproate is not safe to use during pregnancy. It has about a 1 in 10 chance of causing birth defects, including spinal cord defects, and children exposed to valproate in the womb score lower on IQ tests and have a higher risk of autism. We need to switch you to a safer medication - lamotrigine is the preferred alternative - and make sure you are using reliable birth control. An IUD or implant is the most effective option. If you are planning a pregnancy, we should start this transition well in advance."

For Postpartum Psychosis

"Postpartum psychosis is a psychiatric emergency that affects about 1 in 1,000 new mothers. It usually starts within the first few weeks after delivery with symptoms like not sleeping, feeling unusually high or confused, and having thoughts that don't make sense. It is very treatable - almost all women recover fully with the right medications, which usually include a mood stabilizer and sometimes an antipsychotic. The most important thing right now is your safety and your baby's safety, which is why we are recommending hospitalization. With treatment, most women are back to themselves within a few weeks."

For Breastfeeding on Psychiatric Medications

"Most psychiatric medications pass into breast milk in very small amounts - usually less than 2% of what you take. Sertraline is the best-studied and safest antidepressant for breastfeeding. Quetiapine and olanzapine are the safest antipsychotics. The benefits of breastfeeding for you and your baby - including bonding, immune protection, and reduced postpartum depression - generally outweigh the very small amount of medication your baby would be exposed to. We do not recommend stopping your medication to breastfeed, because the risk of relapse is much more dangerous for both of you."

---

Evidence Gaps and Emerging Data

- No RCTs exist assessing antidepressant efficacy or safety during pregnancy; all evidence is observational.[35]

- Postpartum psychosis lacks a distinct DSM diagnostic classification as of 2026, though expert consensus recommends reclassification within the bipolar disorders chapter.[11]

- No REMS for valproate in the US remains a major regulatory gap, with compliance rates for contraception counseling below 15%.[72]

- No active-comparator trials exist for zuranolone versus SSRIs or psychotherapy.[68]

- The quality of lactation pharmacokinetic studies is generally poor - most antipsychotic studies do not meet FDA/ILCA guidelines for correct RID calculation.[97]

- Whether peripartum lithium dose reduction is truly necessary remains debated; recent data challenge this practice.[53]

- Optimal folic acid dose for women on valproate/carbamazepine (0.4 mg vs. 4-5 mg) is unresolved, with a 2026 Nordic target trial emulation suggesting high-dose folic acid (4-5 mg/day) initiated before pregnancy may reduce MCAs by 45%.[49]

## Source: `OPENEVIDENCE RAW FILES TO REVIEW/QTc Prolongation Risk with Psychotropic and Commonly Co-Prescribed Medications_ A Comprehensive Evidence Review.docx`

QTc Prolongation Risk with Psychotropic and Commonly Co-Prescribed Medications: A Comprehensive Evidence Review

Scope and Framing

This review synthesizes evidence on drug-induced QTc prolongation across psychotropic medications (antipsychotics, antidepressants), methadone, antiemetics, and commonly co-prescribed antibiotics. It integrates guideline recommendations from the AHA, ACC, HRS, and FDA safety communications, and concludes with practical tools for inpatient risk stratification. The focus is on adult populations; pediatric data is referenced where it provides unique comparative insights.

---

1. Pathophysiology: Why QTc Prolongation Matters

Drug-induced QTc prolongation occurs primarily through inhibition of the rapid component of the delayed rectifier potassium current (IKr), encoded by the hERG gene, resulting in prolonged ventricular repolarization and increased susceptibility to early afterdepolarizations (EADs) that can trigger torsades de pointes (TdP).[1] The concept of repolarization reserve - the redundancy of multiple ion currents maintaining normal repolarization - explains why TdP typically requires multiple concurrent "hits" (drug + electrolyte disturbance + genetic predisposition).[1][2] Each 10-ms increase in QTc contributes approximately a 5-7% exponential increase in TdP risk, and a QTc >500 ms is associated with a 2- to 3-fold higher risk for TdP compared to normal values.[3]

The following figure from Roden (NEJM 2004) illustrates the cellular mechanisms linking action potential prolongation, EADs, and transmural dispersion of repolarization to TdP - the fundamental substrate that IKr-blocking drugs and electrolyte disturbances exploit.

Figure 2 Postulated Basic Mechanisms in Arrhythmias Related to Long-QT Intervals.

Critically, QTc prolongation is an imperfect surrogate for TdP/sudden cardiac death (SCD) risk. The relationship is not linear, and some drugs with moderate QTc effects (e.g., ziprasidone) have not shown excess mortality in large trials.[5][3] At least one additional risk factor was present in 92.2% of case reports of drug-associated TdP.[1]

---

2. Antipsychotics

Comparative QTc Data

The pivotal Harrigan et al. (2004) head-to-head randomized study evaluated six antipsychotics at steady-state Cmax: thioridazine produced the greatest QTc prolongation, followed by ziprasidone (~15.9 ms), with haloperidol, quetiapine, olanzapine, and risperidone producing smaller effects. No patient on any agent had QTc >=500 ms.[2] The largest network meta-analysis (Schneider-Thoma et al., Lancet 2026, k=66 trials, n=21,022) confirmed that sertindole, amisulpride, and ziprasidone increased QTc more than at least three other antipsychotics, while brexpiprazole, aripiprazole, and lurasidone increased QTc less than at least three others.[2]

Sudden Cardiac Death: The Ray 2009 NEJM Study

The landmark Ray et al. (NEJM 2009) retrospective cohort study (1,042,159 person-years, 1,870 SCDs) demonstrated that both typical antipsychotics (adjusted IRR 1.99; 95% CI 1.68-2.34) and atypical antipsychotics (IRR 2.26; 95% CI 1.88-2.72) were associated with increased SCD risk versus nonusers, with no significant difference between classes and a clear dose-response relationship for both.[6]

The following figure shows adjusted incidence-rate ratios for SCD across six frequently prescribed antipsychotics stratified by dose.

Figure 2 Adjusted Incidence-Rate Ratios for Sudden Cardiac Death among Current Users of Six Frequently Prescribed Antipsychotic Drugs, According to Dose.

IV Haloperidol

In September 2007, the FDA strengthened label warnings for IV haloperidol regarding QTc prolongation and TdP, recommending continuous ECG monitoring.[8] A systematic review identified 70 cases of IV haloperidol-associated QTc prolongation/TdP; 97% had additional risk factors, and cumulative doses ranged from 5 to 645 mg.[8] However, the MIND-USA secondary analysis (JAMA Network Open 2024) found no evidence that haloperidol or ziprasidone caused clinically relevant QTc changes in critically ill adults with delirium who had baseline QTc <550 ms.[9]

The ZODIAC Trial

The ZODIAC trial (N=18,154 schizophrenia patients) - the largest randomized postmarketing cardiac safety study of any antipsychotic - found no elevated risk of non-suicide mortality with ziprasidone versus olanzapine (RR 1.02; 95% CI 0.76-1.39), though it was not powered to detect rare events like TdP.[3]

FDA Black Box Warnings

Thioridazine carries a black box warning for dose-related QTc prolongation, TdP, and sudden death, restricted to treatment-refractory schizophrenia.[10] All antipsychotics carry a class-wide black box warning regarding increased mortality in elderly patients with dementia-related psychosis.[10][11]

---

3. Antidepressants

Citalopram: The FDA Dose Restriction

Citalopram causes dose-dependent QTc prolongation that is the most well-characterized among antidepressants. In a thorough QT study, the maximum mean QTcNi difference from placebo was 8.5 ms for 20 mg and 18.5 ms for 60 mg.[12] The FDA issued a safety communication (August 2011, revised March 2012) restricting citalopram to a maximum of 40 mg/day (20 mg/day for patients >60 years, hepatic impairment, CYP2C19 poor metabolizers, or concomitant CYP2C19 inhibitors).[12][13] A large EHR study (n=38,397) confirmed the dose-response association, with mean QTc increases of 7.8 ms (10->20 mg) and 10.3 ms (20->40 mg).[14]

Escitalopram

Escitalopram demonstrates dose-dependent QTc prolongation to a lesser degree: maximum mean QTcF difference from placebo was 4.5 ms for 10 mg and 10.7 ms for 30 mg (supratherapeutic).[15] Both citalopram and escitalopram are classified as "Known risk of TdP" by CredibleMeds.[5]

Other SSRIs

A meta-analysis of 16 prospective studies (n=4,292) found SSRIs as a class associated with a dose-dependent QTc increase of +6.10 ms (95% CI 3.47-8.73) versus placebo, with citalopram showing significantly greater prolongation than sertraline, paroxetine, and fluvoxamine.[16] Paroxetine appears to have the lowest QTc risk among SSRIs.[17]

Tricyclic Antidepressants

All TCAs cause significant QRS and QTc prolongation through Class Ia antiarrhythmic (sodium channel blocking) activity.[5][18] TCAs were associated with 7.05 ms greater QTc increase than SSRIs in meta-analysis.[16] In overdose, TCAs are among the most cardiotoxic antidepressants, with the primary conduction abnormality being QRS widening.[19] TCAs should be avoided in patients with cardiovascular disease.[18][20]

SNRIs and Other Antidepressants

Duloxetine and desvenlafaxine show no demonstrated QTc prolongation risk.[21] Venlafaxine has a modest QTc-prolonging potential (~3.7 ms) and is classified as "Possible risk".[5][21] Trazodone carries a "Conditional risk" classification with postmarketing TdP events reported at doses as low as 100 mg.[22] Bupropion was associated with QTc shortening in one large EHR study and is not listed on CredibleMeds TdP risk lists, making it potentially the safest option when QTc risk is a concern.[14]

The NCCN Survivorship guidelines provide a comparative table of first-line antidepressants with QTc risk ratings.

SANXDE-E-1 First-Line Antidepressants for Depression or Anxiety in Adults - NCCN Guidelines - Survivorship p. 94 (v2.2026)

---

4. Methadone

Methadone carries the highest QTc prolongation risk among the drugs reviewed, potently blocking IKr channels. A 2025 meta-analysis of 22 observational studies found a pooled QTc prolongation prevalence of 34% (95% CI 24-43%) among patients on methadone maintenance therapy, with pooled TdP incidence of 2%.[22] A prospective double-blind trial showed mean QTc increases of +17 ms at 4 weeks and +34 ms at 16 weeks with methadone versus +6 ms and +10 ms with buprenorphine; 23% of methadone patients developed QTc prolongation (>470 ms men / >490 ms women) versus 0% on buprenorphine.[23]

The APS/College on Problems of Drug Dependence/Heart Rhythm Society (2014) guideline recommends obtaining follow-up ECG when methadone dose reaches 30-40 mg/day and again at 100 mg/day; QTc >=500 ms warrants switching to an alternative opioid or immediate dose reduction.[24]

---

5. Antiemetics

Ondansetron

Ondansetron prolongs QTc dose-dependently: +5.6 ms at 8 mg IV and +19.5 ms at 32 mg IV.[25] In 2012, the FDA removed the 32 mg single IV dose from labeling, capping the maximum at 16 mg IV.[25][24] At standard clinical doses (4-8 mg), the risk appears low - a prospective ED study (n=435) found mean QTc prolongation of only 7.9 ms with no arrhythmias observed.[26]

Droperidol

Droperidol carries an FDA black box warning (2001) for QTc prolongation and TdP, including fatal cases at or below recommended doses.[27] However, subsequent large studies have challenged this: a retrospective study of 20,122 surgical patients receiving 35,536 doses of 0.625 mg droperidol found zero cases of polymorphic VT or death, and an ED study (n=16,546) found TdP incidence of only[28] 0.006%.[22]

---

6. Commonly Co-Prescribed Antibiotics

Fluoroquinolones

All fluoroquinolones prolong QTc via IKr blockade with significant intraclass variability. Moxifloxacin carries the highest risk (mean QTc change +6-14 ms at 400 mg oral; used as the positive control in ICH E14 thorough QT studies).[29][30] A meta-analysis found fluoroquinolone use associated with 85% increased risk of arrhythmia (OR 1.85; 95% CI 1.22-2.81), with moxifloxacin ranking highest.[31] Ciprofloxacin has the lowest QTc risk among fluoroquinolones, with a cardiac safety profile comparable to amoxicillin.[32][33] Risk hierarchy: moxifloxacin >> levofloxacin > ciprofloxacin.[31][32][34]

Macrolides

The landmark Ray et al. (NEJM 2012) study found 5-day azithromycin therapy associated with increased cardiovascular death versus amoxicillin (HR 2.49; 95% CI 1.38-4.50), with an estimated 47 additional cardiovascular deaths per 1 million courses.[35] The FDA updated azithromycin labeling to warn of QTc prolongation and TdP risk.[23] Erythromycin (especially IV) and clarithromycin have higher IKr-blocking potency than azithromycin and carry known TdP risk.[36][37]

---

7. Electrolyte Abnormalities

Hypokalemia

Hypokalemia is the most well-established electrolyte risk factor for TdP, reported in 17-70% of patients who develop drug-induced TdP.[38] The mechanisms are multiple and synergistic: enhanced IKr fast inactivation, dramatically increased drug block potency of IKr (the IC50 for dofetilide shifts ~30-fold between high and low [K+]), hERG channel internalization and degradation, and increased dispersion of repolarization.[39][40][41]

Hypomagnesemia

Hypomagnesemia frequently coexists with hypokalemia and impairs potassium repletion - magnesium must be repleted first.[42] IV magnesium (1-2 g) is first-line therapy for acute TdP regardless of serum magnesium level, likely through suppression of EADs via calcium channel inhibition.[1][43]

Hypocalcemia

Hypocalcemia prolongs the QT interval by impairing calcium-dependent inactivation of L-type calcium channels, specifically prolonging the ST segment (plateau phase).[44] For every 1 mg/dL decrease in serum total calcium, QTc increases by approximately 13 ms.[45] However, TdP from hypocalcemia alone is rare.[3]

Electrolyte Correction Targets

---

8. Congenital Long QT Syndrome

Patients with congenital LQTS have inherently reduced repolarization reserve, making them fundamentally more susceptible to drug-induced TdP.[1][2] Nearly 30% of patients who develop drug-induced QT prolongation carry mutations in one of the 5 major LQTS genes.[1] The 2017 AHA/ACC/HRS guideline assigns a Class III: Harm recommendation: QT-prolonging medications are potentially harmful in LQTS patients.[46]

The CredibleMeds "drugs to avoid in congenital LQTS" list is intentionally conservative and includes essentially all commonly used psychotropic medications.[5][47] Bupropion is the notable exception - not listed on CredibleMeds TdP risk lists and associated with QTc shortening - though it has not been specifically studied in cLQTS populations.[14] A study from the Rochester LQTS Registry found a striking genotype-specific effect: antidepressant therapy was associated with increased cardiac arrhythmic events in LQT1 patients (HR 3.67; 95% CI 1.98-6.82) but not in LQT2 patients.[46]

---

9. Inpatient Risk Stratification: The Tisdale Risk Score

The Tisdale Risk Score was developed and validated by Tisdale et al. (2013) in 1,200 cardiac care unit patients for predicting QTc prolongation (QTc >500 ms or increase >60 ms from baseline).[48]

Risk categories: Low (<=6): 15% incidence; Moderate (7-10): 37% incidence; High (>=11): 73% incidence of QTc prolongation.[48] The C statistic was 0.823 in the development cohort. In a large multi-center study (n=92,383 across 28 hospitals), a modified Tisdale score was strongly associated with inpatient mortality: OR 4.80 for moderate risk and OR 11.51 for high risk.[49]

Limitations

The Tisdale score has high sensitivity but low specificity (97% sensitivity, 16% specificity in one ICU validation), making it better for ruling out risk than ruling it in.[50] It was developed in cardiac care unit patients and has not been validated across all populations.[46] There is no consensus on a single optimal QT correction formula; Bazett is most commonly used but overestimates QTc at faster heart rates; Fridericia is preferred by the FDA and in oncology.[48][33]

---

10. QTc Thresholds for Action

The AHA/ACC 2010 Scientific Statement and 2020 AHA Scientific Statement on Drug-Induced Arrhythmias provide the following framework:[1][3][48]

---

11. Comprehensive Medication Risk Table

---

12. Resident Risk Stratification Algorithm

Step 1: Baseline Assessment (Before Starting QTc-Prolonging Drug)

1. Obtain 12-lead ECG and calculate QTc (use Bazett for clinical practice; Fridericia if HR >100 or <60)[48]

2. Check electrolytes: K+, Mg2+, Ca2+

3. Calculate Tisdale Risk Score (see table above)[48]

4. Screen for: congenital LQTS (personal/family history of syncope, SCD, known LQTS), structural heart disease, HFrEF, bradycardia, hepatic/renal impairment

5. Review medication list for concurrent QTc-prolonging drugs and CYP interactions (check CredibleMeds.org)

Step 2: Risk-Stratified Decision

- Tisdale <=6 (Low Risk): Proceed with drug; repeat ECG after steady state (typically 5 half-lives or 48-72 hours); correct any electrolyte abnormalities[48]

- Tisdale 7-10 (Moderate Risk): Prefer lower-risk alternatives when available (e.g., aripiprazole over haloperidol; sertraline over citalopram; ciprofloxacin over moxifloxacin); if proceeding, obtain ECG at 8-12 hours and at steady state; maintain K+ >4.0, Mg2+ >=2.0[1][48]

- Tisdale >=11 (High Risk): Strongly prefer lowest-risk alternatives; if QTc-prolonging drug is essential, continuous telemetry; ECG every 8-12 hours; aggressive electrolyte correction (K+ 4.5-5.0, Mg2+ >=2.0); cardiology consultation[1][48]

Step 3: QTc-Based Action Tiers

- QTc >450 ms (M) / >460 ms (F): Review medications -> check electrolytes -> reassess risk-benefit -> repeat ECG in 8-12 hours[48]

- QTc >470 ms (M) / >480 ms (F): All above -> consider dose reduction or switch -> correct electrolytes to target -> cardiology consultation if >=2 risk factors[3][45]

- QTc >500 ms OR QTc >=60 ms: Discontinue offending drug(s) -> continuous telemetry -> aggressive electrolyte correction -> defibrillator at bedside -> cardiology consultation -> keep in highest-surveillance unit[1][3][48]

- Active TdP: IV magnesium sulfate 1-2 g -> potassium repletion to 4.5-5.0 -> if refractory with bradycardia: overdrive pacing or isoproterenol -> defibrillation if hemodynamically unstable[42][43]

Step 4: Ongoing Monitoring

- Inpatient: ECG before and every 8-12 hours after initiation/dose change of QTc-prolonging drug; more frequently if QTc prolongation observed[48]

- Outpatient: 12-lead ECG at 1-2 weeks after initiation, then every 3-6 months depending on risk factors[1][52]

- Methadone-specific: ECG at baseline, at 30-40 mg/day, at 100 mg/day, and annually thereafter[24]

- Serial ECGs should be recorded at the same time of day due to ~25 ms circadian variation in QTc[52]

---

13. Monitoring Recommendations Summary

---

14. Evidence Gaps and Emerging Data

Several important uncertainties remain. No RCTs have specifically evaluated potassium repletion for TdP prevention; the evidence supporting specific K+ targets is largely observational and mechanistic.[3] Whether baseline and serial ECG monitoring reduces mortality in patients on QT-prolonging medications remains unproven.[45] The 2025 Lancet network meta-analysis of RCT data found little evidence of clinically significant QTc prolongation with any antidepressant, likely reflecting the younger, healthier populations enrolled in RCTs versus real-world populations.[24] General genetic screening for prediction of drug-induced TdP is not currently recommended, though polygenic risk scores show promise.[1] The Clinical Toxicology Workgroup (2025) concluded that TdP risk is "likely overstated" for quetiapine, olanzapine, and risperidone, and concern should focus on thioridazine, amisulpride, and ziprasidone specifically.[48]

---

15. Summary

Drug-induced QTc prolongation and TdP are rare but potentially fatal complications that require systematic risk assessment, particularly in inpatient settings where multiple QTc-prolonging drugs are commonly co-prescribed. The Tisdale Risk Score provides a validated framework for inpatient risk stratification (C statistic 0.823), though it has high sensitivity but low specificity.[48] Among antipsychotics, aripiprazole and lurasidone carry the lowest QTc risk, while thioridazine carries the highest.[2][51] Among antidepressants, bupropion and duloxetine are the safest choices, while citalopram carries the highest risk with FDA-mandated dose restrictions.[12][14][21] Methadone requires dedicated ECG monitoring protocols.[24] The critical action threshold is QTc >500 ms or QTc >=60 ms, which should trigger drug discontinuation, continuous telemetry, and aggressive electrolyte correction.[1][3] Electrolyte targets of K+ >4.0 mEq/L and Mg2+ >=2.0 mg/dL should be maintained in all patients on QTc-prolonging drugs, with IV magnesium 1-2 g as first-line therapy for acute TdP regardless of serum levels.[1][42]

## Source: `OPENEVIDENCE RAW FILES TO REVIEW/Social Determinants of Health, Structural Competency, and Health Inequities in Inpatient Psychiatry_ A Comprehensive Evidence Review.docx`

Social Determinants of Health, Structural Competency, and Health Inequities in Inpatient Psychiatry: A Comprehensive Evidence Review

---

1. Scope and Framing

This review synthesizes the evidence on how social determinants of health (SDOH) shape psychiatric inpatient outcomes, how structural competency provides a framework for understanding and addressing these forces, and what interventions can mitigate the resulting inequities. The evidence draws from systematic reviews, meta-analyses, landmark trials, APA resource documents, the DSM-5-TR, VA/DoD guidelines, and major conceptual papers. The scope encompasses twelve SDOH domains and their intersection with five key psychiatric outcomes: readmission, suicide risk, medication adherence, ED boarding, and discharge failure.

---

2. Structural Competency: The Conceptual Foundation

From Cultural to Structural Competency

Structural competency, introduced by Metzl and Hansen (2014), shifts clinical attention from cross-cultural understanding of individual patients toward the social, economic, and political forces that produce health inequities at levels above the clinical encounter.[1] The framework was explicitly proposed as an evolution beyond cultural competency, which the authors argued relies on static understandings of culture and demonstrates limited effects on health outcomes.[1][2] Structural competency trains clinicians to recognize how upstream determinants - policies, institutions, economic systems, and power structures - shape how symptoms, attitudes, and diseases manifest in patients.[1]

The Five Core Competencies

Metzl and Hansen define five skills: (1) recognizing structures that shape clinical interactions, (2) developing an extra-clinical language of structure, (3) rearticulating "cultural" formulations in structural terms, (4) observing and imagining structural interventions, and (5) developing structural humility - recognizing the limits of one's own structural knowledge.[1] The critical reframe is that what clinicians typically attribute to "culture" (e.g., non-adherence, missed appointments, treatment refusal) should be understood as products of structural forces (transportation barriers, insurance gaps, food insecurity).[1]

Related Frameworks

Structural vulnerability (Bourgois, Holmes, et al., 2017) operationalizes these concepts for clinical practice through a structured assessment tool that extends the traditional social history to identify patients whose health problems are exacerbated by local hierarchies and power relationships.[3] Structural stigma (Sukhera et al., 2022) provides a four-component educational framework - Recognize, Reflect, Reframe, Respond - for dismantling stigma related to mental health and substance use in clinical learning environments.[4] The APA's DSM-5-TR (2022) formally acknowledges that racism exists at personal, interpersonal, systemic/institutional, and social structural levels, and that structural racism manifests in pervasive inequities in economic resources, power, and privilege.[5]

---

3. SDOH Domains and Their Impact on Psychiatric Outcomes

Housing Insecurity

Housing instability is the single most consistently replicated SDOH predictor of psychiatric readmission. A 2026 systematic review of 15 studies found housing instability was "repeatedly associated with psychiatric readmission across population-based, hospital-based, and clinical registry studies." Effect sizes are large: homelessness at index admission was associated with aHR 2.04 (95% CI 1.65-2.51) for 30-day readmission in a Vancouver cohort; an urban community hospital found an OR of 29 for early readmission among homeless patients; and homeless patients in England had 2.49 times the rate of emergency readmission versus housed patients.[2][6][7][8] Among homeless adults, mean antipsychotic medication possession ratio over 15 years was only 0.41 - well below the 0.80 threshold for clinical effectiveness - with duration of homelessness significantly associated with lower adherence.[3] The prevalence of lifetime suicide attempt among homeless individuals is 28.9% (95% CI 21.7-37.2%).[9]

Poverty and Socioeconomic Deprivation

A Finnish national study found a steep negative income gradient for first psychiatric hospital admissions, with the lowest income decile having incidence rate ratios of 2.94-4.46 compared to the highest decile.[10] Area-level deprivation shows a dose-response relationship with involuntary psychiatric hospitalization.[11] Among patients with schizophrenia, low socioeconomic level independently predicted medication nonadherence (OR 3.68, 95% CI 1.42-9.53).[12] Financial strain disproportionately affects psychiatric medication adherence compared to non-psychiatric medications.[12] Being on income assistance was associated with increased suicide attempt risk in the year after psychiatric discharge (HR 1.17, 95% CI 1.01-1.35).[13]

Cumulative Social Needs: The Dose-Response Relationship

Using the 2017 Nationwide Readmissions Database (n=13.2 million), a dose-response relationship was demonstrated: 30-day readmission was 11.5% with no health-related social needs (HRSN), 27.0% with 1 HRSN domain, and 63.5% with all 5 domains (aOR 12.55, 95% CI 9.04-17.43).[14] This compounding effect underscores that SDOH rarely operate in isolation.

The following figure from a VA study illustrates how social risks independently predict readmission and ED use even after clinical adjustment, with food insecurity, legal problems, and neighborhood deprivation showing the strongest associations.[15]

Racism and Structural Discrimination

Racial disparities in inpatient psychiatry are pervasive, well-documented, and operate across every stage of the care pathway.

Involuntary commitment: A major international meta-analysis (71 studies, 1,953,135 participants) found Black Caribbean patients had OR 2.53 (95% CI 2.03-3.16) and Black African patients OR 2.27 (1.62-3.19) for compulsory admission compared with White patients.[16] A US prospective cohort found Black patients were significantly more likely to be involuntarily admitted (aOR 1.57, 95% CI 1.26-1.95).[1]

Restraint and seclusion: A large retrospective study (n=29,739) found Black patients were significantly more likely to experience a restraint event (aOR 1.85) and had significantly longer restraint duration.[17] Among patients awaiting psychiatric hospitalization in the ED, Black race was associated with nearly 3-fold higher odds of physical restraint (OR 2.84, 1.03-7.84).[2]

Diagnostic disparities: The overdiagnosis of schizophrenia in Black patients is one of the most persistent disparities in psychiatry. A 2024 JAMA Psychiatry meta-analysis (64 studies, 54,929 people) confirmed Black individuals had a pooled OR of 2.07 (1.64-2.61) for schizophrenia diagnosis compared with White individuals, and structured assessments did not fully mitigate the disparity.[18] Critically, a 2025 national study found that after adjusting for a neighborhood Social Vulnerability Metric, the Black-White difference was attenuated and no longer statistically significant (aOR 2.49, 0.63-9.90), suggesting neighborhood-level social determinants partially explain the disparity.[19]

The forest plot from the van der Ven et al. JAMA Psychiatry meta-analysis illustrates the consistency of elevated schizophrenia diagnosis risk among Black compared with White individuals across studies:

Treatment quality: Black patients received disproportionately more PRN antipsychotics (17.7% vs. 8.2% of White patients) and were 58% more likely to receive antipsychotic PRNs over non-antipsychotic PRNs.[20] Black patients were significantly less likely to receive clozapine (OR 0.40) and more likely to receive haloperidol (OR 1.52).[3] Racial/ethnic minority patients were significantly more likely to be admitted to low-safety inpatient psychiatric facilities.[21]

Pathways to care: Black patients had significantly higher odds of police transport to the ED (aOR 1.64, 95% CI 1.57-1.72).[22] In England, Black Caribbean patients had OR 2.64 for police contact during pathways to psychiatric care, while GP involvement was less likely.[23]

Insurance Barriers

Children with government insurance were 18% more likely to be rehospitalized within 90 days than those with private insurance (aOR 1.18, 95% CI 1.04-1.34).[24] Medicaid patients aged 45-64 had the highest adjusted odds of 30-day readmission (aOR 1.67 vs. private insurance).[25] Having health insurance was a strong correlate of mental health treatment use (private insurance aOR 1.63; Medicaid aOR 2.66 for any mental illness), and uninsured individuals were 6.9 percentage points less likely to receive counseling than Medicaid enrollees.[26]

Rural Access Issues

More than half of all US counties - all rural - lack a practicing psychiatrist, psychologist, or social worker, and over 85% of federally designated mental health professional shortage areas are in rural communities.[27] Only 1.6% of rural zip codes have an office-based mental health specialist physician, compared to 17.6% of urban zip codes (UOR 13.52).[28] Psychiatry workforce adequacy in non-metropolitan areas is projected at 34.8% in 2026, declining to below 25% in some states by 2038.[29] Rural Medicare beneficiaries had lower rates of follow-up care after psychiatric hospitalization (HR 0.81, p < 0.001) and greater ED use postdischarge.[30]

The following figure displays the geographic distribution of specialty mental health treatment resources across US communities, demonstrating the stark urban-rural divide:

Criminal Legal Involvement

Approximately 15-30% of county jail inmates have serious mental illness, compared to ~4% of the general community - there are now more than ten times as many individuals with SMI behind bars as in state psychiatric hospitals.[31][32] A 2025 meta-analysis of 131 publications across 43 countries found pooled prevalence of depression at 12.8% and any psychosis at 4.1% among incarcerated populations.[9] Prior incarceration was associated with significantly worse mental health at age 50 (aOR 1.9 for any mental health history; aOR 2.2 for past-year depression).[33] Justice system involvement was among the SDOH most strongly associated with suicide mortality in a 2025 JAMA Psychiatry umbrella review.[9] Suicide is the leading cause of death in jails, at a rate of 46 per 100,000.[32]

Food Insecurity

People with severe mental illness are 2.71 times more likely to report food insecurity than the general population (95% CI 1.72-3.25), with a prevalence of approximately 40%.[34] A systematic review and meta-analysis found food insecurity was the SDOH most consistently associated with lower medication adherence (aOR 0.56, 95% CI 0.42-0.70).[35] Food insecurity is associated with depression (OR 2.74) and anxiety (OR 2.41).[36] State SNAP eligibility expansion policies were associated with reduced rates of major depressive episodes and mental illness at the population level.[37]

Transportation Barriers

Twenty-eight percent of patients across three urban EDs delayed medical visits due to transportation issues, and transportation difficulties were associated with poor medication adherence.[38] Patients with schizophrenia spectrum disorders had 27.9% increased odds of treatment adherence when travel time to facilities was <=30 minutes.[2] Transportation barriers are cited as a major barrier to treatment engagement across racial/ethnic groups, with Black participants particularly noting inability to afford public transportation for appointments and medication pickup.[34]

Digital Access Barriers

Approximately 6 million children and adolescents in the US have inadequate in-person and digital availability of child psychiatric services, with 51% of children in rural counties lacking both forms of access.[39] In 2020, 596 US counties (19%) lacked both psychiatrists and broadband coverage, representing 10.5 million residents; these counties had significantly higher rates of drug overdose mortality (40.9 vs. 11.1 per 100,000) and completed suicide (88.1 vs. 11.3 per 100,000).[2] Despite the promise of telehealth, its expansion has not equally benefited all populations - nonmetro respondents were less likely to use virtual mental health care (AOR 0.74), and older adults, those living in poverty, and those without a high school diploma were significantly less likely to use teletherapy.[40][41]

Family Instability and Trauma Exposure

The 2025 JAMA Psychiatry umbrella review found childhood maltreatment, sexual assault, foster care experience, and exposure to others' suicide were among the SDOH most strongly associated with suicide-related outcomes.[9] Among hospitalized Veterans, food insecurity, legal problems, and neighborhood deprivation were the strongest social risk predictors of 30-day readmission.[15] Lack of family support was associated with antipsychotic nonadherence (aOR 2.01, 95% CI 1.33-3.04).[1]

---

4. ED Boarding: A Structural Crisis

Psychiatric boarding - holding patients in the ED after the decision to admit - represents a structural failure with profound consequences. Psychiatric patients remain in the ED 3.2 times longer than non-psychiatric patients, with average boarding times of 7-11 hours nationally and frequently exceeding 24 hours.[3] A Canadian study found mental health patients' median boarding time was 120% longer than non-mental health patients, and this gap widened over time.[2]

Harms are well-documented: patients boarded >14 hours more frequently required high-observation beds (14% vs. 3.5%), antipsychotics (44% vs. 14%), or sedation (55% vs. 33%).[42] Among older adults, functional decline occurred in 12.6% and restraint episodes in 8.1%, with both events occurring only among those boarding >=24 hours.[43] ED boarding duration is a direct risk factor for developing delirium or severe agitation during subsequent inpatient admission.[44]

Disparities are stark: Black patients boarded significantly longer than White patients for psychiatric admissions, and Medicaid patients were more than twice as likely to remain in the ED >=24 hours compared to privately insured patients.[45][46] Boarding >=24 hours was associated with a significant increase in perceived discrimination, particularly among patients from marginalized racial/ethnic groups.[47]

The following figure illustrates how statewide demand for inpatient psychiatric care correlates with individual boarding outcomes - as more youth board simultaneously, admission rates drop and boarding durations increase substantially:

The following figure displays reasons for patient dissatisfaction during ED boarding stratified by race/ethnicity, showing that non-Hispanic Black patients reported substantially higher rates of not being involved in treatment decisions:

---

5. Post-Discharge Suicide Risk and SDOH

The post-discharge period carries extremely elevated suicide risk - pooled estimates show suicide rates of ~2,950 per 100,000 person-years in the first week after psychiatric discharge.[48] SDOH are critical risk factors: the 2024 VA/DoD Clinical Practice Guideline explicitly includes housing instability, homelessness, exposure to abuse/violence, interpersonal conflict, and financial and legal problems in suicide risk assessment.[48]

The following figure from the Na et al. (2025) JAMA Psychiatry umbrella review summarizes effect sizes of SDOH on suicide mortality, with justice system involvement, exposure to suicide, firearm accessibility, and divorced status showing the strongest risk associations:

Outpatient follow-up within 7 days was associated with HR 0.82 for suicide in a Korean population-based study and aRR 0.44 for suicide over 180 days among Medicaid-insured youth.[48] Non-Hispanic Black youth and those with managed care insurance were less likely to receive timely follow-up.[48] SDOH barriers - transportation, insurance, housing - impede the very follow-up that is protective against post-discharge suicide.

---

6. Interventions That Improve Outcomes

Housing First

Housing First (HF) consistently improves housing stability (SMD 1.24; 95% CI 0.86-1.62) and reduces ED visits (IRR 0.63; 95% CI 0.48-0.82) and hospitalizations (IRR 0.76; 95% CI 0.70-0.83) in meta-analyses of RCTs.[49] Long-term 7-year follow-up of the At Home/Chez Soi trial showed HF with ACT reduced days in hospital (RRR 0.32) and ED visits (RRR 0.57) among high-need participants.[50] However, direct improvements in psychiatric symptom severity are not consistently demonstrated.[49]

Critical Time Intervention (CTI)

CTI is a 9-month, 3-stage intervention that develops individualized community linkages during transitions. The original RCT found significantly lower psychiatric rehospitalization at 18 months (OR 0.11).[51] Brief CTI reduced 30-day readmission from 47% to 28% (p < .001).[52] A 2025 meta-analysis confirmed CTI significantly improved quality of life (SMD 0.23), reduced homelessness (SMD -0.20), and improved psychiatric symptoms (SMD -0.16).[53]

Collaborative Care Model (CoCM)

CoCM has the strongest evidence base among SDOH-responsive interventions, supported by over 90 RCTs.[53] The landmark IMPACT trial (n=1,801) found 45% of intervention patients achieved >=50% reduction in depressive symptoms at 12 months vs. 19% of usual care (OR 3.45; 95% CI 2.71-4.38).[53] The SPIRIT trial - the largest mental health trial in rural primary care - demonstrated large, clinically meaningful improvements (Cohen d = 0.79-0.87) using telepsychiatry collaborative care in FQHCs without on-site psychiatrists.[53]

Assertive Community Treatment (ACT)

ACT reduces hospitalization, particularly among high utilizers. A systematic review with meta-regression (29 trials, 5,961 participants) found ACT works best when baseline hospital use is high.[54] The ACCESS-II study showed sustained 4-year improvements: hospitalization rates of 9-13%, involuntary admissions dropping from 35% to 8%, and significant improvements in psychopathology (d = 0.79).[55]

Peer Support

A 2023 meta-analysis of 28 RCTs found peer support had small but significant effects on clinical recovery (g = 0.19; 95% CI 0.11-0.27) and personal recovery (g = 0.15; 95% CI 0.04-0.27).[56] The Cochrane review found no clear effect on hospital admissions, though one RCT of peer mentors for recurrently hospitalized individuals found participants remained out of hospital significantly longer.[57][58]

SDOH Screening and Referral

The CMS Accountable Health Communities Model screened 482,967 participants and found statistically significant reductions in ED visits.[59] However, navigation services did not significantly increase community service connections or needs resolution compared to referral alone - referrals without ensuring receipt of services may be insufficient.[60]

Jail Diversion and Reentry

Mental health courts show a small effect on recidivism (d = -0.20) in meta-analysis, with MHC completion associated with greater reductions in jail days.[61] Mental health services access after release was associated with significant reduction in reincarceration risk, with each additional month between release and services access increasing reincarceration risk by 4%.[62] The Sequential Intercept Model provides the dominant conceptual framework for addressing the criminalization of mental illness across five interception points.[63]

Telepsychiatry

Multiple meta-analyses demonstrate telepsychiatry achieves clinical outcomes comparable to in-person care, with a 2023 meta-analysis of 32 RCTs finding no significant difference overall (p = 0.248) and superiority for depressive disorders (SMD -0.325).[64] However, telemental health may largely substitute for rather than supplement in-person care, resulting in only modest net increases in total specialty mental health contacts in rural areas.[65]

---

7. Staff Training and Structural Competency Education

Evidence on Training

A scoping review identified only 11 articles meeting inclusion criteria for structural competency training interventions, with most using active learning strategies and researcher-developed evaluation instruments.[65] A qualitative evaluation of structural competency training in a family medicine residency found residents reported positive impact on clinical practice but also feeling overwhelmed by increased recognition of structural influences on patient health.[65] At Vanderbilt, MHS majors who received structural competency education identified and analyzed structural factors at higher rates and in deeper ways than comparison groups.[66]

Teaching Frameworks

Castillo, Isom, DeBonis et al. (2020) proposed replacing or augmenting the ACGME's "systems-based practice" competency with a new core competency centered on health equity, social responsibility, and structural competency.[67] Hassan and Bui (2022) developed a structural analysis framework for incorporating structural competency into everyday clinical reasoning: (1) develop a prioritized clinical problem list, (2) identify social and structural root causes, (3) construct a prioritized structural problem list, and (4) brainstorm solutions to address structural barriers.[68] Weill Cornell developed the first OSCE designed to assess structural competency, focused on premature discharge scenarios.[69] As of academic year 2023-2024, the LCME requires medical schools to include content on basic principles of structurally competent health care.[69]

9. Resident Teaching Framework

The "STRUCTURE" Curriculum Model

A comprehensive resident teaching framework for SDOH in inpatient psychiatry, integrating the evidence reviewed above:

S - Screen systematically. Use validated SDOH screening tools (see checklist below) on every admission. Normalize screening as standard clinical practice, not an add-on.

T - Think structurally. Apply the Hassan & Bui structural analysis framework: for every clinical problem, identify the social and structural root causes alongside the biomedical ones.[68] When a patient is "non-adherent," ask what structural barriers prevented adherence before attributing it to the patient.

R - Recognize racism. Understand that racial disparities in diagnosis (schizophrenia overdiagnosis in Black patients, OR 2.07), involuntary commitment (aOR 1.57 for Black patients), restraint use (aOR 1.85 for Black patients), and treatment quality are well-documented and persistent.[18][1][17] Use structured diagnostic instruments. Question diagnostic assumptions.

U - Understand cumulative risk. Teach the dose-response relationship between social needs and outcomes (aOR 12.55 for 5 HRSN domains).[14] A patient with housing insecurity, food insecurity, and transportation barriers faces compounding - not merely additive - risk.

C - Connect to resources. Know the local resource landscape: housing programs, food banks, transportation assistance, legal aid, benefits enrollment. Referral alone is insufficient - ensure receipt of services.[60]

T - Transition with intention. Begin discharge planning on day one. Schedule outpatient follow-up before discharge. Use Critical Time Intervention principles. Ensure 7-day follow-up, which is associated with reduced suicide risk (HR 0.82) and readmission.[48]

U - Use team-based approaches. Integrate social workers, peer specialists, community health workers, and case managers into the treatment team. Structural problems require structural solutions - they cannot be solved by the physician alone.

R - Reflect on power. Practice structural humility.[1] Recognize how institutional power dynamics (involuntary commitment, restraint, discharge decisions) disproportionately affect marginalized patients. Discuss countertransference and implicit bias in team formulation.

E - Engage in advocacy. Move beyond individual patient care to systems-level change. Identify one structural barrier encountered during each rotation and propose a policy or institutional intervention.[67]

Suggested Curriculum Activities

10. SDOH Assessment Checklist for Inpatient Psychiatry

The following checklist integrates domains from the AHC HRSN Screening Tool, PRAPARE, and the structural vulnerability assessment tool, adapted for inpatient psychiatric settings:[3][70][71]

Admission SDOH Screen

Housing

- [ ] Current living situation (own/rent/shelter/street/doubled up/institutional)

- [ ] Housing stability in past 12 months (any moves, evictions, episodes of homelessness)

- [ ] Concerns about losing housing in next 2 months

- [ ] Safety of current housing (violence, structural hazards, environmental exposures)

Food Security

- [ ] "In the past 12 months, did you worry that food would run out before you had money to buy more?" (USDA 2-item screen)

- [ ] "In the past 12 months, did the food you bought not last and you didn't have money to get more?"

- [ ] Access to cooking facilities and food storage

Transportation

- [ ] Reliable transportation to medical appointments

- [ ] Transportation barriers to pharmacy access

- [ ] Distance to nearest outpatient mental health provider

Financial Security

- [ ] Employment status and stability

- [ ] Difficulty paying for basic needs (utilities, phone, medications)

- [ ] Current or recent loss of income

- [ ] Debt or legal financial obligations

Insurance and Healthcare Access

- [ ] Current insurance status and type

- [ ] Gaps in coverage in past 12 months

- [ ] Established outpatient mental health provider (name, contact)

- [ ] Established primary care provider

- [ ] Barriers to accessing outpatient care (cost, wait times, availability)

Legal/Criminal Justice

- [ ] Current or pending legal issues

- [ ] History of incarceration

- [ ] Current probation/parole status and officer contact

- [ ] Outstanding warrants or court dates

- [ ] Immigration status concerns affecting care-seeking

Safety and Violence

- [ ] Current or recent intimate partner violence

- [ ] Community violence exposure

- [ ] History of childhood maltreatment

- [ ] Firearm access in the home (lethal means counseling)

Social Support

- [ ] Emergency contact and relationship quality

- [ ] Family/friend support available after discharge

- [ ] Social isolation (lives alone, limited contacts)

- [ ] Caregiver burden on family members

Digital Access

- [ ] Access to smartphone or computer

- [ ] Reliable internet access at home

- [ ] Comfort with telehealth technology

- [ ] Phone number likely to remain active after discharge

Education and Literacy

- [ ] Highest education level

- [ ] Health literacy concerns (difficulty understanding medication instructions)

- [ ] Primary language and interpreter needs

Discrimination and Structural Vulnerability

- [ ] Experiences of discrimination in healthcare settings

- [ ] Immigration-related fears affecting care-seeking

- [ ] LGBTQ+ identity and related safety concerns

- [ ] Disability status and accommodation needs

Substance Use Context

- [ ] Substance use patterns and relationship to housing/social stability

- [ ] Access to harm reduction services

- [ ] History of overdose and naloxone access
